en: Preface to the *Xifang huizheng* (Compendium of the Western Vessel):

Now, Dharmakara first opened up the four pure lands, mooring his vessel of vows at the harbor of bliss; Śākyamuni vowed to gather in those of the five turbidities, launching his ship of compassion upon the sea of suffering.
Whether uplifting the high or grasping the low, their sole purpose was to extensively save all living beings; whether praising the superior or refuting the inferior, their intent was...
He vowed to skillfully guide all realms of existence. Alas! When the Buddha, the King of Awakening, appeared in the world, was it not solely for this great cause and condition?

How could he have spared his heart’s blood to preach what is so difficult to believe, and to personally practice what is so difficult to perform? For kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he has never known weariness or fatigue.
Yet, I have heard it said that those who are born through transformation upon lotus flowers in the jeweled ponds of pure lands possess golden bodies and fragrant...
Pure. Her countenance was upright and beautiful; both her merit and wisdom flourished. It is said she dwelt in joy and sovereignty.
Generally speaking, when one experiences results according to their causes, then as the mind becomes pure, the Buddha-land naturally becomes pure.

Those who practice pure deeds must cultivate the mind so that it is as bright and flawless as a lotus, as its fragrant scent reaches far and wide like a lotus, and remains ever pure amidst defilement like a lotus.
Just as a lotus enters the water without being soiled, it subsequently takes root within the womb of a lotus.

At the very moment of first generating the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), there is already a single lotus flower that sprouts its bud within the waters of virtue; whether the flower flourishes or withers depends upon the diligence or indolence of the person.

This principle is self-evident—what further cause for doubt could there be? Moreover, to arise without depending on a sage is itself the mark of the superior class; seeing the worthy, one contemplates them...

Rectification is precisely the urgent task for us today. Therefore, I have compiled the miraculous accounts of the spiritual transformations of various virtuous practitioners from antiquity and hastened to have them carved into woodblocks, desiring that my fellow practitioners of the Lotus Society may together behold these models of the ancients.
I have merely composed these regulations for our journey to the West. In the past, Daozhen’s records were incomplete, so they could not be included in the returning sails;
Tongzhi changed his attire and was only able to follow after the departing ship. As the ancient masters said:

"In the frantic bustle of birth and death at the ancient ferryhead, Amitābha moves the boat that ferries people across. At all times, one should cultivate the thought of this rare encounter, and with joy, board together.

This is the Ship of Liberation. Knowing that the river of craving is vast and surging with the waves of desire, one must employ a boat and oars to cross the treacherous currents and reach the ocean of one’s vows, thereby ascending to the other shore.
For this reason, this work is titled *The Collection for Crossing to the West*. Thus it is said.
On the day of the winter solstice in the year Zhuli Duan’an, recorded by Shi Ruizhang as the preface to the first volume of the *Xifang Huizheng Mulü*.

Commentary compiled by Qiubotang Ruizhang. The Venerable Master Ruihua’s name was Huiyuan;
his secular surname was Jia. He was a native of Loufan in Yanmen. From childhood he was fond of learning; at the age of thirteen—
He followed his maternal uncle, the Liang family, to study in the regions of Xu and Luo. He extensively mastered the Six Classics and was particularly adept at the *Zhuangzi* and *Laozi*.
At the age of twenty-one, he wished to cross the Yangtze River to study under Fan Ning; however, the southern road happened to be blocked.

At that time, the monk Dao’an had established a monastery on Mount Taihang and Mount Changshan. Upon meeting him, [Huiyuan] paid him full respect, regarding him as his true teacher. Initially, he heard that Dao’an frequently lectured on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Upon reading the sutra, he attained sudden and profound enlightenment. He sighed and said, "The divergent doctrines of the nine schools are all mere chaff.

Thereupon, together with his younger brother Huichi, he cast aside his hairpin and received the precepts. He applied himself to contemplation and recitation with such intensity that night followed day. His spiritual insight was brilliant and transcendent, and his will merged with the ultimate principle.
Master Dao’an, presiding over the assembly, often sighed and said, "He who shall cause the Way to flow to the eastern lands must be Huiyuan. Great...

In the sixth year of the Yuan era, he arrived at Xunyang and saw that the space between the peaks of Mount Lu was vast and open, a place where one could set the mind at rest. He therefore established a vihāra there.
Because it was still some distance from water, he struck the ground with his staff and said, "If this place is fit for habitation, may the earth yield a spring.

As soon as he finished speaking, a clear stream gushed forth. During a severe drought in Xunyang, the Master went to the side of the pool and recited the Sūtra of the Sea Dragon King; suddenly, [a cloud appeared...]

A divine serpent emerged from the pond, and immediately thereafter it rained heavily; at the end of the year, there was a bountiful autumn harvest. Consequently, it was named Longquan Jingśe (Dragon Spring Monastery).

Master Huiyong had previously resided at Xilin on Mount Lu and wished to invite [Huiyuan] to live together there, but as the master’s disciples were already numerous, Huiyong said to the Regional Inspector, Huan Yi:
"Master Yuan is just now about to propagate the Way, yet the dwelling where I reside is too cramped."
At that time, the Master dreamed that a mountain deity told him, "This mountain is sufficient for you to dwell; I pray you do not go elsewhere.

That evening there was heavy rain and a peal of thunder. At dawn, the foot of the forest had been widely cleared, with white sand spread across the ground and *pien*, *nan*, and *wenzi* timber strewn everywhere, appearing as if they had arrived from nowhere.
Deeply moved by this, he established a monastery there and named its main hall "The Divine" (Shen).
Because it was located to the east of Master Yong’s residence, it was called Donglin (East Forest).
He once remarked that while the names of samādhis in the various teachings are very numerous, for those seeking high merit with ease of progress, mindfulness of the Buddha (*nienfo*) is foremost.

Subsequently, practitioners who strictly observed the precepts and stilled their minds, as well as guests of pure faith who had severed ties with the mundane world, arrived there without prior appointment: Huìyǒng (who, like Master Ān, previously resided at Xīlín), Huìchí (the younger brother of Master Yuǎn born of the same mother), and Dào...
Tánshùn (both disciples of Kumārajīva), Sēngyuè, Tánhéng, Dàobǐng, Tánshēn, and Dàojìng (all disciples of Master Huiyuan), Buddhayaśas (translated as Juémíng;

a native of Jibin), Buddhabhadra (translated as Juéxián; a native of Kapilavastu), and the eminent scholars Liú Chéngzhī (styled Yímín), Zhāng Yě, Zhōu Xùzhī, Zhāng Quán, Zōng Bǐng, Lèi Cìzōng, and others, formed a society to practice mindfulness.
The Buddha was popularly known as one of the Eighteen Worthies. He further led a group of one hundred and twenty-three people to collectively cultivate the practice for the Pure Land.
They fashioned images of the Three Sages of the Western Paradise, established a vegetarian feast, and made a vow, commissioning Liu Yimin to compose a "Text of Vows.
Wang Qiao and others likewise composed poems on the *Nianfo Sanmei* (Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha) to manifest their resolve. Upon hearing that Kumārajīva had entered [China]...
Guan sent a letter to establish friendly relations. Kumārajīva replied in his letter, saying: "I have received the gift you have transmitted; I have heard something of your reputation and virtue.
The Sūtra says that in the final age, in the East, there will be a Bodhisattva who protects the Dharma. How admirable, O Benevolent One, that you so skillfully propagate its Way!
Śramaṇa Huiyao, finding no water clock in the mountains, erected a twelve-petaled lotus upon the water, which rotated according to the waves to divide the time."

He fixed the lengths of day and night to establish the rhythm for his practice of the Way, which he called the "Lotus Water-Clock. The Master resided in the mountains for thirty years, his traces never entering the secular world;
he devoted himself solely to the diligent recollection of the Pure Land. For the first eleven years, he concentrated his mind and focused his thoughts upon it.
Third, he beheld the marks of a sage; he remained solemn and silent, saying nothing.

Nineteen years later, on the evening of the final day of the seventh month, while rising from meditative absorption in the eastern niche of the Prajñā Terrace, he saw Amitābha Buddha, his body filling the void, within whose halo—
There were various transformation buddhas, with Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta standing in attendance to their left and right.

Furthermore, he saw the light of flowing water divided into fourteen streams, cascading up and down, proclaiming the sounds of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self. The Buddha said to him:
"By the power of my original vow, I have come to comfort you. Seven days from now, you shall be born in my land.

Furthermore, he saw Buddhabhadra, Huichi (who passed away in the eighth year of Yixi), Huiyong (who passed away in the tenth year of Yixi), and Liu Yimin (who passed away in the sixth year of Yixi) standing by the Buddha's side.
They bowed before the Master and said, "Your resolve was made long ago; why have you arrived so late? The Master spoke to Fajing:
Huibao said, "Since I first resided here, I have seen the marks of a Buddha three times during these eleven years; now I see them once more. It is certain that I shall be reborn in the Pure Land.
He further remarked, "The seven-day deadline was merely a gradual one. Thereupon he lay ill and composed his final testament, saying:
"In the past, at an age when I understood the nature of destiny, I entrusted my vocation to this mountain. I have long examined for myself that there is a fixed time for my life’s end."
I then intended to sever all external ties in order to pursue my aspirations; however, because my nature was weak in resolve, I allowed those of similar inclination to draw me along.
My worthy contemporaries and kinsmen moved me through their shared affinity, and before I realized it, my physical form and its momentum had declined. This year I am already eighty-three.
Looking back, I lament the parting instructions [of my teacher], and looking down, I grieve over my own sense of failure. I have merely caused this life to pass in vain.

I decline. Because my grief for the departed is so profound, at the time of the funeral, I shall expose my remains beneath the pine forest and make a mound upon the ridge that is no different from earth and wood;
this is the rite of the ancients, and you must not contravene it. If the spiritual principle is not obscure, I hope my sincerity may reach him.
The World-Honored One of Great Compassion will surely assist me with his Way. As for the disciples, their wailing and lamentation—just as...
Upon the death of his parents, the Master, considering the difficulty of severing worldly ties, established a seven-day period for the expression of grief;
it was only upon reaching that time that he entered final nirvana, specifically on the sixth day of the eighth month in the twelfth year of the Yixi era.

His disciples, unable to bear the exposure of the remains, together with Ruan Kan, the Governor of Xunyang, escorted his entire body to the Western Ridge for burial. They piled stones to form a stupa. As for the sutras and treatises he authored:
The various prefaces, inscriptions, encomia, poems, and records comprise ten fascicles, titled the *Lushan ji* (Collection from Mount Lu).

Examining the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land, although it was transmitted during the Zhen dynasty, it became prominent with Fotudeng. From Fotudeng, one reached Dao’an; among Dao’an’s disciples was Master Huiyuan.
He bore the ultimate teachings and expanded the Great Way; his fame was esteemed by emperors and kings, and the flow of the Dharma spread throughout the world for a hundred generations.
...below [this]. He posthumously promoted the Master as the progenitor of the Pure Land school.
Huiyong was surnamed Pan of Henei; he entered the monastic order at the age of twelve and served the śramaṇa Zhu Tanxian.
Initially, he practiced dhyāna on Mount Heng and, together with Master Yuan, relied upon Dharma Master Daoan. They planned to build a monastery on Mount Luofu, but when Master Yuan...
The Master intended to cross the Five Ridges first, leaving what Master An had left behind. At the beginning of the Taiyuan era, he arrived at Xunyang.
The Regional Inspector, Tao Fan, who had long admired his Daoist character, invited him to stay and rest at Mount Lu, donating his residence to be converted into Xilin Monastery for his service.

The Master wore simple robes and ate vegetarian food, cultivating his mind with self-discipline; his countenance was always smiling, and his speech never harmed others. He established a separate thatched hut on the mountain peak.
At that time, he went there to practice meditation. Those who entered his chamber would constantly smell a wondrous fragrance, and for this reason it was called "Fragrant Valley" (Xianggu).

A tiger lived there with him; whenever people arrived, the tiger would immediately drive them away, but when Master Yuan came, it did not. Later, Huan Yi of Longquan established Donglin Temple for him. For thirty years, his shadow never left the mountain.
The Master resided at Xilin Temple and conducted himself in the same manner. Once, having gone to a nearby town on account of a Dharma service, he returned to the mountain.

At dusk, the commander of the Wujiao garrison was riding his horse along the road under the influence of alcohol. He blocked the Master’s path and would not let him pass. The Master pointed his staff at the horse;

the horse bolted in alarm, causing the commander to fall to the ground. The Master took him up and comforted him, whereupon they returned together. The commander fell ill and went to the temple to repent for his transgression.
The Master said, "This was not my intention; I shall pray for you. He recovered shortly thereafter. Meanwhile, He Wuji, General of the South, was stationed there.

In Xunyang, he reached Huxi. He invited Master Huiyuan and [Hui]si. Master Huiyuan possessed great renown; he was followed by more than a hundred disciples, and his lofty speech and elegant discourse were such that his every movement was worthy of admiration.
Master [Hui]si, however, wore a patched robe that barely covered his shins and carried his staff and bowl as he arrived with a carefree air beneath the pines.
Huikai said to the assembly, "Master Yong’s style of pure detachment actually surpasses that of Master Huiyuan. Master [Hui]si...

He manifested his sincerity and cultivated his vows, always directing his thoughts toward the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang). In the tenth year of the Yixi era, while he was ill, he suddenly adjusted his robes, sought his sandals, and attempted to rise.
His disciples asked him in alarm, "The Buddha has come! As soon as he finished speaking, he passed away. A wondrous fragrance lingered for seven days before it finally dissipated.
He was buried to the southwest of the monastery; he was eighty-three years of age.

Huizhi was the half-brother of Master Huiyuan, born of the same mother. From childhood he devoted himself to reading; what he memorized in a single day would normally take ten days for others to master.
At the age of eighteen, he entered the service of Master Dao’an alongside his elder brother, where he studied the various sutras extensively and attained mastery over the Tripitaka.
When Master Dao’an was in Xiangyang, he dispatched Master Huiyuan and Huizhi to travel eastward, where they eventually settled at Mount Lu. The Master stood eight feet tall and wore a patched robe.

His robes reached down to his knees. He had three hundred disciples, of whom the Master was the leader. Fan Ning, the Governor of Yuzhang, invited the Master to lecture on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Abhidharma-śāstra*.
Disciples gathered from all directions like clouds. Wang Xun of Langya wrote a letter to Fan Ning asking which of the two masters, Huiyuan or Daoheng, was superior.
Fan Ning replied, "I truly consider them both worthy brothers. Wang Xun wrote back again, saying, "As long as it is so..."

"Your younger brother has certainly never possessed such qualities; how much less so one as virtuous as you? When Kumārajīva was in Guanzhong, he held you in profound admiration from afar and frequently sent letters to maintain friendly relations with you.
In the third year of the Long’an era, you took leave of your elder brother to enter Shu. Master Huiyuan detained you, saying: 'In human life, people cherish gathering together.'"
"You alone delight in solitude. The Master said, "Those whose sentiments are stalled in attachment to gathering are fundamentally unfit for the homeless life.

Now that you have severed desire to seek the Way, you shall take the Western Regions as your destination. He then departed with a sense of regret. Arriving at Bei County in Chengdu, he resided at Longyuan Temple and extensively propagated the Buddha-Dharma.
Those who ascended his hall were called "those who have climbed the Dragon Gate. In the eighth year of the Shunxi era...

Sengji died at the age of seventy-six. In his final testament, he charged that the monastic discipline (*vinaya*) be strictly observed and the pure practices (*śukla-karman*) be pursued with single-minded devotion.
He entrusted the scriptures in the eastern chamber to Daohong and the Vinaya texts in the western chamber to Tanyuan.
Because Hong’s conduct was pure and diligent, and Yuan possessed divine intuition and transcendent insight, both were able to carry on the Master’s legacy.

Daosheng was born into the Wei clan and was a native of Julu. In his youth, he followed Zhu Fatai to leave the household life. Upon encountering the scriptures and edicts, he could recite them from memory after a single reading.

While still at the age of *zhixue* (the age of formal study), he ascended the lecture seat; his eloquence and clear discernment were such that even those of long-standing reputation dared not challenge him.

He initially relied upon Mount Lu, where he constantly maintained that the essential way to enter the Path is to take wisdom and understanding as its foundation. Thereupon, together with Sengrui and Hui... [text continues]
Yan Hui, Guan, and others traveled to Chang’an to study under Kumārajīva. The monastic community of Guanzhong all looked up to their divine realization. They once sighed in lamentation, saying:
"Since the scriptures flowed eastward, translators have repeatedly obstructed the transmission; consequently, many texts remain stuck in provisional phrasing, while few penetrate the perfect meaning.
Only when one has discarded the trap to catch the fish can one truly be said to speak the Way. Thereupon, they collated and verified the truths of the conventional and the ultimate.

He refined his understanding of emptiness and existence and investigated the principles of cause and effect, thereby establishing the doctrines that "wholesome deeds do not entail retribution" and that "one attains Buddhahood through sudden enlightenment.

He further composed the *Treatise on the Two Truths*, the *Treatise on the Constant Existence of Buddha-nature*, the *Treatise on the Buddha Having No Pure Land*, and the *Treatise on the Necessity of Conditions*.

These works encompassed previous teachings with profound and subtle insights. Those who clung to the literal letter of the scriptures were filled with resentment and jealousy. The Master, moreover, by means of the Dharma...
It was revealed that the version of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* translated by the Tripiṭaka Master had arrived first, consisting of six fascicles.

The sūtra states: "With the exception of icchantikas, all possess the Buddha-nature. The Master said: "All who receive their physical form from the two polarities (Heaven and Earth) possess the primary cause for nirvāṇa.

How could sentient beings of the icchantika class alone be devoid of Buddha-nature? It is simply because this sūtra has not yet reached its completion. Thereupon, he proclaimed [the existence of the icchantikas].
He declared, "All people of this world shall attain Buddhahood. At that time, the *Daban niepan jing* (Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra) had not yet been transmitted. Guiming was the first to proclaim it.

The established school of monks considered this a betrayal of the scriptures and consequently exposed him before the great assembly, banishing and expelling him. The Master assumed a solemn countenance and vowed, saying:
"If what I have spoken betrays the scriptures, may my body be afflicted with leprosy; if it does not betray the True Reality (*tathatā*), I pray that on the day of my death, I shall sit..."
Śīlādharabhadra (Shizi) then shook out his robes and departed. Later, when the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* reached the "Chapter on Holy Conduct" (*Āryacaryā-parivarta*), it stated:

"Even though an icchantika has severed all roots of goodness, they still possess Buddha-nature. At this, all the masters were filled with shame and submission. Śīlādharabhadra was banished to the south;
he returned to Mount Huqiu, where he gathered stones as his disciples and lectured on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*. When he reached the section concerning the icchantikas, he then preached...

"There is Buddha-nature. He then asked, "Does what I have spoken accord with the Buddha’s mind? Whereupon all the rocks nodded their heads. Within ten days, the assembly of students gathered like clouds.
Suddenly, thunder shook the Qingyuan Garden, and a dragon ascended to heaven from the Buddha Hall; consequently, the temple was renamed Longguang (Dragon Light).
The Master invited a Vinaya master from Kaśmīra to the temple to translate the Mahīśāsaka-vinaya, which was transmitted to the world. Subsequently...
He took his leave of the assembly and returned to Mount Lu, where he joined the Lotus Society. After a long time, he returned to the capital and resided at Qingxia Temple.
Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty convened a great assembly of śramaṇas and personally presided over the feast. When the food had been served for some time, the crowd suspected it was past noon.

The Emperor said, "It is only now reaching midday. Daosheng then remarked, "The bright sun adorns the heavens; since the Emperor says it is just midday, how can it not be midday? Thereupon, he lifted his chopsticks.
He ate accordingly, and the entire assembly followed his example; there was no one who did not marvel at his quick-witted eloquence.
At that time, King Wang Hong, Fan Tai, and Yan Yanzhi all held him in profound respect for his character and conduct, following him to inquire about the Way.

On the *gengzi* day of the eleventh month in the eleventh year of the Yuanjia era, while he was ascending the seat to preach the Dharma at Mount Lu, as he was about to conclude, the assembly saw his fly-whisk fall to the ground in a flurry. He then leaned back against his armrest and passed away.
He appeared as if he had entered meditative concentration. When the various masters heard this, they further believed that his former vow had been verified.

Tanshun was a native of Huanglong; having left home at a young age, he received instruction [in the Dharma]. When Kumārajīva lectured on and interpreted the various sutras, he exhaustively elucidated the profound principles of form and emptiness and non-attachment.
Kumārajīva sighed in admiration, saying, "This youth is a vessel of extraordinary talent. Later, he practiced the Pure Land path together with [Hui]ning at Mount Lu.
The蛮 (Mán) Commandant Liu Zūnxiào established a monastery in Jiangling and invited the Master to initiate its construction. There, he extensively propagated the Way of the Nianfo Samādhi.
In the second year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, he passed away while seated in meditation amidst his assembly; a wondrous fragrance filled the room. He was seventy-nine years of age.
Sengrui was a native of Jizhou. He traveled to various regions to study. Once, while passing through the western borders of Shu, he was plundered by bandits and forced to herd sheep.

A traveling merchant found him extraordinary and suspected he was a śramaṇa; upon questioning him, the merchant discovered that there was no point of Buddhist doctrine with which he was not thoroughly proficient.
He immediately provided gold to redeem him. Later, he traveled through various kingdoms of India and returned to Guanzhong, where he consulted with Kumārajīva regarding the meaning of the sūtras.
When Kumārajīva was translating the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he cited the version by Dharmarakṣa which read: "The heavens see men, and men see the heavens.
Sengrui remarked, "This wording is overly literal. Kumārajīva said, "Is it not rather that humans and devas meet, so that both are able to see one another?"
Kumārajīva was delighted and subsequently adopted his writings. After some time, he entered Mount Lu to rely on Master Huiyuan to cultivate the practice of purity (*śubha-karman*).
Thereafter, he traveled to the capital and resided at Wuyi Temple, where he lectured on various sutras; those who listened were moved to profound admiration and submission.

Liu Yikang, the Prince of Pengcheng under the Song dynasty, invited him to his residence to receive the precepts. The Master said, "According to the rites, one comes to study. The Prince then entered the temple to reverently receive the dharma of the precepts.
The King offered him a sable fur robe to use as a seat-cloth. The King secretly ordered thirty thousand coins to be used to purchase it.

The Master said, "Although this is not something suitable for me to wear, it is a gift from the King and cannot be discarded. Upon hearing this, the King’s respect increased all the more. Xie Lingyun was deeply devoted to Buddhist principles;
he was widely proficient in understanding the dialects and local sounds of various regions. Once, regarding a passage in the sutras...

Regarding the phonetics of characters, he sought verification from his teacher and consequently composed the *Xishiyin Xun* (Explanations of the Fourteen Vowels), in which the Sanskrit and Chinese correspond clearly.
In the sixteenth year of the Yuanjia era, he announced to the assembly without illness, "I am about to depart. He then passed away while facing west with palms joined.
The assembly saw a golden lotus flower within his chamber suddenly vanish. He was eighty-five years of age.

Tandeng was a native of the region east of the Yellow River. Having joined the monastic order under Master Huiyuan while still a youth, he was already able to lecture on the scriptures at the mere age of thirteen.

He was thoroughly versed in both Buddhist and secular classics, and his virtuous conduct was so pure and solitary that all people held him in high esteem and submission. It was common for herds of deer to frequent his dwelling.
He paced reverently around the corner of his seat. After entering Mount Lu, he devoted himself single-mindedly to the practice of pure karma.
In the fourteenth year of the Yixi era, he sat upright with palms joined, reciting the Buddha’s name with a resolute voice, and passed away. He was seventy-two years of age.
Daobing was a native of Yingchuan and belonged to the Chen clan. He left home to become a monk in his youth and became a disciple of Master Huiyuan.

He was thoroughly versed in the sutras and the Vinaya, while also having a profound understanding of the *Zhuangzi* and the *Laozi*. His character and integrity were solitary and lofty; his words and deeds were in perfect accord. He devoted himself to the *nienfo samādhi*, investigating the mind without interruption.

In the fourteenth year of the Yixi era, Wang Qian, the Governor of Yuzhang, entered the mountains to pay his respects and requested that Daobing serve as the head of the monastery. Thus he was appointed.
He succeeded to the seat of Master Shaoyuan; the assembly, recognizing him as a dharma heir of Daoyuan, all looked up to him with reverence.
In the twelfth year of the Yuanjia era, he gathered the assembly for the practice of Buddha-recollection (*nianfo*), and while seated, he passed away at the age of seventy-one.
Tanshen was a native of Guangling. In his youth, he left the household life under Master Huiyuan. He diligently cultivated the practice of purity and was also skilled in lecturing.

He annotated the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*, which circulated throughout the world. He frequently composed the *Qiongtong lun* (Treatise on Adversity and Success) to clarify the results of past cultivation, and wrote the *Lianshe lu* (Record of the Lotus Society) to document those reborn there.

Furthermore, he could distinguish the nature of birds and beasts—whether their coats were fine or coarse, and whether they were sharp-witted or dull—and he possessed profound insight into the branches and growth of plants.
He experienced the flavors of both bitterness and sweetness, and his mastery of their principles was exquisite. It is said that people knew he had attained secret verification [of the Dharma].

In the seventeenth year of the Yuanjia era, he assembled the community and said, "Since the founding of this temple until now, fifty years have passed; my journey to the West shall be the very last of these.
He then sat cross-legged, recited the Buddha’s name one hundred times, and by closing his breath, he passed away at the age of eighty.
Daojing was a member of the Wang clan of Langya. His grandfather, Wang Ningzhi, served as the Prefect of Jiangzhou, and Daojing subsequently followed Master Huiyuan to enter the monastic order.

At the age of seventeen, he had extensively mastered the sutras and treatises, memorizing ten thousand words a day. He often lamented that it is difficult to maintain the precepts perfectly throughout one’s entire life;

thus, he wished to purify the six sense faculties by observing only a single precept, considering this to be the essential means for attaining liberation. Master Huiyuan, recognizing his steadfastness and integrity, granted him permission. He remained devoted to this practice.
He resolved to practice the mindfulness of the Buddha, never flagging day or night. After Master Huiyuan had passed into *nirvāṇa*, he entered Mount Ruoye.

In the first year of the Yongchu era of the Song dynasty, he said to the assembly, "The former master has summoned me; it is time for me to depart. He then sat upright, chanted the name of the Buddha, and passed away.
The assembly saw a brilliant light fill the room, which did not vanish until some time later. He was fifty-two years of age.

Buddhayaśas (translated in the Jin language as "Awakened Clarity") was of Brahmin descent from the kingdom of Kaśmīra. A śramaṇa came to his house to beg for food; his father, who had originally been a non-Buddhist, became enraged and drove him away.
Consequently, [Yaśas] suffered from convulsions in his hands and feet and became paralyzed. A sorcerer said to him, "This is because you have offended a worthy sage.
He immediately invited this śramaṇa to repent for his transgression for ten days, whereupon he recovered. Because of this, Yaśas was led to leave the household life at that age.
13. Following his teacher through a wilderness, he encountered a tiger. Xie She said, "The tiger has already eaten its fill; it will surely not harm us.
As they proceeded along the way, they indeed found the remains of other [victims]. By the age of fifteen, he could recite ten thousand words of scripture each day.

Worried that his practice was being neglected due to his rounds for alms (the Sanskrit term *piṇḍapāta* means "begging for food" in the Jin language), an Arhat came to take his place in begging for food. At nineteen, he could recite [scripture].
He composed several million words. By nature, he was simple and haughty, and thus was not highly esteemed by others; even at the age of thirty, he remained a śrāmaṇera.

He subsequently followed his maternal uncle to study the treatises on the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) and worldly arts and techniques. Upon reaching the kingdom of Śākala, he was treated with great honor.
Later, when Kumārajīva arrived, he studied the *Abhidharma* treatises and the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* under him. Kumārajīva later returned south with his mother.
In Kucha, the Master remained to propagate the Dharma. When Fu Jian dispatched Lü Guang to invade Kucha and capture Kumārajīva, the Master heard of this and sighed, saying:
"I have brought Kumārajīva forth, yet we have not yet fully expressed our mutual intentions. Now he has suddenly been taken captive; when shall we meet again?
Ten years later, the Master traveled east to Kucha and extensively propagated the teachings of the Dharma. While Kumārajīva was in Guzang, he sent a messenger to invite him.
Fearing that the people of the country would stop his journey, the Master took clear water and cast medicine into it, reciting several dozen words of incantation.
He then had his disciple wash his feet; that very night they set out. By morning they had traveled several hundred li, and those who pursued them could not catch up.
The Master asked the disciple, "What did you perceive? He replied, "I heard only the sound of a swift wind rushing by, and there were tears in both my eyes. The Master again incanted over water.

He washed his feet and then ceased. Upon arriving at Guzang, Kumārajīva had already entered Chang’an. Hearing that the Lord Yao had taken him as a concubine, he sighed and said, "Kumārajīva is like fine cotton wool;
how can one allow him to enter a thorny forest? Kumārajīva then urged the Lord Yao to dispatch an envoy to welcome the Master.
Once he arrived, a separate monastery was established within the Xiaoyao Garden, where he was provided with the four requisites of monastic life, yet remained entirely detached from worldly things.
When the time arrived for almsround, he would take but a single meal. At that time, Kumārajīva was translating the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*;

the Master [Saṃghadeva] further cross-examined and resolved its meanings, so that the phrasing and principles were finally established. The Master’s beard was red, and he was skilled at explaining the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*; thus, people of the time called him "The Red-Bearded Śāstrin.
During the Hongshi era of the Qin dynasty, he translated the forty-four fascicles of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and two fascicles of the *Dīrgha-āgama*.
In twelve fascicles. In the eighth year of the Yixi era, he came to Mount Lu to join the community. Later, he took his leave and returned to his native country.
From Jibin, he entrusted one scroll of the *Gaganagañja-sūtra* to a merchant, who brought it to Liangzhou.
Buddhabhadra (translated into Chinese as Juexian) was of the Śākya clan. He was a native of Kapilavastu and a descendant of King Amṛtodana.

Having lost both his parents in childhood, he left the household life as a śrāmaṇera. At the age of sixteen, he had extensively studied the various sūtras and attained a profound mastery of dhyāna and the Vinaya.
He frequently traveled together with Saṃghadatta in Kaśmīra. Once, while Saṃghadatta sat in meditation with his door closed, suddenly—

Seeing his teacher approach, he said, "I am going for a moment to Tuṣita to pay my respects to Maitreya. Having finished speaking, he vanished. Later, as [Dao]yi witnessed even more of his supernatural transformations, he prayed with a reverent heart and questioned him;
only then did he learn that [his teacher] had attained the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmin). At that time, the Śramaṇa Zhìyán of the Yáo-Qín dynasty arrived in Kaśmīra.
Observing the purity of the Dharma assembly there, he looked toward the east with a sigh of regret and said, "My fellow practitioners have not yet encountered a true master."
"How shall I achieve enlightenment? he asked, consulting the assembly: "Who among you can fulfill my prayer to propagate the teachings in the Eastern Lands?
They all responded in unison, saying, "Bhadra is the man for this. Guṇavarman then requested his teacher to prepare provisions for the journey.
They traveled through various kingdoms until they reached Jiaozhi, where they boarded a ship and followed the coast to Donglai in Qingzhou. There, they heard that Kumārajīva was there.
He went directly to Chang’an. Prince Hong of Qin invited the Master to the Eastern Palace to preach the Dharma to a gathered assembly.

There, he debated the meaning of form and emptiness with Kumārajīva. The Master said, "You have only been able to explain the emptiness of form within the fruit [of realization], but you have not explained the emptiness of form within the cause.
Kumārajīva asked what this meant. The Master replied, "Because a single atom is empty, all atoms are empty; because all atoms are empty, [the aggregate is empty]."
"A single atom is empty; within a single atom there are no manifold atoms, and within the emptiness of manifold atoms there is no single atom.

He repeated this back and forth several times. Kumārajīva could not fathom it. Emperor Yao Xing provided for three thousand monks and grandly attended to his worldly affairs, yet the Master maintained himself in meditative stillness.
Suddenly he said to his disciples, "I see five ships setting sail from my native land. Everyone called this a delusory claim. Thereupon—
They were collectively expelled. Thereupon, together with his disciples Huìyán and Huìguān and over forty others, he set out for the Fragrant Valley (Xiānggǔ) on Mount Lúshān.
They lived there in grass huts. At that time, they joined the Lotus Society. Master Huiyuǎn remarked, "The Master’s expulsion was due to a prediction made by his disciple regarding five ships;
however, according to the Vinaya, there was no offense. He immediately dispatched the disciple Tányōng to deliver a letter to the Ruler of Qín on his behalf.

He was released from his banishment and subsequently invited Master [Hui]yuan to Donglin, where they translated various sutras of the Chan and doctrinal schools. From this time on, the region east of the Yangtze River began to take delight in the joy of Chan.
The Master’s ambition was to travel and convert others; he traveled west to Jiangling, where he went on alms rounds. There, he indeed saw five Indian ships arrive at that place.
Later, he returned to the capital and established Daochang Monastery. Previously, Zhi Falin had obtained the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* in Khotan.
The Sanskrit original consisted of thirty-six thousand verses and had not yet been translated.
In the fourteenth year of the Yixi era, Meng Yi, the Prefect of Wu Commandery, and Chu Shudu, General of the Right Guard, requested the Master to serve as the chief translator.
Together with the śramaṇas Faye, Huiyi, Huiyan, Huiquan, and others, they served as scribes. The work was completed in sixty fascicles. Two youths in blue robes followed him from the morning.

He emerged from the pond, swept and cleaned the area, and ground his ink. The Master subsequently translated the *Buddhanusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra*, the *Parinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Pratipattisādhana-śāstra*, and the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* obtained by Faxian, totaling fifteen works.
In the sixth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, he passed away while recollecting the Buddha. He was enshrined in a stupa on the northern ridge of Mount Lu.
Tanyi was a native of Yuhang. Initially, he entered Mount Lu and relied upon Master Huiyuan;
later, he went to Guanzhong to see Kumārajīva, and subsequently returned east to Kuaiji. He entered Qinwang Mountain to recite the *Lotus Sūtra*.

After twelve years, he was moved by the manifestation of the Great Being Samantabhadra in the form of a woman, who arrived before the Master wearing lay clothing and carrying a bamboo basket containing a white pig and two large garlic bulbs, and said:
"I, a humble woman, entered the mountains to gather mugwort. The sun has already slanted, and leopards and wolves roam about; there is no way for me to return home.
I venture to ask for one night's lodging. The Master declined her request. The woman continued to wail piteously and would not cease. He then had her stay upon a grass mat.

At midnight, she cried out, saying her belly was in pain, and asked the Master to massage her. The Master declined on the grounds that he observed the precepts and should not touch a woman with his hands. Her crying became even more intense.
The Master then wrapped his iron staff in cloth and pressed it down from afar. The following day, the woman transformed into a cloud of multicolored garments;

the pig changed into a white elephant; and the garlic blossomed into twin lotuses. They ascended into the air, and she said to the Master, "I am Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, who came specifically to test you.
When Meng Yi, the Prefectural Governor, reported this to the court, an imperial edict was issued to establish Fahua Temple (which is today's Tiantai Temple). At first...

The śramaṇa Fazhi of Yuhang Mountain constantly recited the Lotus Sūtra. A pheasant nested beside his hermitage and would fly about and settle at the corner of his seat as if listening to the teaching.
This continued for seven years. One day, the bird suddenly became haggard; Fazhi said, "Since you are able to listen to the sūtra..."

He will certainly be reborn in the human realm. The next morning, a pheasant died; he buried it immediately. That night, he dreamed of a young boy bowing to him and saying, "Because I listened to the sutra, I have escaped the class of birds.
I am now born as a member of the Wang family before the mountain. Later, when that family prepared a vegetarian feast (*zhāi*), Zhìfāng went to their door.
The boy said, "I have come with you. Zhi patted him and said, "You are my 'pheasant-child' (zhì-ér). He removed his garment and looked under his arm; there were three feathers of a pheasant.
At seven years of age, he was sent into the mountains to leave the household life; at sixteen, he shaved his head.
Because there were feathers under his arm, he was named Yi (Wing).
Tanyong was of the Yang clan and a native of Guanzhong. He stood eight chi tall and possessed a heroic bearing that surpassed others. Having traveled south to Mount Lu, he relied upon Master Huiyuan;
there were no internal or external scriptures with which he was not thoroughly versed. He built a thatched hut on the western side of the mountain to dwell in.
His disciple, Tanguo, focused his mind deeply on the gates of dhyāna. One night, Tanguo dreamed that a mountain deity requested to receive the precepts. Tanguo...
He said, "My teacher is here; you may go and seek him. Suddenly, Yong saw a man wearing a lined robe, whose appearance was dignified and elegant, followed by thirty attendants.
He requested to receive the precepts. Because the Master recalled his previous dream, he knew this was a mountain deity.

He then preached the Dharma for him, and upon completing the bestowal of the five precepts, the deity offered two hoes from a foreign land as a cushion and departed after paying his respects. Later, the Master...
He traveled to Jingzhou to propagate the Dharma and passed away at Zhulin Temple.

When Sengji went to Mount Lu to seek instruction, he attained a profound and subtle realization of the essentials. Master Huiyuan sighed and said, "The restoration and flourishing of the Great Dharma rests upon you.
Later, when he was ill, Master Huiyuan gave him a candle and said, "You may rely on this to establish your mind in peace."
While attending to his teacher, he held a candle and focused his mind in meditation. He invited monks to chant the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.

By the fifth watch of the night, he passed the candle to his disciple Yuanbi and followed the monks in circumambulation. Shortly thereafter, he dreamed that he was holding a candle himself and walking through the air.
He saw Amitābha Buddha receive him upon the palm of his hand and saw him serve all the Buddhas. After a brief moment, he awoke and said with joy: "In a single night..."
As he formed this thought, he was immediately received and guided [into rebirth]. The following day, he again saw Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in the sky, who said to Bi:

"The Buddha is coming. He immediately raised his head and looked toward the west, passing away in a single breath. At that time, the weather was intensely hot, yet his body did not change for three days.
A rare fragrance wafted forth in profusion.
Huigong was a native of Fengcheng in Yuzhang. He studied with the same purpose as Sengguang, Huikan, and Huilan;
while Guang and the others could not equal Gong in their scholarly exertion, they surpassed him in their focused contemplation upon the Pure Land. Hui’an said to Gong: "Although you..."
He was diligent in his studies and possessed vast learning. Did he not know that the Sūtra says: "It is like a deaf person playing music;
they delight others but do not hear it themselves"? Daogong said: "If awakening cannot be attained, who could remain alive without being muddled and ignorant like a fool?

Seven years later, Hui-lan and the others passed away, each at the time of their death manifesting extraordinary responses. Five years after that, Daogong fell gravely ill and said: "The Great Way winds and turns; how..."

"It is time to stop. Amidst birth and death, coming and going, where shall I find refuge? Thereupon, he struck his head in worship and wept like rain, vowing his heart to the Land of Ultimate Bliss with mindfulness never ceasing for even a moment.
Suddenly, he beheld Amitābha Buddha welcoming him forward upon a golden platform; he respectfully ascended it.
He saw Lan and the others within the radiance upon the dais, who addressed him, saying: "Elder, you have already been reborn in the highest grade;
we do not trouble ourselves with words of consolation or joy for you. We only regret that the five turbidities linger on so long, and that our mutual dependence was late.
On this day, he informed the assembly and, with joyful vigor, entered parinirvāṇa. This was the eleventh year of the Yixi era.
Faan initially relied upon Master Huiyuan as a disciple; he was exceptionally skilled in lecturing on the sutras and concurrently practiced the discipline of dhyāna.

He maintained his person with rigorous adherence to the precepts, such that his conduct was particularly refined. During the Yixi era, there was a ferocious tiger in the village shrine of Xinyang that lived beneath the trees of the spirit temple.
In the past and present, there had been hundreds of instances where such creatures harmed the people. When Dao’an traveled through that village, the residents all closed their doors early.
He then sat in meditation beneath a tree. After a short while, a tiger arrived carrying a person on its back; upon seeing Dao’an, it was startled and leaped down to prostrate itself before him.

Dao’an then preached the Dharma and conferred the precepts upon it, after which the tiger departed after a brief time. The next morning, when the residents saw Dao’an, they declared him to be a divine being and proceeded to pay him homage in a body.
He subsequently converted the shrine into a monastery and invited [the master] to dwell there in retreat. He donated his surrounding fields and gardens to serve as the property of the temple.

Once, wishing to paint an image but fearing he could not obtain the necessary copper-green pigment (t’ung-ch’ing), he suddenly dreamed of a person kneeling before his bed who said, "There is a bronze bell beneath this spot.
Upon waking, he immediately dug there and indeed found two bells. He took the green from them to complete the image, using the remaining copper to assist in other works.
Master Huiyuan cast a Buddha image, but his final whereabouts remain unknown.
During the end of the Jin dynasty, Huigian resided at Mount Lu; seeing the great flourishing of Master Huiyuan’s virtuous deeds, he sighed and said, "I am a man, and he is a man.
He subsequently went to Jiaxiang Temple in Shanyin, where he gathered disciples to lecture on the sutras, saying to the assembly: "I wish to rely upon these lectures on the Way..."
He used it to offer to Amitābha. Five years later, knowing that his time had come, he said, "The time has arrived when the lotus blossoms and one beholds the Buddha.
That evening, during a brief nap, the nun Jingyan saw Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta together with hundreds of thousands of followers.
Descending from the sky, Yan asked the Mahāsattva, "Where are you going? He replied, "I am merely going to welcome Master Qian at Jiaxiang.
Master Qian had also previously perceived these auspicious signs and informed his disciples; he then suddenly passed away, and a strange fragrance did not cease for ten days.
Tanjian lived in Jiangling during the Song dynasty. While in meditative concentration, he was moved by the Buddha, who sprinkled water on his face, saying, "I wash away your dust and grime;
I purify your mental thoughts. One night, while walking along the corridor reciting the Buddha’s name, he sat cross-legged at dawn and passed away.
At that same time, Daohai of Jiangling, Tanhong of Huainan, Daoguang of Dongyuan, and Daoguang of Hongnong all beheld a golden platform at the moment of their deaths.
This was the sign of his coming to welcome him.
Tanhong traveled south to Jiaozhi, where he recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* countless times. In a mountain thicket, he gathered firewood and performed self-immolation, from which śarīra were obtained.
Several hundred people saw Hong’s body turn golden as he mounted a golden deer and departed toward the west.
During the early Yongming era of the Qi dynasty, Huijin was at Gaoseng Temple in Yangzhou. He made a vow to recite the Lotus Sūtra in order to adorn and purify the Pure Land.

As soon as he took up the scroll, he fell ill; thereupon, he produced one hundred copies of the sūtra to repent for his past karmic obstructions. Once the volumes were complete, his illness also subsided.
He heard a voice from the air saying: "Your task is finished; your vow has been fulfilled. You shall be reborn in the Pure Land."
If it were not you, who else could it be? One day, while reciting the Buddha’s name without illness, he passed away.
During the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty, Daozhen resided at Mount Lu. Admiring Master Huiyuan, he set his mind upon the Pure Land.

On another occasion, he saw ten people in a boat with oars floating upon the sea in a dream. When asked where they were going, they replied, "We are heading to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang). Daozhen said, "I wish to attain [this land as well]."

He followed him there. The monk replied, "The merit of one day's cultivation surpasses that of eternal kalpas. You have not yet recited the *Amitābha Sūtra*, nor have you ever bathed the Sangha; how can you seek to go?
Zhen then prepared a grand bathing ceremony and devoted himself to reciting the *Amitābha Sūtra*.
Two years later, someone arrived carrying a silver platform and said, "By the merit of the Dharma Master, you ought to receive a golden platform. Why is it that your initial resolve [has wavered]?"
He was hesitant; therefore, he stopped here. Zhen said: "If one perceives that the foundation for seeing the Buddha is gradual, why must it necessarily be the Golden Terrace?
On the evening before his death, a thousand torches of fire blazed upon the mountain cliff where he resided, greatly startling the local villagers. By morning, they learned that Zhen had passed away.
Tánluán was a native of Yànmén. In his youth, he traveled to Mount Wǎitái, where he was moved by its spiritual wonders and left the household life.
By nature, he was fond of the pursuit of longevity and received the ten fascicles of the *Cinnabar Scripture* from Táo Yìnjū. Upon returning to Luòxià, he encountered Bodhiruci, to whom he asked:

"Does the Buddha-dharma contain the art of longevity? Bodhiruci smiled and said: "Longevity and immortality—this is precisely my Buddha-dharma. He then bestowed upon him the *Contemplation Sutra*, saying:

One who can understand this will no longer be born within the three realms, nor will they again transmigrate through the six paths. As for their lifespan, even the kalpas of the Ganges sands or the indestructible stones cannot compare to it;
this is the longevity of our Golden Immortal (the Buddha). Luan was greatly delighted and subsequently burned the immortal scriptures.

Day and night he devoted himself exclusively to reciting the *Amitābha Sūtra*, cultivating the three meritorious deeds, and visualizing the nine grades [of rebirth]. Whether in cold, heat, or illness, [he remained steadfast].
He suffered pain, yet he never slackened even slightly. The ruler of the Northern Wei dynasty admired him and bestowed upon him the title Shenluan (Divine Luan).
By imperial decree, he was stationed at Xuanzhong Temple in Fenzhou. One night, while he was engaged in his recitations, he saw a foreign monk enter the room.

The monk said to him, "I am Nāgārjuna. Because you possess the aspiration for the Pure Land, I have come to see you. Luan asked, "How may you instruct me? The monk replied, "That which has already passed cannot..."
"Furthermore, the future cannot be pursued; as for the present, where is it? The white colt is difficult to turn back. Having spoken these words, he vanished.
Knowing that his time had come, Sengluan gathered the assembly and instructed them, saying: "The toil of life is incessant; there is no day when it shall cease.
One must not fail to fear the various sufferings of hell, nor must one fail to cultivate the pure karma of the nine grades. He then commanded his disciples...
He recited the Buddha’s name with a loud voice and passed away while prostrating toward the west. The assembly heard celestial music coming from the west, which ceased only after a long time.

Huiguang lived in Luoyang during the Northern Qi period; he authored commentaries on the *Avataṃsaka*, *Nirvāṇa*, and *Daśabhūmika* sūtras, exhaustively elucidating their provisional and ultimate meanings.
Regarding the essence of his realization: one day, while ill, he saw celestial beings coming to welcome him. Huiguang said, "My vow was simply to return to An-yang.
Shortly thereafter, transformation Buddhas of the Pure Land filled the void. Huiguang said, "I only pray that my Buddha will receive me and fulfill my original vow.
He then snapped his fingers and cleared his throat; at that moment, both speech and breath ceased.
Fali was a native of Jinyuan. He regularly recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* (*Guanjing*), during which he frequently saw a monk of immense stature standing before him.
In the second year of the Jianwu era of the Northern Qi dynasty, he fell ill. He had a vision of a Buddha and two Great Beings (Bodhisattvas) seated upon lotus flowers beneath a jeweled tree;
Fali was greatly comforted and filled with joy. At midnight, he heard the sound of a bell. When the assembly went to look at him, he passed away on his mat.
Sengrou studied the various Mahāyāna sūtras. During the reign of Emperor Wenxuan of the Qi dynasty, he was summoned to Ye. Sengrou devoted himself solely to the practice of pure karma.

On the day of his death, he saw thousands of transformation Buddhas, and a wondrous fragrance was perceived both inside and outside his room. As he turned westward to pay respectful homage, his spirit immediately departed.
Huiming was a native of Changsha during the Northern Zhou dynasty. At fifteen, he began reciting the *Lotus Sūtra*, completing one entire fascicle in just seven days.

He and Fayin were companions in their pursuit of the Pure Land. One night, as they walked hand-in-hand under the moonlight, they looked at each other and laughed, saying, "If the time has come and we do not depart, it is because of our greed for life.
The Western Land awaits; I am about to go. Fayin said, "Could you not wait for me for ten days? [Huiming] then commanded his servant to...

Liangzhi said, "Beyond this, it cannot be. Two days later, he indeed passed away. The assembly saw celestial beings descend, accompanied by extraordinary fragrances and marvelous music, some of whom cried out, "Excellent!
Ten days later, Yinyin also died; the auspicious omens were entirely consistent with those of his own life.
Sengya was at Duobao Monastery in Yizhou during the Northern Zhou dynasty. Having resolved to offer his five fingers by fire, ten thousand people crowded to witness it.
He said to his disciples, "After I am gone, you must provide for the sick and the deformed with great care; these are all the skillful manifestations of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

At the time of his death while seated in meditation, the assembly saw precious flowers falling profusely. The Master, wearing his patched robe and holding his staff, chanted the name of the Buddha aloud.
Accompanied by several dozen monks, he ascended into the air and departed.
Zhishun entered Mount Lu to follow Master Huiyuan’s practice of pure karma. While lecturing on the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*, as soon as he finished, he manifested signs of illness.
He saw parrots and peacocks reciting the Buddha’s name and the Dharma, all with exquisite voices. He told his disciples, "Today I shall attain rebirth in the Pure Land."
Soon thereafter, he indeed passed away. This was at the beginning of the Daye era of the Sui dynasty.

At that time, Zhenhui resided at Magu in Puzha, where he consumed yellow atractylodes and abstained from grain. He constructed a pure site and erected a four-pillared precious banner to venerate the Three Holy Ones.
Every time he relied upon an image to practice contemplation, he would straighten his body and align his mindfulness, remaining invariably solemn and reverent.
However, one night he said to his disciples, "I see now that lotus flowers are opening and closing repeatedly, as if they were about to support my feet.
A short while later, the sound of bells was heard and a celestial fragrance drifted in from the west. A wondrous light suddenly burst forth, and soon after, Huì passed away.
Zhìtōng was a native of Hé-dōng during the Sui dynasty. He constantly recited thirty verses of praise for the Buddha composed by former sages.

At each of the six periods of the day, he would face an image of the Buddha and chant aloud with a resonant voice; his delivery was so detailed and poignant that those who heard it were moved to grief.

In the seventh year of the Dàyè era, while chanting the name of the Buddha in unison with his disciple Dǐnggài, he suddenly beheld a radiance and extraordinary jeweled banners and flowered canopies. He said to Gài: "I..."
He was reborn in the Pure Land; his fulfillment occurred this very evening. He passed away while seated in the hall of repentance.
The assembly saw a thousand-tiered pavilion ascending into the sky and departing, like mist or clouds.

Huisi came to reside at Mount Nanyue during the Chen dynasty. He specialized in the recitation of the *Lotus Sūtra*. Once, he dreamed that Amitābha Buddha and Maitreya Buddha preached the Dharma to him.
At the conclusion of the summer retreat, as he observed the *varṣa* ceremony, he attained a sudden and great awakening to the *Lotus Samādhi*.

Scriptures he had never heard before were understood by himself without doubt. Later, when his end approached, he gathered his disciples and taught the Dharma for several days. Sitting upright, he proclaimed—
The Buddha arrived; [the master] immediately joined his palms and passed away.
The Great Master Zhìzhě, whose posthumous name was Zhìyǐ, was surnamed Chén. He was a native of Yíngchuān. His mother dreamed of five-colored incense smoke swirling and entering her breast.
On the evening of the child’s birth, a divine light illuminated the room. At the age of seven, he entered Guòyuàn Monastery, where he engaged in hearing, contemplation, and meditation.
The Master was staying at Mount Daisu, so [Huisi] went there to pay his respects. Zhiyi said, "In the past, we listened to the Lotus Sūtra together on Vulture Peak;

pursued by our karmic affinity from that former life, you have come here once again. He then showed him the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra’s place of practice and expounded for him the Four Practices of Peaceful Bliss.

The Master entered into meditative contemplation for twenty-one days. His body and mind became suddenly expansive and clear; his latent supernormal powers were secretly awakened, and he beheld the single seat upon Mount Lingyan as solemnly present as if the assembly had not yet dispersed.
He reported what he had realized to his teacher, who sighed in admiration and said: "Were it not for you, this could not have been realized; were it not for me, this could not have been recognized.
This is the *prathama-āvartā-dhāraṇī* of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*. In the first year of the Dajian era, he went to Jinling to propagate the teachings. Once...

Clad in a single tattered robe, he preached the Dharma at Tiantai for over twenty years. He composed commentaries on the *Amitābha Sūtra* and authored works such as the *Ten Doubts*, the *Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra*, and others.

He exhorted people to advance in the practice of Pure Land cultivation. Later, before the stone statue at Shicheng, as he was about to pass into parinirvāṇa, he instructed his disciples to chant the name of Amitāyus Buddha and the title of the *Amitābha Sūtra*. With palms joined, he praised it, saying: "The Forty-eight Vows."

The Pure Land is adorned with lotus ponds and jeweled trees; though it is easy to go there, few do so. Even when the signs of the fiery chariot appear, one may still attain rebirth there by repenting for a single thought.
How much more so for those who cultivate through precepts and meditative concentration and possess the power of practicing the Way—such efforts are truly not in vain. Furthermore, he said:
"My teachers, friends, and attendants, all following Avalokiteśvara, have come to welcome me. Having spoken thus, he sat cross-legged and chanted the names of the Triple Gem. As...

He entered into samādhi. Later, there was a monk who sought to know the place where the Master had been born. [The Master] then dreamed of the golden countenance of Avalokiteśvara, several *zhang* in height, with Zhi-zhe following behind him.
The Bodhisattva addressed the monk, saying, "Do you still harbor doubts? When the monk further verified this regarding Zhi-zhe, he realized that [the Master] had been reborn in the Western Land.
Huicheng resided in Zhiyang. He recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* and practiced the contemplations of the Western Paradise for thirty years, remaining constantly seated without lying down.

Whenever he entered meditative absorption, he beheld the lotus pedestals and jeweled trees of the Pure Land. On the evening of his death, someone dreamed that Cheng was riding upon a lotus flower, fading away toward the west.
The Venerable Hui-ming was a native of Xiancheng. At the time of his death, he instructed his disciples to be diligent in their pure conduct.
Suddenly, the assembly saw Amitābha Buddha leading a multitude to welcome him; the Master followed behind the Buddha and departed toward the west.
Guanding, a person from Zhang’an, manifested illness when his end approached. A rare fragrance filled the room.

After he had finished instructing his disciples, he suddenly rose, joined his palms, and recited the names of Amitābha Buddha and the two Great Beings (Mahāsthāmaprāpta and Avalokiteśvara). He then passed away in an instant.
He constantly practiced the Fangdeng (Vaipulya) liturgies and repentances with the joy of the Dharma. Once, a pheasant came to claim its life;

a divine being rebuked it, saying, "This Dharma Master is destined for rebirth in the Pure Land; how could he repay your life? Later, while ill, he made a vow to dedicate all the merit of his lifelong practice toward the Pure Land.
As he recited the Buddha’s name with a sincere heart, he immediately saw the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas coming to welcome him. Straight...
He passed away while seated.

Dengguan resided at Tiantai Mountain, where he constantly recited the *Lotus Sūtra*. One night, after bathing, he sat cross-legged facing west, reciting the names of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Zhiyi.
He further expounded upon the Dharma-gate of the Three Contemplations; having finished speaking, he passed away.
Fajun resided at Bijian Temple and practiced the Lotus Samādhi, whereby he immediately attained realization.
On the day he manifested his passing, celestial music filled the air and divine incense spread across the fields. The assembly saw him ascend into the void and depart toward the west.
Dao Yu resided at Kaijue Temple, where he recited the name of Amitābha Buddha day and night without ceasing. He fashioned a statue of the Buddha that was barely three inches tall.

Later, while in meditative concentration, he saw the Buddha, who said to him, "Why have you made my image so small? Dao Yu replied, "If the mind is great, it is great; if the mind is small, it is small.
As soon as he had spoken, the Buddha's body appeared to fill the entirety of space. The Buddha then told him, "Return now to your original place."

He bathed in perfumed water, and when the morning star appeared, he said, "I shall come to welcome you. At that time, he was moved by a transformation as a Buddha came to welcome him, his radiance filling the room.
Shou Hong was a native of Fenyang who constantly kept the Western Paradise in mind. As he was about to die, he saw a youth from Tuṣita Heaven coming to welcome him.
The Master said, "My heart aspires to go to the West; I shall not be reborn in the heavens. He then immediately led the assembly in reciting the Buddha's name.
Suddenly he declared, "The Buddha comes from the West! Having finished speaking, he passed away.
Fazhi resided at Guoqing Temple, where he single-mindedly recited the Buddha’s name. He frequently experienced Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta descending to illuminate his body with light.
He said to those close to him, "The day will come when I am born in the Pure Land; who can prepare a meal to see me off? The assembly prepared it for him.
After he had finished eating, nothing extraordinary occurred. The assembly suspected he was mocking them, so they stayed overnight in his room to wait for him. Before midnight had passed—
Suddenly, he sat upright upon his bed and passed away while reciting the Buddha’s name. A golden light came from the west, causing fishermen on the river to mistakenly think it was dawn.
During the Daye era of the Sui dynasty, Huǐhǎi resided at Ānluò Monastery in Jiāngdū; he devoted himself single-mindedly to the practice of pure karma and attained the Way under Master Dào of Qízhōu.
He reverently paid homage and performed repentance before the statue of Amitābha Buddha that Quan had left behind. Suddenly, the statue emitted light.
From then on, his earnest seeking for rebirth became even more intense. One day, facing west and sitting in the lotus posture, he recited the Buddha’s name and passed away.
Two śrāmaṇeras from Wenshui were fellow practitioners of nianfo (Buddha-recitation). After five years, the elder one passed away first and attained rebirth in the Pure Land.
Seeing the Buddha, he was filled with joy and said to him, "There is a junior śrāmaṇera who practiced together with me; I do not know if he may also attain rebirth.
The Buddha said, "Originally you had no intention to practice nianfo, but it was because of his exhortation that you did so. You should now return and apply yourself even more diligently."
"Practice pure deeds. Three years hence, you may come here together. When the appointed time arrived, the Buddha and the assembly of sages came from the west to welcome them.
The great earth shook, and celestial flowers drifted and danced. At that moment, the two śrāmaṇeras both attained transformation simultaneously.
Shanzhou was a native of Boye who was diligent and devoted to the practice of purity. He frequently saw images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas emitting light that illuminated his body.
One night, while suffering from illness, he suddenly rose and joined his palms in prayer, saying: "The Buddha has gathered sentient beings such as myself through his forty-eight vows;
I surely hope that at this very moment, it shall be according to the Buddha’s original vow. Thereupon, he told the assembly: "The Buddha’s light has shone upon me; my aspirations shall not fail."
Having finished speaking, he passed away.
Faxiang resided at Daxingguo Temple in the capital of Yangdu for thirty years, cultivating the practice of An-yang (Sukhāvatī).

Whatever benefits he performed, he invariably dedicated toward [rebirth in that land]. While he was ill, his disciples heard their master chanting the name of the Buddha with great intensity; they also saw his room...
On the western wall, there appeared a light like a mirror, manifesting the景象 (xiàng) of the Pure Land with a *piṅgala* bird flapping its wings; the auspicious sign vanished in an instant.

Sengzhan had long aspired to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*). Some criticized him for doing so late in life, but Zhan said, "If the merit of ten recitations can lead one to see the Buddha, why should I have any anxiety?
Later, while ill at Xingshan Temple, he prepared a vegetarian feast to bid farewell to the monastics and the laity. At that time—
The Vice-Presidents Fang Xuanling and Du Ruhui were both present at the assembly. When noon had passed, he straightened his deportment and suddenly said, "The Buddha is coming!
The two Great Beings also arrived; then, with body erect and palms joined, he passed away.
Daocuo was a native of Wenshui in Bingzhou. He entered the monastic order at the age of fourteen and studied the sutras and śāstras. Later, he served under Meditation Master Zan to study Chan.

Subsequently, he entered Xuanzhong Temple in Bigu Valley, the former residence of Tanluan. There, he dedicated himself single-mindedly to the practice of nianfo (Buddha-recitation), setting a daily quota of seventy thousand recitations.
He exhorted the people of Bing and Fen to practice nianfo, using beans to mark those who had reached the number ten thousand.
On the eighth day of the fourth month in the second year of the Zhenguan era, he gathered monastics and laypeople for a celebratory assembly on the Buddha’s birthday.
Suddenly, a phoenix was seen in the sky riding a boat made of the seven treasures, which said to Daochuo: "The halls and buildings of your Pure Land are now complete.

The assembly further beheld transformed Buddhas and Bodhisattvas floating and drifting through the air; all were filled with joy, admiration, and marveled at the wonder. This occurred whenever his fellow practitioner Daofu [was present].

Whenever they met, they invariably pointed to the Pure Land as their destination. Three days after Daocuo passed away, Sengfu heard of it and said, "I have always expected to go first, yet now I am behind.
If I apply myself with one more breath of effort, I shall be able to catch up and see the Buddha. He then [proceeded] before the image.
He prostrated himself with his head to the ground to present his petition, then withdrew to his seat and passed away.
During the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, the Dharma Master Shandao saw the Chan Master Chuo of Xihe lecturing and reciting the *Amitābha Sūtra* at the Nine Grades Practice Hall;
he was greatly delighted and said, "This is truly the essential ford for entering the Buddha-way. To cultivate other practices is circuitous and difficult to accomplish."
"This contemplative gate alone enables one to swiftly transcend birth and death. Thereupon, he applied himself with diligent and arduous effort, performing prostrations and recitations day and night.

He continued his journey to the capital, where he inspired the fourfold assembly. Whenever he entered his room, he knelt on his right knee (*huku*) and recited the Buddha’s name, never ceasing until his strength was exhausted.
Even during the coldest weather, he would perspire profusely. Upon leaving his quarters, he expounded the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land for others for over thirty years.

He did not sleep even for a moment, but practiced the *pratyutpanna-samādhi* (walking meditation). He performed prostrations before the Buddhas according to the Vaipulya sutras and upheld the categories of precepts without violating them by even a hair’s breadth.

When fine food was sent to the kitchen, he would serve himself coarse and poor-quality fare; milk, curd, and clarified butter never passed his lips. Whatever offerings were made to him as undergarments, [he would give them away].

He copied one hundred thousand scrolls of the *Amitābha Sūtra* and painted three hundred wall murals depicting the transformation scenes (*pariṇāmanā*) of the Pure Land. Wherever there were ruined temples or collapsed stupas, he renovated them upon arrival.
He lit lamps to maintain continuous illumination, never allowing them to be extinguished for years on end. As for his three robes and alms bowl, he did not allow anyone else to carry them for him.

He practiced apart from the crowd, fearing that talk of worldly affairs would hinder his progress. Among the noble families of Chang’an, those who transmitted the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land were beyond counting.

Those who followed his transformation included some who recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* one hundred thousand to five hundred thousand times, and others who made it their daily practice to chant the Buddha’s name ten thousand to one hundred thousand times. Some even attained the Samādhi of Buddha-remembrance and departed for the Pure Land.
Those who were born in the Pure Land cannot be fully recorded. Someone asked, "Is it through reciting the Buddha's name that one is born in the Pure Land?
The Master said, "As you have recited, so shall your wish be fulfilled. He then recited the name once himself, and a ray of light issued from his mouth;

as he recited from ten up to a hundred times, the light did likewise. His verse for exhorting the world says: "Gradually the skin becomes like chicken skin and the hair turns white like a crane; look, look..."
When one’s gait becomes faltering and decrepit, even if gold and jade fill one’s halls, how can one avoid decay, decline, aging, and illness?
No matter how manifold one’s pleasures may be, impermanence will inevitably arrive. There is only the practice of the direct path: simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha.
Later, he said to others, "This body is loathsome; I shall return to the West. He then climbed a willow tree and, facing west, prayed: "May the Buddha receive me;
may the Bodhisattvas assist me, so that I may not lose right mindfulness and attain birth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).

Having spoken, he threw himself down and passed away. Emperor Gaozong learned of these events and bestowed upon the temple the plaque name "Guangming" (Radiance). It is traditionally said that this was an emanation of Amitābha.
He established himself as the Second Patriarch of the Lotus Society.
Zhiyan resided at Wupiu, where he gathered monastics and laypeople to practice the contemplations of the Pure Land. They assembled once every month, numbering over five hundred people.
Later, while ill, he saw a foreign monk holding a precious vase who came before him and said, "I am Amitābha."
"Furthermore, the one later referred to in the Pure Land as the King of Merit-Jewels (*Guṇaratnarāja*) is none other than I.

Yan then discussed this with the assembly of the monastery, saying, "The Great Being Amitābha (Boundless Light) and Śrīkṣetra (Potent Virtue) are the King of Merit-Jewels; that shall be my name upon attaining Buddhahood.
Shall I not return to the West? That very evening, he passed away.

Master Shen had formerly resided in Puzhou, where he lectured on the *Abhidharma-samuccaya-vyākhyā* and the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*. He vowed to attain rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang) at an early date.

Later, while ill, he instructed his disciples to read the *Amitābha Sūtra* (Guan jing); he sat in meditation and listened. When the reading was finished, he chanted the names of the Buddhas and Great Beings several times from beginning to end.
At midnight, he sat upright and passed away.
His merit was far-reaching, and he was a man from Junyi. He practiced the Samantabhadra Repentance, remaining without leaning against anything for thirty years.
One day, Samantabhadra appeared, riding a six-tusked elephant, and the ground became entirely silver in color. In his later years, he specialized in lecturing on the *Lotus Sūtra*;

whenever they reached the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter, the heavens would invariably send down rain. He also composed a commentary on the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, vowing to dedicate the benefits of its exposition toward rebirth in the Pure Land.
The soil solidified, and five-colored rays of light shone through his chamber. He said, "To attain this at such a time and behold the Buddha amidst the light—my vow is fulfilled.
Thereupon, he focused his mind on the West and passed away without food.

Daowang habitually practiced the Pure Land teachings. One day, as he ascended the high seat to admonish his disciples, he suddenly made a gesture of greeting and said, "Why have those celestial hosts come in such a throng?
The heavenly realms have never been my aspiration. If the Pure Land comes to welcome me," [he continued].

He immediately replied, "I shall obey your command. He then closed his eyes for a long while and said, "The light of Amitābha Buddha shines upon me, and the various transformed Bodhisattvas have also come to this assembly.
Thereupon, he took up the incense burner and prostrated himself to express his gratitude; suddenly, the burner fell and he passed away.

Shandao was a native of Linzi. Upon entering the Great Canon (Tripitaka), he reached for a scroll at random with his hand and obtained the *Sūtra on the Visualization of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life*.

He then devoted himself exclusively to practicing the sixteen sublime visualizations (*ṣoḍaśa-vipaśyanā*). Later, when he visited Mount Lu to observe the traces left by Master Huiyuan, his contemplation expanded suddenly and profoundly.
Subsequently, he withdrew to Zhongnan Mountain, where he practiced the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi* for several years; there, the Jewel Pavilion and the Jade Pond appeared vividly before his eyes.
