Zhongming resided at Ba’en Monastery in Shanyin. He had never previously observed the precepts or maintained self-restraint. Once, while suffering from an illness, he said to his fellow student Daoning, "My consciousness is now scattered and confused;
what medicine can cure this? Daoning replied, "Simply recite the Buddha's name in accordance with your breath;

this is the supreme medicine. Zhongming then recited the Buddha’s name according to that method. When the seventh day arrived and his strength was already exhausted, Daoning further instructed him to visualize the Buddha before his eyes.
After some time, he suddenly saw two bodhisattvas, followed by the Buddha himself coming to welcome him; with eyes closed, he passed away.

Hui-chong and Fayi resided at Jingguang Monastery in Qiantang, where they drew blood to transcribe the seven sutras on the Pure Land, further inscribed the *Lotus Sūtra* in gold, and carved images of the Three Holy Ones of the Western Paradise.
Relying on the methods of meditation through the *Mohe Zhiguan*, they recited the name of Amitābha Buddha. One day, Fayi fell ill.
He took no medicine. Holding incense, he repented before the Buddha and requested the assembly to assist him in reciting the name of the Buddha and chanting the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.
Upon reaching the passage on the Western World, he passed away peacefully and suddenly.

The Master Fanzong relied upon Guangci at Leifeng Peak to study the teachings. Employing the methods of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, he practiced the Great Compassion Repentance for nine years, offering his five fingers as an offering to the Buddha.
Every month, he led forty-eight monks to collectively practice the Pure Land Repentance.
After a long time, he dreamed that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas came to welcome him. Three days later, he passed away while gazing toward the west with palms joined.
Xi Zhan was a native of Shan-yin. In his youth, he was a Confucian scholar, but suddenly grew weary of the world and left the household life.

Together with the lay practitioner Ying, he joined the community at Wan-sha to construct a hall for Amitābha Buddha and devoted himself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism. He never turned his back toward the west while seated.
After some time, he frequently beheld visions of the Three Holy Ones. One night, facing west, he chanted the sutras while sitting upright; forming a meditative mudrā, he passed away.

Tanyi resided at Jingzhu Monastery in Qiantang, where he practiced medicine as his livelihood. In his later years, he paid homage to the Lotus Sūtra and cultivated the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha.

He used the wealth he had accumulated throughout his life to make offerings to the Buddha, provide meals for the monastic community, commission the creation of Buddhist images, and establish bathing facilities for them. He continued these practices in this manner for twenty years.

Later, he fell slightly ill and refused to take medicine. He invited seven monks who were practitioners of the *li-xing* (expedient practice) to recite the Buddha’s name to assist him in his rebirth in the Pure Land.
On the following day, he saw a lotus flower as large as a house. Another day, a monk from India arrived at his bedside to offer greetings.
At midnight, the assembly heard the sound of his reciting the Buddha’s name grow faint; he then passed away peacefully.
When Taimei was a child, he went to Dharma Master Fajian of Qiantang. Initially, when he was first taught the *Amitābha Sūtra*, he was able to recite it from memory.

Upon receiving full ordination, he vowed to shut himself in his room to practice mindfulness of the Buddha as a means of non-retrogression. While the monks were often strolling about, Taimei suddenly heard the sound of a flute on a boat from behind the mountain;
he attained sudden enlightenment and subsequently kept a flute for his own amusement. There was also a certain Inspector Ling, who likewise practiced [the Way].
Jingye was known as the District Magistrate of the Pure Land (*Sukhāvatī*). One day he knocked at the door and said, "Brother District Magistrate of the Pure Land, let us meet.

Jingwei replied, "We may meet tomorrow in the Pure Land; today I am too preoccupied with my recitation of the Buddha's name. The next morning, people marveled that he had not gone to the morning gruel.
When they went to look for him, they saw that his staff, alms bowl, and meditation chair had already been burned, and he sat there in the full lotus posture.
He passed away while seated on the ground.
Sīcóng resided at Fǎ'ān in Qiántáng; he recited two sections of the Lotus Sūtra daily and spent the remainder of his time chanting the Buddha’s name, never speaking of worldly affairs.
Suddenly, he said to his disciples: "Last night, I saw the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas coming together to welcome and guide me. His disciples...
[Cheng] said, "I fear this may be a demonic realm; you must not follow it. [Wang] Cong said, "At the time of my death, there shall be a lotus flower upon my chest as proof.
Two nights later, he ordered the sounding of a *qing* bell and the recitation of the Buddha's name. [Wang] Xi said, "The Buddha has come! and he immediately passed away in a state of composure.
Upon examining his chest, there was a mark about the size of a palm; it was reddish and lustrous, appearing like a blooming lotus flower.
Liaoyi, styled Mumen, was the great-grandson of the Junior Master Zhongli. At fifteen, he took the jinshi examination. Upon traveling to Jinling, he met Master Baoning Ji;
hearing the Dharma, he attained awakening and immediately underwent tonsure. Wherever he went, he inscribed his name as "Zuomeng" (Last Night's Dream).
Moment by moment, he directed his mind toward the Western Pure Land without ever ceasing. When Master Xiang traveled to Huangbo, he invited Liaoyi to accompany him. One night—
In an auspicious dream, the Master came to bid farewell, saying, "I am returning to the West. He was then seen again, as Buddhas and Bodhisattvas presented him with a golden platform.

Three days later, while sitting in meditation after burning incense, he passed away with a smile on his face. He once visited Mount Wutai and suddenly felt himself following a multitude of Bodhisattvas.
Later, while walking in the path, two men wearing purple sashes and gold seals followed behind him. The Master questioned them regarding their names, and one monk led him forward.
Beside the Hall, one may observe a jade tablet with the two names Wang Gu and Ge Fan inscribed in golden characters.

Huicheng resided at Zisheng Temple in Qiantang; he recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and paid homage to the Buddha of the Western Paradise. He once experienced a spiritual journey to the Pure Land.

Having personally beheld the countenance of the Buddha, he went into hiding on a mountain ridge. He piled firewood to form a shrine-casket and entered within it to recite the Buddha’s name. He then set fire to himself.

The Patriarch resided at Mount Nanyue to the south, where he drew blood to transcribe five hundred scrolls of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, one hundred scrolls of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāpāramitā Sūtra*, and ten sets of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
Over twenty-seven years, he used his own blood for all of them, constantly reciting the Buddha’s name with the aspiration [for rebirth].

He was reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*Sukhāvatī*). Toward the end of his life, his blood dried up and he became a mere skeleton; yet the sound of him reciting the Buddha’s name did not cease for a single day.

When he reached the age of facing his death in the abbot’s quarters, he spoke no other words. He sat upright and passed away, with *śarīra* relics bursting forth from between his eyebrows, which grew back as soon as they were taken.

Fayin resided at Sizhao Guangshou Monastery for thirty years, devoting himself to silent meditation and pure practice. Once, while he was ill, he gathered the assembly to chant the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* and recite the Buddha’s name for three nights.
He then said to his disciples, "I am about to depart. When someone requested that he leave behind a verse of farewell, he replied:
He wrote this for himself: "I and Amitābha are fundamentally non-dual; both duality and non-duality are transcended.
Now, seeing Amitābha in this way, the resonance between cause and response is inconceivable. He sat upright with his body straight, formed a mudrā, and passed away.
Liaoran, styled Zhiyong, resided at Bailian for twenty-four years. He dreamed that two dragons were sporting in the sky;

one transformed into a divine being who produced a scroll from his sleeve and said, "Master, you shall depart in seven days. Upon waking, he gathered the assembly to preach the Dharma and wrote in large characters:
"By the power of mindfulness of the Buddha, I have attained rebirth in the Land of Bliss. All of you, should you not exert yourselves? Immediately bathe!"
He changed his robes and gathered the assembly to recite the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*. When they reached the passage on the Western World, he suddenly passed away.
All the practitioners of the Way of the Buddha heard the sound of celestial music, and auspicious light ascended toward the heavens.

Zhixian was styled Zhijiao. He resided at Bailian Temple and lectured on the Way for thirteen years. He practiced the ten recitations facing west throughout all twelve periods of the day, never failing to do so.
One night, he fell slightly ill and requested the practitioners of the Guantang Hall to recite the *Amitābha Sūtra*. Before the scroll had even finished, he passed away while sitting.
The practitioners of Nengren Temple all heard the harmonious sounding of celestial music. It was not until dawn that they learned the Master had died.
Sishi of North Pass, Qiantang, was surnamed Yu. He constantly recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* and never ceased his mindfulness of the Buddha.

He was skilled at painting Buddhas, always requiring that he first purify his chamber and engage in visualization for one day before painting. When he painted a sixteen-foot Amitābha Buddha, he first beheld the Buddha’s radiance, whereby he realized the subtlety of brushwork.
Consequently, people called him "Yu Mita" (Yu Amitābha). He established the Lan-yuan named Miaoxing (Wondrous Practice) to provide food for wandering monastics, where he passed away.

His body was followed by three million people. Suddenly becoming silent, he sat upright with his mind directed toward the Western Quarter. On the seventh day, approaching the end of his life, he requested incense to offer to the Buddha;
then, sitting in the full lotus posture, he passed away. A wondrous fragrance lingered for ten days.
Like Zhan, who attained liberation through the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he traveled extensively among the teaching seats and resided at the Pagoda Cloister in Wuzhen.

Daily, he recited two sections of the Lotus Sutra and twenty thousand invocations of the Buddha’s name. One night, while sitting upright in mindfulness of the Buddha, he passed away. His writings on the meaning of the teachings were titled the *Jiaming ji* (Collection of Provisional Names).
While he was contemplating dwelling on the Western Mountain (Mount Wutai), an astrologer said to him, "On the full moon of the sixth month, you, Master, will pass away.
The Master replied, "How can the Creator control one who cultivates the Way? You say I shall die in the sixth month; I shall instead depart in the eighth.
When the time arrived, he bathed, sat within his meditation niche, gathered the assembly, and while sitting upright, passed into extinction.
Wenhui resided at Qīnglóng Monastery in Jiāhé. His poetic style was lofty and archaic, and he was a friend of Běifēng Yìn. Běifēng also enjoyed composing verse;
Wenhui took his brush away from him and rebuked him, saying, "My elder brother is a pillar of the Great Dharma; why must you concern yourself with such things?

Běifēng was moved by this and subsequently humbled himself to pursue study, eventually becoming a man of renown. Wenhui devoted himself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land, continuing with even greater diligence as he grew old.
He was diligent. At the time of his death, he heard a voice from the sky saying, "You shall be reborn in the Middle Grade.

Huiming, whose style name was Huian, studied under Huiguang, the Chief Monk (Senglü). In his later years, he relied on Changzhao Temple on Mount Jing, where he practiced the Pure Land path together with Zhiye.
Daily, he recited the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, and the *Awakening of Faith*; he maintained the sacred name of Amitābha Buddha by the tens of thousands.
In the spring of the Jiwu year of the Qingyuan era, he manifested illness. He said to his disciples, "I have studied the Mahāyāna and sought rebirth in the Pure Land;
now my vow has been fulfilled. Thereupon, he sat with his feet crossed and passed away. The assembly heard celestial music coming from the west, lingering above his head.
After the cremation, there were śarīra relics of five colors, beyond measure.
Zhili resided at Huadu Monastery in Shangyu. Initially, he traveled extensively to study under the masters of the Chan school; in his later years, he focused his mind solely on the Western Pure Land.
In the eighth month of the autumn of the first year of the Qianyuan era, he wrote a verse to bid farewell to the assembly, saying:

"In my dream, I saw Amitābha Buddha surrounded by a great multitude preaching the Dharma, saying: 'All you superior and virtuous people, you must single-mindedly cultivate pure karma; you shall come to be born in my land.'"
Having finished speaking, Guo vanished. Having witnessed these signs, I knew my rebirth was certain; I immediately turned my body toward the west, performed mudrās, and passed away while seated.
Jingguan resided at Jiguang Hermitage in Jiahe for over ten years practicing the Pure Land Repentance Method. He said to his disciples:
"I shall depart on the twenty-seventh day of the coming month. Two days prior to that, I saw red flowers;
the following day, yellow flowers filled the room, all of which were spontaneously born. At the appointed time, the child was dressed in celestial robes and entered the coffin, sitting within it.
He commanded the assembly to recite sutras and chant the Buddha's name. After a short while, he passed away."
Lixian resided at Xincheng Fahui Temple. Daily he recited the Lotus Sūtra, performed his ritual chants, and practiced mindfulness of the Buddha.

At midnight, his voice became piteous and urgent as he looked upward and lamented the extreme suffering of the Sahā world, praying that the Buddha would swiftly grant him guidance so that he might achieve rebirth in the Pure Land.

In this manner, ten years passed. In his later years, he frequently experienced auspicious signs. Suddenly, he manifested illness in a dream and commanded the assembly to recite the Buddha’s name. Facing west, he gazed intently with a composed countenance.
He passed away while seated.

The Master had studied under Wuzhen Pujing and thoroughly mastered the essential tenets of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. He practiced the Amitābha Repentance and meditated upon the Pure Land for twenty years, never ceasing day or night.
Although he suffered from many illnesses throughout his life, at the moment of death he suddenly became alert and vigorous, and said to his disciples:
He said, "The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have already descended; I shall now depart. He then sat upright and passed away.

Like Bao Shou of Ye-chuan, who attained the Flower of Enlightenment through his practice, [the Master] heard of the story of how Zen Master Zhen of the past dreamed of performing a ritual bath and thereby attaining rebirth in the Pure Land.
Consequently, he resolved to establish a long hall for bathing for twenty years and constructed an image of the Buddha, vowing to seek rebirth there.
At the age of eighty-one, he invited the assembly to drink tea and took his leave. Suddenly, the sound of a bell was heard once; the assembly was all struck with wonder.
He immediately sat in the full lotus posture facing west, joined his palms, gazed intently, and passed away.

Xian Chao was a native of Bozhou. He personally received from the Tripitaka Master Jin Zongchi the methods for the *Huiji* (Vimalakīrti) mantra recitation, through which he healed the sick and resolved grievances.
The offerings and benefits he received amounted to fifty thousand strings of cash, all of which he deposited into the permanent endowment of Yongshou Monastery.

Later, while ill, he saw Buddhas and Bodhisattvas coming forward to welcome him amidst a profusion of lotus flowers and the sounding of various musical instruments. His disciples all urged the Dharma Master to remain.
He saved the world from suffering. As the manifestations of the Pure Land gradually faded away, he remained for another fifteen years, reciting mantras to save sentient beings.
One day, celestial music and extraordinary fragrances arose; the Buddha and the assembly of sages came to welcome him as before. He then sat in the full lotus posture facing west and passed away.
There was a man named Kai who resided at Qianbu Monastery in Xiachuan. He devoted himself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism, never failing in his morning and evening devotions.
At the beginning of the year, he invited the assembly to recite the Buddha’s name and chant sutras until they reached the section on the Western World; thereupon, he closed his eyes and passed away.

Daosheng resided at Xingfu Monastery in Changshu. He commissioned a sixteen-foot image of Amitābha Buddha, for which he received financial support from Mei Ruren, the Magistrate of the county, to provide the pigments and decorations.

He immediately gathered the assembly to chant sutras and recite the Buddha’s name while making his formal petition. Weeping bitterly as he took his leave of the Buddha, he returned to his room, wrote a gatha, and passed away while seated.

When he observed that the people of Jiu’anzhen were gathering for a great assembly, he organized ten thousand people to practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name, each person chanting it one hundred thousand times, vowing to lead those who first attained rebirth in the Pure Land to follow in succession.
The Master requested the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Sūtra of the Light of Wisdom*, completing one hundred copies daily;
over twenty years, he recited these sūtras six million times, vowing to adorn the pure karma of all sentient beings. One day, while he was emptying his bowl...
He came to visit me and accompanied me for the midday meal. Suddenly, he asked for a brush and wrote a verse, then sat in the lotus position and passed away.
Tan Yi resided at Longquan in Yuao, where he recited the *Lotus Sūtra* five thousand times and the *Sūtra of the Practices of Samantabhadra* and the *Amitābha Sūtra* ten thousand scrolls each.
He worshipped the Buddha in his quiet chamber without ceasing day or night. When he suddenly fell slightly ill, he gathered the assembly and said, "I am at peace."
His life was to have its appointed end; he then faced west, placed his feet one upon the other, and passed away.
Yuanzhao was of the Lu clan of Siming. He was a descendant of Lu Tian, a renowned scholar of letters. In his youth, he studied the Vinaya and read through the Great Canon (*Tripitaka*).
He recited the *Lotus Sūtra* ten thousand times and also transcribed a copy of the *Lotus Sūtra* and three commentaries on the Vinaya school using his own blood. This was during the Jianyan era.

In the fourth year, when the Jin invaders broke into Siming, the Master was residing at Lake Xin. As the invaders pressed him to travel north, he reached Nanxu and said to his attendants, "I shall now return to the West.
Immediately, the sound of flutes and singing was heard; at that moment, both soldiers and civilians saw it clearly.
The Master gazed toward the west, recited the Buddha’s name, and passed away.
Zhijin resided at Jiyuan Monastery in Xiachuan, where he constantly contemplated the Pure Land day and night without interruption. While ill, he gathered the assembly to chant the *Amitābha Sūtra*.
As soon as it was finished, he sat in the lotus position, joined his palms, and passed away.

He practiced the perfection of precepts, studied the Vinaya, and settled his mind in meditative cultivation. Later, he resided at Jile (Ultimate Bliss) in Yu’ao. While ill, he composed a final letter to bid farewell to his friends and former associates.

He instructed the assembly to recite the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*; when they reached the section on the contemplation of the Dharma-body, he called the Buddha’s name with a forceful voice, sat cross-legged, and passed away.
Daochen’s sobriquet was Yuanbian. He was the eighth-generation patriarch of Nanhu. While seated in meditation during the Amitābha Repentance, he beheld the Venerable Fazhi;

during the Lotus Repentance, he saw Samantabhadra emitting light. Every twenty-third day of the month, he established a Pure Land assembly as his regular practice, attended by both monastics and laypeople.
One day, manifesting illness, he vowed that on his ordinary days, [he would maintain] even a single hair’s breadth [of diligence].
He dedicated these merits toward rebirth in the Pure Land. He gathered the assembly to chant the *Amitābha Sūtra* without interruption for seven days.

Addressing the head monk, he said, "I have already beheld the Buddha’s body and heard a wondrous fragrance. Thereupon, he bathed, changed his robes, and wrote this verse: "The Pure Land is but the mind; fundamentally, there is neither delusion nor enlightenment.

When not a single thought arises, one immediately enters the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*). He then further ordered the chanting of the "Peaceful Practices" chapter until they reached the section on "profound entry."
In meditative concentration, he beheld the Buddhas of the ten directions and passed away with a sigh of contentment.
He had a friend named Muguan (Pastoral Hermitage) who resided at Nanhu. One day, while sitting in the Qingyu Pavilion, he requested a practitioner to recite the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*.
Upon reaching the contemplation of the True Dharma-body, he further led the great assembly to chant the Buddha’s name. He left behind a verse and passed away while seated.
Miao-yun of the Yang family of Si-ming, surnamed Cishi, retired from Nan-hu to live at the Wu family hermitage by the creek.
One day, after bathing and sitting in the lotus position, she said to her attendants: "I have a fragrant incense stick that I have kept hidden for thirty years; I intended—"

He was to be cremated at the time of his death as an offering to repay the Buddha’s kindness; now that very moment had arrived. While the fragrant flames were burning most fiercely, he rose, addressed the Buddha to state his intention, and passed away while seated.

Xiyan (Hsi-yen), whose courtesy name was Shengtú (Sheng-t'u), was a native of Siming. Throughout his life, he was unwilling to dwell in the mountains; in his later years, he resided at the Li family hermitage in Taoyuan.

For over ten years, he devoted himself single-mindedly to the recitation of the Buddha’s name. He once inscribed a small window with the characters "Recalling the Buddha" (Yìfó) and composed a verse which says:
Following the waves and chasing the ripples, it drifts away; in the snap of a finger, seventy years have passed. Have you not known how to recollect the Buddha since long ago?
As you grow old, you must apply yourself with even greater vigor. I pity myself for this deep longing for the Buddha in my final years;

save for the Buddha, there is none who can express my heart. Who says that ten thousand pieces of gold are better for a guest? In the end, a single meal in the groves of one’s own home is superior. (At the time of death, bathe.)
He changed his robes, sat upright, and passed away while reciting the Buddha’s name.
Liaoxuan studied at Baolin Temple in Siming; he entered Guangyan Hall at Nanhu to read the Tripitaka and participated in the Lotus Sutra ritual repentance.
In the twenty-seventh year [of the era], he was on very good terms with the lay practitioner Rong. One day, he went to Rong’s quarters and sat in silence.

Dongrong questioned him about this. The Master said, "The time for my return to the West is approaching; I cannot forget our bond of righteousness and virtue, and I hope to meet you again in the Pure Land.

Dongrong said joyfully, "This is exactly what I have prayed for. Suddenly, he manifested illness and requested that the assembly chant the *Amitābha Sūtra*. While they were reciting the Buddha's name, [he passed away].

Sitting upright, he wrote a verse, saying: "Nature and form are forgotten; oneness and threefoldness have no resting place. The winds of breath cease and do not move—this is Mahāśrī. With palms joined, he passed away.
During the intense heat of summer, his remains stayed in the shrine for seven days; his complexion remained ruddy and moist, with a slight amount of saliva at the corners of his mouth.
Those who observed him wrapped it in a cloth, from which a wondrous fragrance wafted toward people. When the officials and commoners heard of this, they flocked from the entire city to wrap it;
the fragrant exudation became even more abundant. At the site of his cremation, there were countless śarīras.
Shanrong was of the Zhou family from Xiaoxi in Siming. He entered the Guanshi hall at Nanhu sixteen years ago, where he read the Tripitaka and practiced the ritual of repentance.

He transcribed the Lotus Sutra, the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, the Complete Enlightenment Sūtra, the *Guangming* (Radiant Light) Sūtra, and other scriptures in gold ink. He also fashioned an image of Amitābha.
Whenever he encountered a Dharma assembly, he would distribute his possessions as offerings. He himself painted a water-ink image of Avalokiteśvara and gave it to anyone who requested it.

Three years after Master Xuán passed away, he suddenly took his scriptures and images and distributed them among his relatives and acquaintances. He invited the assembly to chant the *Bhadracari-praṇidhāna Sūtra* and the *Amitābha Sūtra*.

Amidst the sound of the recitation of the Buddha’s name, he sat cross-legged and passed away. At that time, it was believed that he had fulfilled his promise to join Master Xuán in the Pure Land. His younger brother—
His disciple Haiyin’s lofty conduct was like his own.
Zuohui resided in the Buddhist pavilion within the city walls of Siming County; whenever he encountered people, he would say only, "It is Amitābha Buddha who speaks.

Because he could not find anyone capable of repeating his words, he ultimately referred to him as the "Master Who Cannot Be Quoted" (Shuobude). The Magistrate of Yin, Wang Yongxiang, and his wife were his patrons.
He visited him frequently. One day, he went to his home and took his leave, saying, "I shall depart tomorrow.
When all the donors had assembled, he entered the shrine and sat upright. He asked for sweet melons and ate one whole; then, reciting the Buddha's name, he passed away.

Jian Siming was like a mountain of pagodas. Having twice read through the Great Canon and constantly recited the Lotus Sutra, he devoted himself single-mindedly to the mindfulness of the Buddha, never flagging day or night.
In his later years, he lived in a hermitage; suddenly falling ill, he invited the monks from neighboring huts to focus their minds on him as he faced west.
He passed away sitting cross-legged with a smile upon his face.
The Master newly received his training at Fuyuan in Siming. Wearing simple robes and eating coarse food, he maintained a life of austere practice.

Not far from the monastery, there was a man of prominent lineage surnamed Fang, who invited him to a hermitage. Thereupon, at Fuyuan, he established a Pure Land Hall, fashioned images, and planted lotuses.

On the eighth and eighteenth days of each month, he gathered monastics and laypeople to focus their mindfulness. One day, he went to take leave of the abbot, saying: "On the fifteenth day of the second month..."
On this day, as I was about to return to the West, I came specifically to pay my respects and bid farewell. My withered entrails longed for a bowl of noodles; the host granted his wish.
Having finished eating, I went before the image in the Jōdo-in and prostrated, saying: "The Patriarch is about to depart; I respectfully take leave of the Honored Image."
He immediately returned to the hermitage and gathered the assembly to recite the Buddha’s name. Suddenly emerging from the group, he inquired after them, saying:

"Master Xinyu has already paid his respects to the honored image of the Tathāgata and bid farewell to the abbot of Fuyuan. Now I take my leave of you, my fellow practitioners. On the fifteenth day, I shall certainly depart.

I pray that all of you, virtuous ones, will diligently recite the Buddha’s name so that we may soon meet again. He then sat cross-legged in meditation and recited the Buddha’s name, suddenly exclaiming:
The Buddha had already arrived here; [the Master] joined his palms and passed away.

The Venerable Zhongfeng, whose name was Mingben, was a native of Qiantang. He received the Dharma from Gaofeng of Tianmu. His wisdom and eloquence were unimpeded, and he secretly cultivated the practice of Pure Land.
He composed one hundred poems on the aspiration for the Pure Land. His virtue and character were revered by all like the towering peaks of a mountain range.
Dragons and elephants mingled there. The imperial court repeatedly dispatched envoys to bestow gold and silk, and by imperial decree he was titled National Teacher Puying.
At the age of sixty-two, on the day he manifested parinirvāṇa, a brilliant radiance shone forth. He was interred in a stupa at Mount Tianmu.

Shanzhu, whose courtesy name was Yunwu, was a native of Suzhou. By nature he was lofty and pure, remaining aloof from fame and profit. He shut himself within his room for six periods of the day to recite the Buddha’s name, upheld the Mahāyāna scriptures, and performed prostrations and repentance.
He did not falter even during long illnesses. Among those who cultivated the Pure Land in the Wu region, he was one of the most prominent.

The Master was the most eminent; both monastics and laypeople drew extensively from his teachings. At the time of his passing, a rare fragrance filled the room. His *An-yang chuan gu-xiang ji* (Record of the Oral Tradition of the Land of Peaceful Nurturing) remains in circulation.
Tianru Weize was a native of Luling who received the Dharma from Zhongfeng. His wondrous realization surpassed that of ordinary men.

He established the Shizilin Bodhi Zhengzong Monastery in the city of Suzhou, which contained two chambers named "Lying in the Snow" and "Standing in the Snow," where he sat daily to recite the Buddha’s name.

Students of the Way followed in his footsteps one after another. Beyond his practice of holding up the single phrase for direct pointing, he further composed the *Jingtu huo wen* (Questions on the Pure Land) to exhort others.
At the time of his passing, auspicious signs appeared in manifold ways. He was sixty-nine years old; his stupa was erected on the plains west of the river.
Pudu was a native of Danyang. He entered the monastic order in his early twenties. Initially, he studied under Chan Master Huì of Bǎoshān, who held him in high esteem.
He resided at Dōnglín Monastery on Mount Lú and excelled in the Fǎtáng. He was devoted to the practice of the *nienfo* samādhi and authored the ten-fascicle *Lianzong baojian*.
He propagated the teachings at Fǎwáng Monastery in the capital; National Preceptor Guǎndǐng presented his work to the throne, and an imperial edict was issued in praise of it.
He traveled throughout the world, instructing and guiding beings of the human and heavenly realms, continuing the Buddha’s life of wisdom and reviving the legacy of Donglin.
At the time of his death, he took leave of the assembly and passed away while reciting the Buddha’s name. He was renowned in the world as the Patriarch Yudantan.
Miaowen left home at the age of nine and first appeared in the world at thirty. His unimpeded eloquence was like a torrent rushing down a gorge or a river surging through a ravine.

Later, he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of the *nienfo* samādhi. At the end of his life, knowing in advance that the time had come, he instructed his disciples to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha aloud;
facing west and sitting in the lotus posture, he passed away.
Pangu’s physical appearance was unremarkable, yet his ambition and spirit were transcendent. By nature he was devoted to mountains and waters, once saying:

"My footprints have covered half the world, and my poetic fame fills the realm. At that time, the Prince of Shen in Goryeo, having heard of the Master’s virtue and reputation, invited him to lecture on the Avatamsaka Sūtra.

The seven classes of followers were all moved to submission, and the Prince of Shen was greatly delighted. Later, he went to Song County, where he constructed a vihāra and diligently cultivated the practice of purity.
He daily recited the Buddha’s name as his regular discipline. At the age of seventy, free from illness, he announced the time of his passing in advance; sitting upright, he manifested parinirvāṇa.
Chu Shi Fanqi was a native of Shu. He was a devoted believer in the Western Paradise. While traveling to Yanjing, he attained great enlightenment upon hearing the sound of the drum atop the tower.

At the beginning of the Hongwu era, he was summoned three times to preach the Dharma in the capital, for which the Emperor’s heart was greatly pleased. Later, he built a residence called Xizhai (Western Studio) and dedicated himself single-mindedly to the practice of pure karma.
He composed a poem titled "Recalling An-yang" (Recalling the Land of Peaceful Nurturing), which says: Day and night I long to return, yet I have not returned; A traveler at the edge of heaven.
The soul soars in dreams; upon awakening, where does the cry of wild geese pass? Gazing toward my homeland, all is cut off as letters from home grow rare.

How many times have I opened the window to watch the setting moon? For a lifetime, leaning against the railing, I have sent off the slanting light. Within the golden pond, there are lotus roots like boats; I imagine their blossoms must span dozens of fathoms.
I have seen great lotus flowers filling the world, with Amitābha Buddha at its center and the assembly of sages surrounding him.
Surrounded by his disciples, as he was about to pass into parinirvāṇa, he addressed the assembly, saying, "I am going. Someone asked, "Where will you be reborn? He replied, "In the West.
Again they asked, "There is a Buddha in the West; is there no Buddha in the East? Thereupon, he let out a single, stern shout and passed away in stillness.
Master Zuxiang was a native of Xinyu in Jiangxi. He had been diligently cultivating the Pure Land practices at Longtan Temple in Shandong.

A layman named Wang Jie built a hermitage to invite him there. Before long, he told Jie that he would return home on a certain day. Although his family members tried to detain him, he insisted on leaving.

Xiangyun returned to the An-yang family home. When the appointed time arrived, she arranged her seat and sat facing west, passing away. Her coffin was carried into the mountains, where it spontaneously ignited in flames.
Huiri styled Dongming had the surname Jia; he was a great-grandson of Sima Xidao of the Song dynasty. When Xidao was demoted to military exile, [Huiri followed him].

At that time, the Master was still young, yet his resolve was set on seeking the life of a renunciant. During the Zhizheng era, a disaster struck Southern India. Gao Nalun, a high-ranking official of the Yuan dynasty, requested the Master to rebuild it.

In the second year of the Hongwu era, the Emperor summoned him to appear before the Fengtian Hall. With a ruddy countenance and white eyebrows, the Master presented a comprehensive report that fully met the Emperor's expectations.
Emperor Taizu looked toward the assembly of monks and said, "Why do you not consult this man regarding the profound meanings of the scriptures?"
The Dharma Master Bai-mei was subsequently summoned for an audience, after which he was addressed solely by his nickname, "White-Brow.
Later, when he returned to Shang Tianzhu Monastery, he practiced the *Amitābha* repentance ritual to perfect his pure karma. One night, he dreamed that a blue lotus grew from within a square pond;
upon waking, he told the assembly, "The auspicious sign of my rebirth in the Pure Land has appeared. Four days later, he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture with palms joined.

The Dharma Master Lianchi, whose name was Zhuhong, was a member of the Shen family of Hangzhou. Having set his mind upon the Buddha-vehicle at the age of twenty, he received the tonsure under Wumen Xingtian in the *bingyin* year of the Jiajing era.
He subsequently received full ordination and traveled with only a single gourd and a pair of sandals, visiting numerous spiritual teachers throughout the land.

At that time, Bianrong and Xiaoyan were the most prominent figures of the two Chan lineages; he went to study under them and attained much accord with their teachings. He traveled north to Mount Wutai, where he was moved by the manifestation of Mañjuśrī’s radiance.
In the *Xinwei* year of the Longqing era (1571), seeing that the mountains and waters of Yunqi were secluded and tranquil, he eventually settled there in a thatched hut for the rest of his life.

Tigers were a frequent scourge in the surrounding hills; the Master recited sutras and performed the *shishi* (food-offering) rite for them, and the threat of tigers was thereby pacified. During a drought, he followed the irrigation channels across the fields.
He practiced the recitation of the Buddha's name (*buddhānusmṛti*). Wherever his feet traveled, timely rains fell in abundance. From this point on, his path of transformation flourished greatly.
The Master alone opened the single gate of the Pure Land (*Sukhāvatī*), synthesizing the Three Baskets (*Tripiṭaka*) and pointing toward the mind-only (*cittamātra*) as the ultimate destination.

Monastics and laypeople from the four quarters followed one after another to prostrate and inquire about the Way. Prominent officials and high-ranking dignitaries, such as Lu Guangzu, Zhang Yuanbian, Feng Mengzhen, Tao Wangling, and Yu... [text continues]

During the Chunxi era, figures such as Song Yingchang were all so moved that they surrendered their hearts in refuge to him. By nature, the Master was profoundly filial; whenever he traveled while carrying his ancestral tablet, he would prepare offerings for its sustenance.
He provided relief to the solitary and destitute within the monastic community, invariably making offerings on behalf of his ancestors of the Shen clan for the sake of those in the dark realms.

Having personally practiced the *Yankou* (Feeding the Hungry Ghosts) ritual, he constantly presided over its performance himself. There were frequent instances where those who saw him perceived the form of the Tathāgata manifesting upon his seat.
This was due to the power of his contemplation. To save the lives of sentient beings, he composed the "Essay on Refraining from Killing and Releasing Living Creatures.

He established ponds for releasing living creatures both inside and outside the city, as well as within the mountains. During the Wanli era, Empress Dowager Cisheng sent an eunuch to inquire about the Dharma and bestowed upon him purple robes and gold.

The messenger brought out the gold and returned it to the monastery’s permanent endowment; the robes were enshrined in a high pavilion and never worn on his body. The Master carried them upon his shoulders.
He upheld the True Dharma and cultivated the four practices of peaceful bliss. Through the *nien-fo* samādhi, he universally gathered his three faculties.

He authored more than twenty types of commentaries on the *Amitābha Sūtra*, including the *Shuchao* and the *Yunqi Fahui*, which have circulated in the world. Fifteen days before his passing, he entered the city to bid farewell to his old friends.
His disciples, including Song Shouyi and others, said, "We shall go elsewhere; returning to the mountain to part from the assembly will be as it was before."
The community, believing that the Master intended to decline visitors, found him instead residing at Changshou Hermitage; none could fathom the reason for this.

When the appointed time arrived, he faced west and recited the Buddha’s name, passing away while sitting upright. The assembly mournfully requested his final instructions. Closing his eyes, he opened them again and said, "Recite the Buddha's name with sincerity;
do not change the subject. This was on the fourth day of the seventh month in the forty-third year of the Wanli era; he was eighty years of age.

There was one whose monastic seniority reached fifty years; he was the patriarch of the Lotus School. From Mount Kuang to Zongze, the eight [patriarchs] within the realm were determined to be in accord with one another, counting this master as the ninth patriarch.

Baizhu frequently traveled between the prefectures of Hangzhou and Jiahe. Wearing but a single robe throughout both winter and summer, he sustained himself by begging for food and had no fixed dwelling.
In his daily life, he never ceased to recite the Buddha’s name; when someone called out to him, he would only respond briefly before immediately resuming the continuous chanting of the Buddha’s name.
He spoke no further words. One day, he told the assembly, "I am going. After requesting a bath, he passed away.
Zhenqing left home at the age of nineteen and took up the "Mu" (No-Word) kōan. Upon hearing the sound of a boat striking the shore, he attained realization.

Later, he moved to Mount Tianzhu on Huading Peak, where he practiced the Great and Small Amitābha Repentances. In a dream, he beheld the Three Holy Ones of the Western Paradise. This occurred in the *guisi* year of the Wanli era (1613).
In the first month, his end approached. The assembly asked, "In which grade of rebirth will the Master go? He replied, "I shall be born in the middle grade of the middle level.
They said, "Why not be born in the upper grade? He replied, "I have been perfumed by the fragrance of the precepts; my station stops at the middle grade. Having finished speaking, he passed away.
The Buddha Stone was titled the Elder Fayu. His mother dreamed that a monk covered her body with a *kāṣāya* robe before he was born.
In his youth, he detested the smell of meat and pungent flavors. At fourteen, he shaved his head and donned the dyed robes; at eighteen, he received full ordination from Master Lianchi.

At thirty, he visited Chan Master Zibo in Jinling and personally received a prophetic transmission from him. By nature, the Master was solitary and eminent, never attending to worldly affairs. In his later years...

In his later years, he declined visitors and took up residence on the summit of Wulin Peak. There he constructed a single room and excavated a burial pit, saying, "This shall serve as my dwelling when alive and my tomb when dead.
After some time, he manifested illness. His disciples requested that he leave behind a verse, and the Master wrote it with a swift hand:
"A single phrase of Amitābha for fifty years— Clearly digging in the earth to seek the blue sky. Now there is this truly excellent news: Half..."
The sound of the night bell reached the traveling boat; he set down his brush and passed away.
In Huangzhou, Hubei, there was an unnamed monk who specialized in reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha, never ceasing day or night.
Whatever he saw, he would call out "Amitābha Buddha. In the *Chongzhen* era, the year *Guiwei*, General Huang Ding defended the prefectural city. The Master...
He chanted the Buddha’s name with a loud voice. As he passed through the military lines, they seized him. It happened that Zhang Xianzhong was attacking Huangzhou;

the Master remained upon the city walls, chanting the Buddha’s name throughout the night and repeatedly calling out to awaken those who were sleeping. The soldiers resented this and bound him, throwing him down from the wall.

Shortly thereafter, he was again on the city walls chanting the Buddha’s name. This occurred four times in total; whenever he was thrown down from the eastern wall, he would reappear on the western wall, and from the southern wall...

Descending, he went up onto the northern wall of the city. The commander of the central army informed the Generalissimo, who then paid him respectful homage. At that time, Huangzhou was suffering from a great famine, and people were eating one another.

When the Master went outside the city, a starving man holding a knife sought to have the Master sacrifice his body. The Master took off his robe and showed it to the crowd, saying, "Wait until I have recited the Buddha’s name a thousand times, and then you may eat me.
When he had reached three hundred recitations, the crowd grew anxious and rushed forward, eager to strike him with their blades.
Suddenly, troops arrived from the sky, and the starving people scattered in terror; yet the Master was already within the city.
A hunter in the mountains had captured a large tiger, and the Master sought to ransom it for release. The hunter demanded thirty pieces of gold, but the Master could only obtain four.
The hunter said, "If you can hold the tiger's ears and circle it three times without being harmed, I shall give it to you."
The tiger. The Master then bestowed a prophecy upon it; he grasped the tiger by its ears, circled it three times, and released it. The escaped tiger took refuge with the Master and would not leave.

The Master lived together with the tiger in the Vajra Cave on Mount Hwangma. While Lu Gudeok, the Inner Minister, was leading troops past Hwangju, he went to the mountain to visit the Master and wished to see the tiger.
The Master told the tiger to stop; the tiger merely poked its head out from the outside as Lu wished to see it.
His entire body was covered in [tiger] stripes. The tiger then let out a great roar and leaped away; Lu also took refuge [in him].

One day, while the Master was walking through the streets, he saw a rooster chanting the Buddha’s name with a loud voice; the rooster also chanted along with the sound. In the year Gengyin, the Master wished to travel to Wulin.

On his way, he passed through the White Gate (Nanjing) and stayed by the Qinhuai River. During the Dragon Boat Festival, he saw a pleasure boat where there was a prominent gentleman surnamed Qian, who had previously taken refuge [in the Dharma].
He called out to his teacher, "Does Master Qian Amitābha Buddha also reside on this boat? Upon disembarking and seeing his teacher, the teacher asked those traveling with him, "Do you know who he is?
He was [recognized as] so-and-so. So-and-so then wailed aloud, saying, "Sentient beings take such suffering to be happiness!"
Qian earnestly requested instruction on the essentials of practice. The Master said, "Single-mindedly recite the name of Amitābha Buddha.
He further said, "After I have passed away, if you have any doubts, you may ask Juelang; he is a man of clear vision.
Shi Haibao of Tianting Monastery in Jinling, upon first encountering spoiled vegetables in the meditation hall, would invariably set aside the rotten greens every morning when he rose.

He carried several loads of these items to the temple gate and waited for passersby to solicit money to place upon them; once they were restored, he would have the sellers take them away. He would then carry the first batch inside to provide for the monks.
When he encountered those who were unwilling to give, he would follow them for a distance of several *li*, earnestly exhorting them to change their minds.

He did not treat people with contempt. His tattered robes were so full of lice that they swarmed over them; when he had leisure, he would sit on the ground to recite the Buddha’s name, constantly picking up the lice and moving them from one side of his body to the other. In total...

He did not leave his body behind. After more than a year, he sought out withered vegetables and rotten wood from outside; furthermore, he begged for small increments of money until he had accumulated several taels.

He would then earnestly request the assembly to recite sutras. Once the liturgical repentances were completed, he would recite the Buddha’s name and dedicate the merit. He continued in this manner for many years.

During the Chongzhen era, Zheng Zuochang of the literary academy invited the Master to visit the South Sea. The Master declined the invitation. After the boat had departed, [the author] frequently saw the Master there.
He proceeded by land, but could not catch up with him. When he reached the mountain and entered the hall, he saw the Master again burning incense above;
he dispatched messengers to watch for his return, but they found no trace of him. Upon arriving at the prefecture, Zheng went directly to the temple to wait for the Master.

A disciple said, "The Master has been lying in bed for over a month, consuming neither tea nor water; only yesterday did he finally ask for a drink and rise. Zheng then recounted the Master's spiritual manifestations.
The people of the commandery consequently came to revere and trust him. One day, Liao Juke came to take his leave.

The Master instructed him, saying, "On such-and-such a month and day, we shall meet again to conclude our worldly ties. Liao arrived as scheduled. The Master brewed tea and poured it out, saying, "I trouble you, Layman, to paint a small portrait of this old monk for me.
Juke painted it; not only was the form and spirit remarkably lifelike, but even the worn-out robes [were rendered with fidelity].

The lice on his robes were also vividly perceived moving about; it was truly like the brush of a divine artisan. After more than ten days, he passed away while sitting in the lotus posture reciting the Buddha’s name.
Master Ouyi Zhixu, whose style name was Suhua, had initially studied under the Chan school, but later, due to a severe illness, resolved to travel westward.

He returned home and diligently cultivated pure karma. He authored works such as the *Essential Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra*, the *Mysterious Texts of the Buddha-peak*, the *Collection from the Hall of Pure Faith*, and *Celestial Music Resounding in the Void*.
At the time of his passing, auspicious signs were manifold.
During his years at Shisō, he left home to become a monk at Buttsuji. He applied himself diligently to ascetic practices and oversaw the monastery’s permanent assets.

He performed whatever tasks arose before him and devoted himself to the practice of *nenbutsu*. Whatever he received, he gave away immediately, never retaining any surplus wealth. He did not quarrel with others, nor did he ever show a look of anger.
In the autumn of the *jinshin* year (1212), one day he suddenly said to those around him, "I shall depart for the West tomorrow. Thereupon, he borrowed...
An elderly man of Yunqi sat in his coffin. On the following day, he bathed, put on fresh clean robes, and while his hair had not yet been fully shaved, he passed away while seated.
Daoshu was a native of Renhe;
he constantly exhorted others to take the recitation of the Buddha’s name as their vanguard, and in his daily life, he recited the Buddha’s name with great vigor.
Unstained by worldly conditions, in the year of the Yiwei cycle (1655), he dreamed that he ascended the summit of Mount Yuping with a divine monk.
In the sixth month of the Bingshen year (1656), he manifested illness. On the morning of the twenty-sixth day, he said to the assembly, "Last night I dreamed that a divine monk came to welcome me;
could this be the same one who ascended Mount Yuping with me? At the hour of Xu (7–9 p.m.), he suddenly saw banners and canopies filling the sky and lotus flowers carpeting the ground.
He immediately sat cross-legged with palms joined and recited the name of Amitābha Buddha more than a hundred times before passing away peacefully.

A wondrous fragrance filled his funerary chamber. Jugu was a native of Wuxi; he tirelessly instructed others through the samādhi of buddha-recitation. In the Jihai year of the Shunzhi era, he manifested illness.

He bathed at the appointed time and put on only a single sandal, secretly manifesting his intention to return to the West. Having finished reciting the *Amitābha Sūtra*, he chanted the name of Amitābha Buddha ten times.
Raising his brush, he wrote these large characters: "Vast and empty is the numinous void; there is no place of coming or going.
He then cast down his brush and passed away.
His posthumous name was Dazhen. He left home as a youth at Lianju Hermitage in Wulin and received the Dharma from Master Shaojue.
While practicing the *pratyutpanna-samādhi*, at the time of his death, his disciples all saw him together in a dream. Devas filling the sky held incense and flowers and proclaimed:
"We welcome the Great Master to be reborn in the Western Land. When dawn broke, the disciples gathered to await him;
the Master’s body was healthy, and they conversed with him as usual while he recited the Buddha's name. After three days had passed, he suddenly sat in meditation and passed away.

Lingu Gu was a native of Shaoxing. He resided on the western border of Luoshan. Wearing tattered robes and hempen sandals, he exhorted people solely that the recitation of the Buddha’s name was their essential duty.
At the time of his death, he saw white clouds standing still as the Buddha came to welcome him, whereupon he passed away. The local people subsequently renamed his hermitage.
Her name was Baiyun (White Clouds).
Her secular surname was Qiao, and she was a native of Changxing. She was pure and harmonious by nature; in her daily life, she did not become angry when reviled, nor did she feel joy when praised.
For several decades, she had exclusively recited the name of Amitābha Buddha. In the sixth month of the second year of the Kangxi era, she passed away without illness.
Suddenly, he bound himself within a grass hut. On the sixth day of the ninth month, he entered the hut and passed away while sitting in the lotus posture.
Benchong was a native of Hangzhou who resided at Zhangjiasi Temple; he had long been dedicated to the Dharma seat, guiding the ignorant masses.
In the ninth month of the eleventh year of the Kangxi era, he manifested illness and announced his end. After a short while, he revived and said to the assembly: "In my daily life, I lacked..."

Regarding his practice of mindfulness of the Buddha, he said, "From now on, I shall have no sitting place. You all should assist me in reciting the Buddha's name. The assembly then joined their palms and chanted together.
After some time had passed, he passed away.

His posthumous name was Guangzhi. A native of Kuaiji, he retired from secular life and built a thatched hut at Huangjin Cave on Mount Tiantai, where he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land cultivation.
Yin Tiancheng of Wushan in Suzhou visited Mount Tiantai to provide a meal for the monastics; impressed by the Master’s spiritual conduct, he invited him to reside at Jieyin Hermitage on Wushan.
There he remained for over thirty years, guiding and transforming others according to their capacities, directing them toward rebirth in the Pure Land. Many followed him and received [his teachings].

Those who returned to the precepts numbered over a hundred. He once established a period for reciting the Buddha’s name, continuing day and night without the sound ever ceasing. His disciples built a shrine there;
upon seeing the place where their master had practiced walking meditation (*caṅkrama*), they saw the words "Amitābha Buddha emits golden light" inscribed in large characters.

Astonished, they questioned the master about it. The master said, "This is simply the manifestation of your own original radiance. On the full moon of the fourth month in the twenty-sixth year of the Qianlong era.
He requested four disciples to go to the hermitage to make offerings to the Buddha. Upon their departure, he said, "You should come to see me off tomorrow before noon.
When the appointed time arrived, the assembly gathered; they burned incense, recited the *Amitābha Sūtra*, and chanted the Buddha’s name a thousand times. He then sat upright and passed away.
Shiding Haowenxue was a native of Shanghai. He formerly presided over Chan Yuan Temple on Mount Tianmu. Later, he arrived at Wensheng Pavilion in Suzhou.

Having thoroughly penetrated the source of the Dharma, he responded to circumstances to benefit sentient beings with unhindered wisdom and eloquence. At that time, for the sake of students, he advocated the practice of the Buddha-remembrance (nianfo) method, composing a verse on nianfo which says:
"Remind yourself of the Buddha; remind yourself of your own mind. The essence of mindfulness is fundamentally empty and still. When... (text ends)

He contemplated that there is nothing upon which to rely; in every moment of mind, there is no Buddha separate from it. He also said: "The Western Pure Land is opened; do not be stained by worldly sentiments.

On the path ahead there is no one who knows you; you must travel alone. Furthermore, he once composed one hundred and eight poems on the Pure Land, extensively expounding the principle of "mind-only" and universally exhorting people to give rise to the mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). In the forty-first year of the Qianlong era...
He returned to Xiangshan Temple in Jiangyin. At the end of the year, he fell ill. On the third day of the first month of the following year, he entrusted his final affairs to others.

At dusk, he sat up, called the assembly together, and ordered hot water to be prepared. After washing his hands twice, he repeatedly recited the name of Amitābha Buddha and, after speaking a verse, passed away.
Shi Yuanming, surnamed Fu An, was a native of Suzhou. At over thirty years of age, he entered the Tianzhu Hermitage at Shangjin Bridge to become a monk.
Subsequently, he resided at the Great King Temple by the northern moat, making the recitation of the Buddha’s name his daily practice.

Whenever he received money, he would immediately purchase incense and flowers to offer to the Buddha and release fish and birds. In the forty-first year of the Qianlong era, he fell ill. Three days before his passing, he sent away his disciples.
He went to Shilin Temple and requested monks to perform the Pure Land Repentance ritual and a single session of the *śrāddha* (offering of food).
When the period was complete, he withdrew from the assembly, recited the names of the Buddhas, burned three incense sticks, and at noon, saying "I am going," he sat upright and passed away.
Master Luting, whose name was Jiuhui, was a native of Jia County. He received the Dharma from the elder Wenxue.
His spiritual acumen was swift and sharp; he once presided over Chan Yuan Monastery and later went to Wenshengge in Suzhou.

He stated that while at Xifang Hermitage on Mount Tianmu, he cultivated the samādhi of buddha-remembrance (*nienfo*), such that the sounds of the wind, the water, the birds, and the insects all became the chanting of the Buddha’s name.
He chanted the Buddha’s name while remaining in seclusion behind closed doors, composing a verse that said:

"I sever the path of birth and death for those in the world, And open a separate realm beyond this mundane sphere. I know not whose footstep is firm; Casting aside body and mind, one enters this gate.
In the forty-sixth year of the Qianlong era, he suffered from diarrhea and spoke to his precept-disciple, Shen Jingfu, saying: "Day and night, ten thousand recitations of Amitābha."
Each sound flowed forth from his own breast; only then did there arise a slight degree of resonance.
How could one have the leisure to speak? He spoke of idle matters and managed trivial affairs. He then instructed his attendant to prepare hot water for a bath. The following day, he passed away.

Xiangfeng Dawa was a native of Wumen. In the winter of the fifty-sixth year of the Qianlong era, while he was in retreat at Wensheng Pavilion practicing the *nienfo* samādhi, he dreamed one night that three people entered his room and sat facing south.
One wore monastic robes, flanked by two laymen (*upāsaka*), their countenances solemn and dignified.
A white light shone above them, covering their heads. Dawa prostrated himself and asked the Great Virtuous One, "From what place have you come?"

[The Master] said, "Are you still speaking falsely? [The disciple] said, "I am truly not speaking falsely. The Master said, "All sentient beings take the false for the true and cling to the provisional as real;
therefore, they undergo the cycle of rebirth. If there were one with wisdom who knew these things to be empty and false, there would be no cycle of rebirth.
Do not lose yourself in delusion regarding your own fundamental true mind. You should know that the true mind is mindless, and true knowing is without [subjective] knowing."
"Awareness is the absence of awareness; therein lies both the demon and the Buddha. You should believe and accept this; do not harbor doubt.

The text continues with an awakening statement: "This is truly the inconceivable Dharma of the Buddha. He asked again, "Since you have come from the land of the Buddha, have you ever seen Amitābha Buddha?
The person on the left replied, "I have told you before, but you ultimately did not believe me. You must..."
He saw them with his own eyes. Only then did the three men rise together and, each placing their hands upon the crown of Mañjuśrī’s head, recite a verse:
"One should be diligent and energetic, cultivating all pure deeds; when the cause is deep, the fruit is substantial—be careful not to give rise to doubt. They spoke again:
"All phenomena arise from the mind; all phenomena cease within the mind. The nature of the mind is originally empty; grasping and rejecting are unattainable. He further said:
"The arising of the Buddha-mind and its dharmas is like the objects within a dream, like the samādhi of illusion. You have already understood a small portion of this.
When the verse ended, he immediately ascended into the air and departed toward the west. From the sky, the sounds of music were clear and resonant. This occurred at dawn.

Upon awakening, this dream serves two purposes: first, it enables those who cultivate pure karma to understand the ultimate truth—that there is thought within non-thought and birth within non-birth—and thus, without lingering on the middle path, they proceed directly to the precious realm.

Second, it allows those of reckless Chan to realize that there is the single gateway of the Pure Land, thereby inspiring them to seek supreme bodhi and practice the illusion-like samādhi, so that they may become true eyes for the Lotus School.

The nun Jingyin was a person of great brilliance whose aspirations were set upon pure cultivation. She vowed to be reborn in the Pure Land. Whenever she entered her chamber to perform prostrations and recitations, she would first don clean robes and hold aloeswood incense in her mouth.
Emperor Wen’s consort held her in high esteem. On the day of her death, the assembly suddenly smelled the fragrance of aloeswood filling the entire room.
Suddenly, a radiance like a cloud appeared, dimly fading away toward the west.
Fasheng resided at Daochang Temple in Jinling, where he practiced the visualization of the Sixteen Contemplations. One night, while prostrating before an image, he fell asleep due to illness;
he saw the Great Being (Mahāsattva) riding upon a cloud of various flowers, emitting precious-colored light, coming forward to welcome him. At that time, the nuns were [in attendance].

When Sengmen went to inquire after his illness, he saw radiant light bursting forth and overflowing everywhere. Sengsheng said, "The Buddha and the Bodhisattvas have emitted their light to deliver me," and having finished speaking, he passed away.
Daoyuan was a native of Danyang who, prior to this, had commissioned seven large statues for various purposes, striving to make them as exquisitely beautiful as possible. He also cast...
He fashioned an image of Amitāyus Buddha out of gold and copper. Suddenly, from between its eyebrows, it emitted a great radiance, and the ground became entirely golden.
The image then granted him a prediction, saying: "When you cast off this body, you shall surely be born in my land. He then sat upright before the image and passed away.

Dharmarakṣa resided in Jinling, where he applied himself with diligence to the practice of Buddha-recollection. During the night, he saw Buddhas and Bodhisattvas come to console him, their radiance illuminating the monastery.
He then suddenly passed away.
Jingzhen resided at Jixian Temple in Chang’an. Wearing patched robes, he begged for his food and recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* one hundred thousand times.
He was single-mindedly devoted to the practice of nianfo (reciting the Buddha’s name). He told his disciples, "Within this fifth month, I have seen the Buddha ten times.

On two occasions, I saw children playing upon precious lotus flowers in the Pure Land. I have already attained rebirth in the highest grade. Having said this, he sat cross-legged and passed away amidst auspicious omens.
Guangman Temple.

Wuxing resided on Mount Lu and practiced the recitation of the Buddha’s name, vowing to seek rebirth in the Pure Land. Suddenly, he heard music from the air and said to those around him, "I have attained rebirth in the Middle Grade.
I see that all my fellow practitioners who were diligent in their recitation of the Buddha's name each have a lotus flower; they shall be born there."
In the jeweled pond, she waited for her rebirth. Having finished speaking, she passed away.

Nengfeng was a person from Qiantang who specialized in the practice of Pure Land Buddhism. She often dreamed that the Buddha’s light shone upon her body, or heard various nuns speak words of virtuous inspiration.
One day, without illness, she told her disciples: "When the time comes for my rebirth, wait for a short while until you hear Feng..."
Hui recited the Buddha’s name with a forceful, urgent voice as he hurried there to look; he found [the deceased] sitting facing west with palms joined, having passed away.

A wondrous fragrance filled the room, and the sound of music drifted toward the west. Hui’an resided at the Yang family hermitage by Xiaxi in Shiming. He was a disciple of Da Kuai Yao Ying and others.

He specialized in the Western [tradition] and recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* without altering his practice regardless of cold or heat. He often sat within his room, illuminated by the light of a Buddha’s radiance.
One day, he manifested illness; sitting upright, he moved his hand back and forth and instructed the assembly not to make noise. After some time, he said:
The Buddha arrived. He instructed the assembly to recollect the Buddha, and in an instant, he passed away.
His lifespan was ninety-six years. Wuwei was the daughter of the Li family from Xiaoshan; from her youth, she vowed not to marry. She maintained a vegetarian diet and recited the Buddha’s name.

At the age of twenty, she shaved her head and lived in a thatched hut, where she devoted herself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land for thirty years. Later, she traveled to various regions to study under different masters. In every place she visited, there were those suffering from illness.

He would take [the medicine] according to the specific ailment; by boiling it in water and drinking it, one would immediately be cured. During the Jiajing era, there was a widespread epidemic within the palace that reached the imperial court by rumor.

He was summoned, and his treatments proved effective. Consequently, he was bestowed with the title "Chan Master Wuweixin" (Master of Non-Action Mind) and sent back to his former dwelling. When he was about to pass away, he said:
A divine monk came seeking lodging. Wude refused him repeatedly, but the divine monk exhorted and admonished him until he finally allowed him to stay temporarily.
As Wude was waking from sleep on his meditation seat, he did not realize it was the divine monk who had been there. The divine monk then rose and sat up, reciting a verse:

"After sixty-four years of worldly life, today I cast aside my burden and return to the West. Having attained the samādhi of Bodhi, I am once again amidst the bright moon and clear breeze," and then he vanished.
A single mass of *śarīra* relics was cremated and enshrined in a stupa on Guanshan.
His original name was Qisong; he was a native of Wuxian. Having suffered from many illnesses since childhood, he made a vow to leave the household life at the age of twenty-five.

His parents sent him to the Yuantong Hermitage within the city, where he shaved his head and subsequently received full ordination. He purchased several rooms to dwell in, naming it Guanhuan (Contemplating Illusions).

His observance of the precepts was pure and clear, and he diligently cultivated meritorious deeds. He visited various famous monasteries, making offerings to the Buddhas and providing meals for the Sangha, dedicating the merit toward rebirth in the Pure Land.
In the eighth month of that year, returning from Mount Jiuhua, he established a retreat to perform the Great Compassion Repentance.

Scarcely two weeks had passed when he suddenly felt a slight illness and said, "Are my life-conditions coming to an end? He then ceased his ritual repentances and concentrated solely on reciting the Buddha’s name.
By the beginning of the tenth month, he lay upon his bed for seven days, reclining on his right side facing west, reciting the Buddha’s name without interruption.
Thereafter, he gave instructions regarding his final affairs and commanded his disciples to recite the *Amitābha Sūtra*. When they had completed three cycles, he passed away in silence.

Suqin Hao Yuecheng was a native of Wuxi. He entered the monastic life at the age of nine. Upon reaching maturity, he encountered a nun who inspired him to single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name, doing so without interruption whether walking or standing.
He subsequently resided at the Baiyi Hermitage in Nanyuan, Suzhou, where he renovated the halls and pavilions;
his practice of nianfo became even more earnest. At the age of fifty, he first received full ordination, continuing until he reached fifty-five in the fiftieth year of the Qianlong era.
In the third year, on the third month, at the first crowing of the cock, he summoned his disciples and said, "I am about to depart. His disciples replied, "The Master has no ailment;
why do you speak such words? Thereupon they wept. The Master said, "Fools! What benefit is there in weeping for me? It is better that you take this as a true occasion to recite the Buddha’s name.
He then sat cross-legged facing west, and together with them, they chanted the Buddha’s name until the incense sticks were exhausted, at which point he passed away.

The Vinaya master styled Shengke was a native of Jiading. He lost his mother at the age of three; his grandmother took him to the Yuantong Hermitage in the city of Suzhou, where he subsequently underwent tonsure and received full ordination.
In his youth, he delighted in making prostrations to the Buddha, and as he grew older, he practiced the *Lotus Sūtra*.

Distressed by his inability to comprehend its meaning, he went in indignation to Jinshan and Chongfu in Hangzhou, where he engaged in intensive study for several winters. Upon returning, he devoted himself exclusively to cultivation.
Jingye frequently visited various famous mountains to make offerings to the Buddhas and provide meals for the monastic community.

At the age of fifty-three, he contracted a coughing illness and subsequently closed his retreat quarters, refusing to go out, with the Western Paradise as his ultimate goal. When he reached the age of sixty-four, on the full moon of the first month, he gathered all the monastics and laypeople.

They recited the Buddha’s name together. When the sun reached its zenith, he looked around at those on his left and right, exhorting them to diligent practice with words that were both intense and poignant.
He then raised his hand and called out the name of the Greatly Compassionate and Greatly Merciful Amitābha Buddha of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss;
he did this three times. He then sat in the lotus posture and passed away, while the fragrance of lotuses filled the room.

Foji (佛琦), styled Jianlin (見琳), was a native of Changzhou. From his youth, he had no desire for a household life. Upon reaching adulthood, his mother sent him outside the Chang Gate to Yuhua Monastery (雨華庵) to undergo tonsure.
He subsequently received full ordination (*upasampadā*). Later, he received the entrustment from the nun Daojian (道堅) of Chongfo Monastery (崇佛庵) within the city and succeeded her as the abbess.
He solicited over a thousand taels of gold to craft sandalwood images of the Three Holy Ones of the Western Paradise.
The statue was eight *chi* in height. Every year, they established a seven-day period for the ritual field, gathering monks of pure conduct to hold a Buddha-remembrance assembly (*nianfo hui*).

They traveled to various famous mountains to make offerings to the Buddhas and feed the Sangha, and they purchased several *mu* of land for Tianning Temple in Changzhou. In his later years, he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land.
Three days before his passing, he saw a Bodhisattva appear with two youths attending him. Some say he heard [the sound of] chrysanthemums.

There was the fragrance of flowers. The Master said, "This is the fragrance of blue lotuses. On the final day of the eighth month in the fifty-sixth year of the Qianlong era, a laywoman came to inquire after his health.
The Master had her helped up, assembled the congregation, and burned incense, chanting the name of the Buddha approximately two thousand times.
He then passed away.

*Xifang Huizheng*, Volume Two.
Commentary compiled by Ch’u-po-t’ang (Ch’ui-chang). Residing amidst the dust of the world, his conduct was exemplary.
During the leisure moments from the myriad affairs of state, the King of Wu-chang was deeply fond of the Buddha-dharma. He once said to his ministers: "I am a man..."

The Sovereign, though enjoying blessings and happiness, could not escape the suffering of impermanence—birth, old age, sickness, and death. Having heard of the Buddha-land in the West, he vowed to settle his spirit there.
Thereupon, day and night, he applied himself with diligence, recollecting the Buddha and practicing the Way, while extensively practicing charity to benefit and bring joy to sentient beings.
Every day he provided a vegetarian feast for one hundred monks; the King and his consorts personally served the food with their own hands. At that time, he invited those of renown...

The monk had inquired into and sought the sublime Dharma for over thirty years with unflagging devotion. One day, while in the palace, he beheld Amitābha Buddha and the holy assembly from the West coming to welcome him.
Various auspicious signs appeared, and he passed away while sitting upright, his countenance serene and joyful.

Liu Chengzhi, courtesy name Zhongsu, was a native of Pengcheng. He was a descendant of Liu Bang, the Prince Yuan of Chu during the Han dynasty. He was exceptionally skilled in the teachings of Laozi and Zhuangzi and had a broad mastery of the various schools of thought.
Orphaned at a young age, he served his mother with such filial piety that it became renowned. Confident in his own talent, he did not involve himself in worldly affairs.

Initially, upon leaving the plain white robes of a student, he served as a military aide (*canjun*) to a provincial governor. Xie An and Liu Yu both admired his worth and recommended him to higher office, yet he declined both offers resolutely. By nature, he was fond of...
Fuli then went to Mount Lu and devoted himself to Huiyuan with all his heart. Huiyuan said, "Your official rank is lofty;
what would you not do for it? Fuli replied, "If ruler and subject harbor mutual suspicion, why would I do such a thing?
Because Liu Yu could not bend him, he honored him with the title "Yimin" (The Relict). He was joined by Lei Cizong, Zhou Xuzhi, Zong Bing, Zhang Quan, Bi Yingzhi, and others.
When they arrived at Mount Lu, Master Huiyuan said to them, "Now that you have come here, how could you forget the journey to the Pure Land?

Chengzhi then engraved a text of vows upon a stone to commemorate the event. Subsequently, he established a separate meditation hall north of the Xilin Brook, where he cultivated his aspirations amidst poverty, diligently investigated the profound principles of the Dharma, and concurrently observed the prohibitions and precepts. Zongzhang and the others all sighed in admiration and looked up to him with reverence.

He once sent a letter to Guanzhong, engaging with Kumārajīva and Sengzhao in a detailed discussion of scriptural meanings. He composed the "Verses on the Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection" (*Nianfo Sanmei Shi*) to express his intent to practice single-minded recitation and seated meditation.
After less than half a year, while in a state of meditative concentration, he beheld the radiance of the Buddha, and the ground all around turned the color of gold.
Having practiced for fifteen years, while in the midst of his correct recitation of the Buddha's name, he beheld the light from the jade-like brow-hair (*ūrṇā-kośa*) of Amitābha Buddha.
The Buddha reached down his hand to comfort and receive him. Cheng said, "How may the Tathāgata rub the crown of my head and cover me with his robe?
Immediately, the Buddha rubbed his head and drew out his *kāṣāya* to clothe him. On another day, as he was recollecting the Buddha, he again saw himself entering a pool of seven treasures;
the lotuses were blue and white, and the water was limpid and deep. There was a person there with a halo around the neck and a *svastika* (*śrīvatsa*) emerging from the chest, pointing [at him].
The pond water said, "This is water of eight meritorious qualities; you may drink from it. Chengzhi drank the water, which was sweet and delicious.
Upon waking, he still perceived a wondrous fragrance emanating from his pores. He then comforted himself, saying, "The conditions for my rebirth in the Pure Land have arrived.
He further requested that monks recite the *Lotus Sūtra* nearly several hundred times. Later, when the monks from Mount Lu had all assembled, Chengzhi faced them...
Thus, burning incense and prostrating twice, he made this vow: "By virtue of the Bequeathed Teaching of Śākyamuni, I know that there is Amitābha Buddha.
This incense shall first be offered to Śākyamuni Buddha, next to Amitābha Buddha, and thereafter to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
It is by the merit of this sutra that I have been able to be born in the Pure Land; therefore, I pray that [all beings] may..."
