All sentient beings were born together in the Pure Land; thus he was distinct from the multitude. Facing west with palms joined, he passed away.
He instructed his son, Yong, to pile up earth for a tomb and not to use a coffin or outer casing. This was in the sixth year of the Yixi era. He was fifty-nine years of age.

Zhang Ye, courtesy name Laimin, resided in Chaisang, Xunyang. He was related by marriage to Yuanming (Tao Qian). Zhang Ye’s learning encompassed both Chinese and Buddhist traditions, and he was particularly skilled in literary composition.
By nature filial and fraternal, he ceded all his fields and houses to his younger brother and shared every delicacy with his nine branches of kin.

He was recommended as a *xiucai* by the province and served as the *gongcao* of the South Zhonglang Commandery. Following his appointment as *zhizhong* of the provincial administration, he was summoned and appointed as a *sanqi*.
He repeatedly declined appointments as a court attendant. He entered Mount Lu and relied upon Master Huiyuan, where he and Liu Rong both esteemed the practice of pure karma.

When Master Huiyuan passed away, Xie Lingyun composed a stele inscription for him and Wang Yan wrote a preface, both of whom praised him at the outset as a member of the lineage who had served its teachings for generations.
In the fourteenth year of the Yixi era, he took leave of his family, entered his room, sat upright, and passed away. He was sixty-nine years of age.
Zhou Xuzhi, whose courtesy name was Daozu, was a native of Yanmen. His father later crossed the Yangtze River and settled in Yuzhang.

At the age of eight, he lost his mother; his grief and sorrow surpassed those of a full-grown adult. At twelve, he went to Fan Ning to receive instruction, mastering the Five Classics and the Five Waijing (Five Supplements).

He was thus known as the "Ten Classics Boy. He cultivated his will in seclusion, exhaustively researching the *Laozi* and the *I Ching*. Although high officials repeatedly summoned him for office, he did not accept any appointment.

He entered Mount Lu and served Master Huiyuan, joining the Lotus Society. Believing that while the body cannot be cast aside, all other worldly entanglements should be severed, he remained unmarried for the rest of his life, wearing coarse cloth and subsisting on simple vegetarian food.
When Liu Yi was stationed at Gushu, he summoned him to serve as Commandant of the Army; later, Liu also appointed him as a Doctor of the Imperial Academy, but he declined both positions.
He wrote a commentary on the *Biographies of Eminent Recluses* by Xi Kang, establishing the correct standard for when to enter or withdraw from public service.

Commentary: During Emperor Wu of the Song dynasty’s northern expedition, the Crown Prince remained in charge of the defense of the capital. [Huiyuan] was welcomed and lodged at Anle Temple, where he entered to lecture on the *Book of Rites* for over a month before returning to the mountains.
Liu Liu, the Governor of Jiangzhou, recommended him to Emperor Wu, who summoned him as a staff member (chuan) of the Grand Commandant (Taishou). He did not accept the appointment.

After Emperor Wu ascended the throne, he summoned him to the capital and provided him with lodging outside the eastern gate. When the imperial carriage went on an excursion, the Emperor questioned him regarding the *Liji* (Rites Classic), but [Huiyuan] remained haughty and did not respond.
He could have lived long. At the age of nine, he participated in the archery contest at Ju-pu, where his analytical insights were exceptionally refined and profound;

the Emperor was greatly pleased. Someone asked him, "You are a retired scholar (*chushi*), yet you frequently attend the royal court. Why is this? He replied, "For one whose mind is already racing toward the imperial gates, the rivers and lakes become shackles.

For one whose feelings have reached a state of dualistic forgetting, even the marketplace and the court are but mountain caves. At that time, he was known as Tongyin Xian (The Recluse Who Penetrates Both).

Sheng suffered from chronic wind-paralysis and was no longer able to lecture. He subsequently moved to Mount Zhongshan to recuperate and passed away in the first year of the Jingping era at the age of sixty-seven.

Zhang Quan, courtesy name Xiushuo, was a descendant of Zhang Ye. He cherished a spirit of lofty detachment and was deeply devoted to the classics and histories. Even while plowing his fields, he would not set aside his scrolls of scripture.
When the court summoned him to serve as an Attendant-at-Large (Sanqi Changshi), he did not rise to accept the post. Yu Yue, noting his poverty, appointed him as Magistrate of Xunyang.
Zhang laughed and said, "The ancients considered a space sufficient for their knees to be a place of peace. If I were to bend my will to pursue official emolument..."

What cause for such great honor? He subsequently entered Mount Lu and relied upon Master Huiyuan, where he investigated and exhausted the depths of the Buddhist scriptures until he attained profound realization.
In the first year of the Jingping era of the Song dynasty, without any illness, he faced westward, recited the Buddha’s name, and passed away while lying peacefully. He was sixty-five years of age.

Zong Bing, courtesy name Shaowen, was a native of Nanyang. His mother was intelligent and eloquent, possessed of extensive learning and knowledge, and she instructed her sons until they all achieved success.

Zong Bing was exceptionally skilled in the lute and calligraphy, and he was particularly refined in his mastery of the profound principles (*xuanli*) of metaphysics. Both Yin Zhongkan and Huan Xuan summoned him as their secretaries (*zhubushu*), but he declined both appointments.
When Liu Yu took command of Jingzhou, he again summoned him as secretary, to which Bing replied: "I shall dwell among the hills and drink from the streams..."
He lived in the mountains for thirty years, whereupon he entered Mount Lu to build a hermitage and join Master Huiyuan’s Lotus Society.

After some time, his elder brother Zang became the Governor of Nanping and pressured him to return with him to Jiangling. There he dwelt in seclusion, transcending the mundane world; subsequently, Liu Yu summoned him as a staff member of the Grand Marshal.

He did not accept. After his two elder brothers passed away, his dependents were very numerous; he thus engaged extensively in farming. Emperor Wu issued an edict to the Governor of Nanjun to provide him with regular offerings and gifts.

When Prince Yijì of Hengyang was in Jingzhou, he personally visited his residence. Sengbing wore a horned headband and cloth garments; the Prince summoned him for an audience, but he did not prostrate.
The Prince asked, "Is it appropriate to place a gentleman such as you in a position of high emolument? He replied, "Emoluments are like autumn grasses—[they flourish for a time and then wither]."
If left for too long, it would rot. When the Song dynasty received the abdication of the throne, he was summoned to serve as a *taizi sheren* (Palace Attendant to the Crown Prince).

At the beginning of the Yuanjia era, he was summoned to serve as a *tongzhilang* (Attendant Censor). Later, when the Crown Prince was established, he was summoned to serve as a *zhongshuzi* (Junior Secretary), but he declined both appointments.

His wife, Lady Luo, also possessed lofty aspirations. Upon her death, Sengbing grieved for her excessively; however, his sorrow soon dissipated, and he said to the śramaṇa Huijian: "Death and life..."

The distinction between these states is not easily reached. Only after repeatedly reflecting upon the ultimate teaching can one finally cast off sorrow. Having a refined love for mountains and waters, he would invariably forget to return once he went there.
He traveled west to Mount Jing and Mount Wu, and south to Mount Heng; there he built a dwelling among the peaks, cherishing the aspiration of Shang Ping.
Returning to Jiangling due to illness, he sighed and said, "Old age and sickness have arrived together; I can no longer ascend the famous mountains.

I shall only clarify my mind to contemplate the Way, traveling through them while lying down. He drew maps of all the places he had visited and traveled upon his walls, saying to others, "When I play the lute and move its strings, I wish to make all the mountains resound.
He passed away in the twenty-fourth year of the Yuanjia era at the age of sixty-nine.
Lei Cizong, courtesy name Zhonglun, was a native of Nanchang in Yuzhang. He was widely learned and proficient in the Odes and the Rites.

He entered Mount Lu and joined the Lotus Society, establishing a residence to the east of Donglin Temple. In the fifteenth year of the Yuanjia era, he was summoned to the capital, where he established an academy on Mount Jilong and enrolled one hundred students.
He was appointed as a Secretariat Drafter (Gishizhong) but did not accept the post. After some time, he returned to Nanchang. Duke [Yuan Hong]... [text ends].
Your Excellency has provided a parting send-off on the road. Your letter to me, your nephew, says: "In my childhood, I already harbored far-reaching ambitions.

At the age of twenty, I took refuge at Mount Lu to serve the Śramaṇa Master. For over twenty years, I have wandered the Way and nourished myself on its spirit. Now that my profound teacher has passed away,"
Furthermore, together with you all, I returned to cultivate the ancestral graves. Dwelling in the mountains and drinking from the valleys, ten years suddenly passed.

Even now, before I am old, it is still possible to rouse my will and become a bridge for those returning to the West. From this day forward, let no matter of household affairs, great or small, concern me at all.
In the twenty-fifth year, he was summoned and appointed as an Attendant-at-the-Horse (Sanqi Changshi), but did not accept. He was again summoned to the capital and [ordered to] build...
His studio was on Zhong Mountain, which he called the "Hermitage for Summoning the Recluse.

He would frequently travel from Hualin Garden to the Yanxian Hall to lecture on the Book of Rites for the Crown Prince and various princes. That year, he passed away without illness at the age of sixty-three.
His son, Su zhi, inherited much of his father’s scholarly legacy and served as the Vice Governor of Yuzhang Commandery.

Què Gōngzé entered the White Lotus Society on Mount Lú. After he passed away, a fellow member of the society went to Bǎimǎ Temple in Luòyáng and performed a memorial service for Gōngzé during the night.
Suddenly, at that moment, the trees, forests, and temple buildings all turned the color of gold.
A voice from the air said, "I am Gue Gongze. I prayed to be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and now I have attained rebirth there.
Having spoken these words, he vanished without a trace.
Yu Xian was a native of Xinye. Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty summoned him to serve as Palace Attendant, but he did not go. Six times a day he recited the name of the Buddha.
One night, he saw a Daoist practitioner who called himself Master Yuan; he addressed Yu Xian as "Master Shangxing" and departed after bestowing upon him incense.

After four years, he wished for the Master to return, but the Master subsequently passed away into transformation. From the sky, a voice proclaimed: "Master Shangxing has already been reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).
Gao Haoxiang was a native of Dongping; he lived in seclusion behind closed doors, sitting in stillness and specializing in the recitation of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.

Within his visualization, he saw red lotuses floating upon a jade pond, yet at first he did not see the Buddha. Thereupon, he directed his whole heart toward the flowers and paid homage with reverence, gazing afar at the Buddha.
Jinrong’s countenance was radiant, its brilliance shining afar. One night, he saw a multitude of bodhisattvas coming to welcome him, and he passed away suddenly.

During the Song dynasty, Pu Sui was a man from Hengzhou who counted his recitations of the Buddha’s name using small beans until they filled thirty *shí*. He then held a vegetarian feast for celebration.
Two great bodhisattvas transformed into three monks and came to the assembly to beg for food. Pu said, "I, your disciple, vow to be reborn [in the Pure Land]."

In the west, the Master came to attend the meal, which deeply fulfilled his own aspirations. When the ceremony was concluded, he immediately beheld celestial flowers and extraordinary fragrances traveling through the air.
Not long after, Manfu sat facing west and passed away in the state of samādhi.
Li Bai, whose courtesy name was Taibai, produced a depiction of the Transformation of the Western Pure Land using gold-encrusted clay, along with a preface, which states:
"To the west of our Buddha’s Golden Heaven, where the sun sets, ten thousand billion *kṣetras* away from the Middle Kingdom, lies the World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*).
The Buddha of that land is sixty million billion *yojanas* in height; between his eyebrows, the white tuft of hair curls gracefully to the right."
It revolves like five Mount Sumerus. His eyes are clear and white like the waters of the four oceans. He sits upright preaching the Dharma, serene and eternally present.
A pond shines with golden sand; precious trees line its banks. Nets cover it everywhere, and railings are set out on all sides.
Mother-of-pearl and lapis lazuli serve as ornaments for the towers and palaces; crystal and agate illuminate the splendor of the steps and paving stones. All these are [the abodes] of the Buddhas.

It is testified that there are no empty words here. Whether one has already made the vow or has not yet made it, whether one is already destined for rebirth or has not yet reached that destiny, if one maintains focused mindfulness for seven days, one will certainly be born in that land.
One’s merit shall be boundless, so brilliant as to be difficult to name. In praise, it is said:

To the west, where the sun sets, I gaze afar upon the face of Great Compassion. The eyes are as pure as the waters of the four oceans; the body’s radiance is like a mountain of purple gold. With diligence...

I shall surely attain rebirth; therefore, it is called Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*). With jeweled nets and precious trees, celestial flowers scattered upon fragrant pavilions—these images appear as if before my very eyes.
I vow to take refuge in that sacred site (*bodhimaṇḍa*). By this ocean of merit, may there be secret protection as a bridge for crossing over.
May the sins of eighty billion kalpas be swept away like light frost by the wind. Thus, may I behold Amitāyus and forever gaze upon the light of his jade-like *ūrṇā*.

Bai Juyi was titled the Layman of Mount Xiang. Holding the office of Grand Preceptor of the Crown Prince, he initially exhorted one hundred and forty-eight people to form the "Assembly for Rebirth Above" (*shangsheng hui*).
They practiced the recitation of Maitreya’s name and meditated on Maitreya’s countenance, vowing that in a future life they would surely be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven.

In his later years, however, he suffered from wind-stroke and paralysis; consequently, he focused his resolve solely on the Western Paradise, praying for rebirth in Sukhāvatī. He thus painted a transformation tableau of the Western Pure Land.
The circumstances were identical. He made a vow, saying: "In the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, there are no evil realms nor any sufferings.
May those like my body who suffer from illness be reborn together with me in the realm of Amitāyus Buddha.
One night, while reciting the Buddha’s name upon his bed, he suddenly passed away.
Wei Wenjin was appointed as an Observation Commissioner (Guancha Shi). He established a Western Paradise ritual site (Daochang) and practiced the recitation of the Buddha's name with earnest vows.
One day, while in the midst of his recitation, he suddenly sat cross-legged facing west and passed away. A wondrous fragrance filled the room, perceived by everyone both inside and outside.
An old man from Fenyang in Bingzhou was staying overnight in a borrowed room at Faren Mountain reciting the Buddha’s name. Suddenly, a great light shone everywhere;
people saw him ascend a lotus pedestal and depart.
Zheng Muzheng was a native of Yongyang. His entire family recited the Buddha’s name. During the Kaiyuan era of the Tang dynasty, when he fell gravely ill, someone urged him to consume fish and meat;
he resolutely refused. Holding an incense burner in his hand, he prayed for rebirth in the Pure Land. Suddenly, a wondrous fragrance filled the air, and he passed away peacefully.
His maternal uncle, the Minister Su Ting, dreamed of a jeweled pond where lotuses were blooming, and upon one of them sat Muzheng.
Zhang Yuanxiang was a native of Chang’an. He constantly recited the Buddha’s name without ceasing. One day, he urged his family members, saying, "The Sage of the Western Land awaits me;
once my meal is finished, we shall go together to the Pure Land. When the meal was concluded, he indeed requested incense and candles, sat cross-legged facing west, and passed away.

Li Zhiyao was a native of Chang’an. He led a multitude in performing the Five Assemblies of Buddha-recitation (during the Dali era of the Tang dynasty, Master Fazhao established the Five Assemblies of Buddha-recitation at Hengzhou;

Li Zhiyao’s current practice of the Five Assemblies likely followed Fazhao’s model. The "Five Assemblies" presumably refers to holding one assembly every five days). Suddenly, he left the hall and prostrated toward the sky.
A voice from the air said: "I inform you, Li Zhiyao: your merit has borne fruit and you have invited this result yourself. I shall lead you to the Pure Land;
let us ascend the golden bridge together. Immediately, he sat upright upon his bed and passed away, as a fragrant celestial incense filled the air.

Ma Ziyun was a filial and upright scholar during the Tang dynasty. He served as a magistrate of Jing County. While escorting a grain transport convoy to the capital, his boat encountered a storm and sank;
he was subsequently imprisoned. Thereupon, he devoted himself single-mindedly to the recitation of the Buddha’s name. Five years later, he was released by imperial amnesty.

He then entered a mountain temple in Nanling, where he observed the practice of eating only one meal a day. Suddenly, he said to those around him: "My life has been full of misfortune, so I have diligently upheld the Inner Teachings. Now, in the West..."
His karma was fulfilled; he was destined to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang). On the following day, having bathed and donned new robes, he sat upright with palms joined.
A wondrous fragrance filled the room, and he said joyfully, "The Buddha has come to welcome me. Having finished speaking, he passed away.
During the reign of Empress Wu of the Tang dynasty, Yu Chang served as the Recorder (Lùshì) of Bingzhou. By day he adjudicated civil affairs; by night he adjudicated matters in the underworld.

He was constantly aware of impending calamities and disasters, and would secretly prepare for them without ever speaking of it. This continued for six years. Upon the death of his mother, he recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and no longer served as an official of the underworld.
When he reached the age of eighty-four and was about to pass away, he suddenly smelled a wondrous fragrance and immediately called to his left...
The man on the right said, "A sage came to welcome me to the Western Land; I immediately recited the Buddha's name and passed away.
Yuanzi was then residing at Guanyin Temple in Runzhou, where he was reciting the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* and practicing mindfulness of the Buddha. Suddenly, he fell slightly ill.
One night, he heard fragrant incense and the sound of music in the air, as if someone were saying: "The coarse music has already passed; the subtle music follows now. You shall..."
He departed; as he recited the Buddha’s name, he passed away. A wondrous fragrance did not dissipate for several days.
Yuan Ziping resided at Guanyin Temple in Jingkou, where he recited the Buddha’s name and chanted sutras. Suddenly, he heard music from the air and immediately sat facing west to pass away.
A wondrous fragrance continued without ceasing for several days.
Zhang Kang served under the Shi Jin dynasty as a Hanlin Academician. He recited the *Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī* one hundred thousand times, vowing to be reborn in the Western Paradise.
One day, while suffering from illness, he did nothing but chant the Buddha’s name. Suddenly, he said to his family members, "The Pure Land of the West is right here at the western side of this hall.
Amitābha Buddha is seated upon a lotus flower; see my father and son in the golden lotus pond."
On the sandy ground, he performed prostrations and played; after a long while, he passed away while reciting the Buddha’s name. Weng’er was his grandson.
Zhongli Jin was a native of Kuaiji and held the rank of Junior Master (Shaoshi). In his youth, he served his mother, Lady Ren. The lady had cultivated the Pure Land practices with great diligence;
at the age of ninety-eight, her daily activities remained as usual. Suddenly, she admonished Jin, saying: "Every person has their own Amitābha."
How could one cast this aside? Every thought is none other than the Land of Ultimate Bliss, yet one does not understand how to return.

The following day, as I was about to depart, he rose at dawn, burned incense, and recited the Buddha’s name more than his usual practice; then, with palms joined, he passed away. Jin performed twenty meritorious acts daily as his routine.
Later, while serving as the magistrate of Jishui, he took a concubine. When she married her daughter, he investigated the matter and found it was the daughter of a former magistrate.
The daughter informed her relatives, who suggested that the betrothal gifts be accepted slowly so that she might first be sent back to her former magistrate.
Her relatives wrote again, saying: "How can you, sir, alone maintain such high principles? I have a nephew; let us divide the dowry equally and allow him to go together to welcome the bride.

The magistrate followed this advice. Suddenly, he dreamed that his former magistrate came to thank him, saying: "Your humble son has been taken under your care; I have already reported this to the Supreme Deity. He shall attain [the rank of] a *shou* (ten-thousand)..."

There is a land in this world. Yet, after another twelve-year cycle, the Duke was destined to be born in the Pure Land. Subsequently serving as the Intendant of Zhexi, he discussed the essential points for rebirth in the Pure Land with the Master of Repentance, Ciyun.

His pure cultivation became even more earnest. Since his wife had possessed a sandalwood Buddha image which she would constantly wear upon her head while practicing the Way, the Duke followed her example.
Suddenly, several grains of *śarīra* emerged from between the eyebrows of the image. Not long after, [the Duke passed away].
While serving as the Governor of Kaifeng, he suddenly rose at midnight and said to his family, "My lady has informed me that the time for my rebirth has arrived.

He then sat in the lotus posture and passed away. On the day before, the entire household had dreamed that the official was riding upon a seat of blue lotuses, accompanied by celestial music and extraordinary fragrances, as a multitude from the sea welcomed him westward. Calculating the years, it was exactly twelve years since [the initial dream].

Zhongli Jingrong was the younger brother of the Seventh Patriarch’s son. He held the official rank of Chaoqing Dafu. He constantly recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* and never ceased his mindfulness of the Buddha.
Hanging up his official cap and abandoning his career, he built a thatched hut beside the East Garden in Yizhen. He once said: "If you recognize Amitābha, Amitābha, Amitābha;
if you do not recognize Amitābha, what can be done, what can be done? If you do not recognize Amitābha, Amitābha is even further to the west."

Beyond the mundane world, he realized Amitābha; Amitābha was found to reside only within his own home. One evening, he instructed the monk Miaoying to recite the "Chapter on the Vows of Samantabhadra.
Once the incense had been lit and the recitation completed, he formed mudrās with both hands and passed away.

From the time of Ren Shi, the Junior Grand Master, through three generations, they attained rebirth in the Pure Land. His great-grandson, Songju, resided in Wuyuan; during the Qiandao era, he served as a ritual attendant.
In Wu Commandery, he formed a religious society with his teacher Baoji and Lü Ji of Dongping to practice the recitation of the Buddha's name.
Without any illness, he suddenly sat upright facing west, joined his palms, and passed away.
Wen Lubu, whose courtesy name was Yanbo, while serving as the governor of Luoyang, once observed a fast and went to Longshan Temple.

Upon entering the hall to pay homage to the Buddha, he suddenly saw that a statue had collapsed to the ground; he showed it no sign of reverence. A monk questioned him about this, and Wen replied, "Since the statue is already broken, what benefit is there in gazing upon it?
The monk said, "The statue has neither newness nor antiquity; the Way is neither born nor extinguished. Upon hearing these words, Wen attained a realization.

Having paid his respects, he departed. Later, he attended upon Dharma Master Jingyan and vowed to assemble a gathering of one hundred thousand people for a Pure Land assembly, universally encouraging them to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
When his end approached, he passed away without illness, mindful of the Buddha as he transformed.
Su Shi was styled Dongpo. While serving as Hanlin Academician, during his banishment to the south, he painted an image of Amitābha on a single scroll and wore it with him wherever he went.
When people asked about it, he replied, "This is my birth certificate for the Western Paradise.

After his mother, Lady Cheng, passed away, he used her remaining assets—her hairpins and earrings—to commission the artisan Hu Xi to paint an image of Amitābha as an offering for her rebirth in the Pure Land. Furthermore...
Old Quan once commissioned images of the Six Bodhisattvas at Jile Temple; this was because the Su family had long been devoted to the Triple Gem.
When Dongpo was nearing death, he composed a verse: "Birth and death are like the bending and stretching of an arm;
For those like us, who cling to worldly attachments, there is but bitter sorrow. Le-tian is no longer a guest of Penglai; I rely upon the Western Paradise as my host."

Yang Jie, courtesy name Cigong, was a native of Wuyuan. He held the office of Director of the Court of State Ceremonial and traveled extensively through the Chan monasteries to seek out enlightened masters.

In his later years, he painted images of the Buddha of the Western Paradise and practiced mindfulness while traveling with them. On the day he passed away, he experienced the Buddha coming to welcome him.
He passed away while sitting upright in meditation.
Ma Liang, serving as a Palace Attendant (*shilang*), was stationed in Hangzhou; he visited Mount Ling and studied the practices of the Pure Land.

Ciyun composed for him the *Jingtu xingyuan famen* (Dharma Gate of Vows and Practices for the Pure Land) and the *Jingtu wangsheng lüe zhuan* (Brief Biography of Rebirth in the Pure Land). Upon his death, he recited the Buddha’s name and passed away.

Zi Yu, the Chao-feng, also applied himself according to the *Ten Doubts Treatise*. While serving in office, he read the Tripitaka, recited the sutras, and practiced mindfulness of the Buddha with regular daily routines.
One day, he suddenly changed his clothes, sat upright while reciting the Buddha’s name, and passed away. A vapor like a blue canopy emerged from him.
He exited his room and ascended into the air, departing toward the west. At times, auspicious light manifested from his funeral altar.

Yu’s son, Yongyi, was appointed as an Official of Propagated Doctrine; he regularly practiced the *ṣoḍaśa-bhāvanā* (Sixteen Contemplations) for thirty years. Suddenly, he saw the Three Holy Ones coming to welcome him;
he passed away while forming mudrās. His crown felt warm, and a rare fragrance filled the air.

Hu Yin, whose courtesy name was Guanyi, was the son of Minister Hu Ze. In his later years, he retired from official service and lived in carefree laughter by West Lake, where he was on very good terms with the Vinaya Master Qingzhao.
One day, falling ill, he asked the Master, "How is it that reciting the name of the Buddha once can extinguish the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas?
The Master replied, "The Buddha possesses great majestic power; when sentient beings recite [his name] even once..."
His name alone was enough to cause his karmic defilements to vanish naturally, like frost and dew before the high noon of a blazing sun. Chen Da was profoundly moved and awakened;

with single-minded devotion, he recited the Buddha’s name and invited monks to assist him. One day, when a Vinaya Master arrived, Chen Da said, "I am deeply grateful that you two Great Beings have graced me with your presence for so long.
Please perform a repentance ceremony for me and help me make vows. Suddenly, he recited the Buddha’s name with a powerful voice and passed away while sitting upright in meditation.
Ge Fan was a native of Chengjiang. Having passed the civil service examinations in his youth, he rose to the rank of Chao-san.

Whenever he occupied an official residence or a private dwelling, he would invariably adorn a pure chamber and install a Buddha image there. Every time he entered the room to perform prostrations and recite scriptures, śarīras would descend from the air.

He universally exhorted both monastics and laypeople to cultivate the karma of purity, and all submitted to his transformation. There was a monk who, while traveling through the Pure Land in meditative concentration, saw Fan together with King [Bimbisāra].
Formerly, when the Senior Secretary Wang Gu was strolling among the rows of trees by the Jewel Pond, he suddenly heard that Fan had passed away without illness.
Wang Gu was a man of true integrity; he served as the Minister of Rites and was a fellow practitioner of Chan with Huitang and Yangqi.

He once composed the *Jiuzhi Jingtu Jueyi Ji* (A Collection for Resolving Doubts Regarding the Direct Pointing to the Pure Land), for which Yang Jie wrote a preface. He also augmented and supplemented the *Wangsheng Jingtu Zhuan* (Biographies of Those Who Attained Rebirth in the Pure Land); both works...
He lived in the world with his usual aspirations set on rebirth in the Western Paradise. At the time of his death, he experienced no suffering;
suddenly, the entire room was filled with radiance, and he passed away while sitting upright. There were those who dreamed that he mounted a lotus flower and departed toward the west.
Jiang Gongwang was a native of Diaotai who served as an Imperial Censor. Having passed the imperial examinations in his youth, he maintained a vegetarian diet and practiced pure cultivation.

He composed the *Bodhi Treatise* and the *Expedient Means of Buddha-Recitation* to exhort both the clergy and the laity. His son died prematurely and appeared in a dream to his maternal uncle, saying:
"I wish to petition you, my lord, to request that we attend the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* at Tianning Temple; by this merit, I may be reborn in a favorable realm. My lord, please practice [this].

He practiced until his achievements were complete. In the underworld, there was a golden plaque that read: "Jiang Gongwang of Yanzhou, though dwelling in wealth and honor, aspired to the truth of suffering and emptiness.
He personally engaged in cultivation and meditation; his mind was free from attachment. Whether in motion or stillness, he never forgot the Buddha-Dharma."
In his speech and discourse, he never deviated from the ancestral style; by name, he was already liberated from the dark barriers of the underworld. His body would surely return to the Pure Land.
At the end of the Xuandao era, while serving as the Prefect of Guangde Commandery, one morning he passed away without illness, sitting upright facing west.
The King resided at Gushan on Qiantang, the former site of Lin Hejing. Living in seclusion to his heart’s content, he was summoned as a recluse during the Zhenghe era;

the court subsequently conferred upon him the title of Chushi (Retired Scholar). Later, his official rank reached that of Chaosan Dafu. He devoted himself deeply to the Pure Land practice and attained profound realization.
Daily, he recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* seven times and chanted the Buddha’s name ten thousand times. This continued for nineteen years without ceasing.
He had occasionally withdrawn from worldly affairs. One day, without prior illness, he bathed, faced west, sat in the lotus posture, and passed away.

Zhang Di resided in Qiantang and served as an Assistant Professor (*Jiàozhù*). He received the Bodhisattva precepts from Vinaya Master Yuanjing and inquired about the dharma-gates of Pure Land practice.
He vowed by burning his arm as incense; whenever he recited the Buddha’s name, he did so with a loud and courageous voice, continuing even until his voice failed.
This continued for some time. One day, he said to Yuanjing, "Recently, while in my meditation chamber, I saw a white *piṅgala* bird fluttering and dancing before me.
Furthermore, within my visualization, I saw an infant with green hair joining his palms in greeting. Three years later, he passed away while facing west in mindfulness of the Buddha.
Jia Chunren was a native of Xichuan. He served as the Vice Prefect of Yingzhou. He devoted his heart to the pure practices of Buddhism, maintaining a lifelong fast and reciting the Buddha’s name.
Due to a slight illness, he sat facing west in meditative composure and passed away. A circular halo of white light appeared upon the crown of his head, and a wondrous fragrance filled the room.
Mei Ruren was a native of Changshu. He served as a district magistrate and had long harbored aspirations for the practice of Pure Land Buddhism.

One night, he suddenly dreamed that a monk gave him a hundred sheets of paper, which he tore into sixteen pieces of eight characters each. He asked Master Dongling Zhao about this, and the master said, "Two eights make sixteen;
could this not refer to the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (The Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations)? Just then, another monk appeared and handed him the sutra, but suddenly vanished. From that point on...
This recitation of sutras and mindfulness of the Buddha is termed "rebirth" (wangsheng), as evidenced by your own intent.

Because Master Daosheng of Poshan in your district had fashioned a sixteen-foot image of Amitābha, you were able to contribute one million coins to adorn it and to provide offerings for a vegetarian feast and repentance ceremony.
Before the hall, a single double-headed white lotus grew from the pond; its flower had a hundred petals. That very winter, you—
He was able to pass away peacefully and without illness. Not long after, Daosheng also died.
Feng Jia was a native of Suining; he styled himself the Layman Budong (Immovable). Having passed the examinations at the Imperial Academy, he initially sought the Way within the Zen forests.

In his later years, he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism. He composed liturgical texts for the Western Paradise and a ritual manual for the *Maitreya* (Amitābha) Repentance.

Upon returning to his native district, he established a Pure Land assembly (*jìngtǔ huì*). Therein, he experienced a white light extending to the heavens from within the incense burner, and śarīra relics manifested as auspicious signs.

During the military calamities of the Jìngkāng era, many scriptures stored at famous mountains were destroyed by fire. He pooled his accumulated stipends to produce forty-eight sets of the *Mahāpiṭaka* (Great Canon) and four sets of the *Kṣudrapiṭaka* (Small Canon).

The sections also comprise forty-eight collections (*piṭaka*). He fashioned a sandalwood image of Amitābha for rebirth through the nine grades of transformational birth (*upapāduka*), which he personally venerated and made offerings to.
Later, serving as a Court Attendant (*shigongshi*), he went to the region south of Lu. There, he led both monastics and laypeople to hold a *xiannian* (mindfulness) assembly.

Upon being stationed in Changsha, he arranged a high seat within the main hall; donning monastic robes, he ascended the seat, expressed his gratitude to the officials, and rested his staff crosswise upon his knees.
Above, there was Hua Ruzi Cai, whose courtesy name was Xinsou. A native of Suzhou, he studied together with his disciple Zhang under Yunwu, receiving the Dharma-gate of *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation).
He practiced with unceasing diligence. After Ruzi Cai retired from official service, he prepared a coffin in advance and slept within it at night.
He had the youth strike the coffin and sing: "O Wu Xinsou, return! In the three realms there is no peace;
one cannot dwell therein. The Western Pure Land has the lotus womb; Hurry back home before it is too late. Wu himself followed along, singing in harmony with him.
One day, he instructed his family members to listen quietly to the air, and they heard the sound of celestial music. He then said, "I have lost mindfulness and come here from the Pure Realm.
Now that the golden platform has arrived, I shall depart. Having spoken these words, he passed away.
Qian Xiangzu’s monastic residence in Tiantai was named Zhian (Cessation Hermitage).
While serving as the governor of Jinling, he sought the Way from Bao-ning Chan Master Quan Wuyong and took the authentic practice of the Pure Land as his primary concern.

He once established ten reception centers throughout his native prefecture, all of which were named after the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. He also founded the High Monks’ Quarters at Zhian as a place for inviting monks to discuss the Way.

After the Left Minister resigned and returned home, he devoted himself even more to the practice of pure karma (*śukla-karman*). In the second month of the fourth year of the Jiading era, he suffered a slight illness and wrote a verse, saying:
"The fragrance of the lotus comes from the Buddha-land; Upon the ground of lapis lazuli, not a speck of dust remains.
My mind is pure and transcends that realm; Today I know from afar that one flower has blossomed. Two days later, when a monk came to inquire after his health, the Master said, "I am no longer..."
He felt no greed for life, nor did he fear death; he was not reborn in the heavens, nor did he become a human, but sought only birth in a Pure Land.
Having finished speaking, he sat in the full lotus posture and passed away. At that time, celestial drums resounded and a wondrous fragrance wafted through the air.

Before his end, his sons, nephews, and the people of the district all dreamed together that a voice from the sky proclaimed: "The Minister Qian shall be born in the Western Lotus Palace as the Bodhisattva Ciji."

Wang Zhonghui was a man from Wuwu who served as a *canshen* (participating military officer) in the Ministry of Justice. Through Yang Jie, he was taught the Dharma of the Pure Land, and his practice of mindfulness of the Buddha (*nianfo*) progressed further.
Seven days before his death, he took leave of his old friends and passed away while sitting upright. At that time, Yang Jie was serving in Danyang;
he dreamed that Zhonghui returned to thank him, saying, "I previously received your instruction, and now I have attained rebirth in the Pure Land," after which he bowed twice and departed.

Shortly thereafter, news arrived that Zhang Yu, the Regional Commander-in-Chief of the Two Zhe Circuits, had passed away. He had vowed to be reborn in the Pure Land and exerted himself with diligence in the recitation of the Buddha’s name.

All members of his household, both old and young, followed his transformation. They excavated a pond and planted lotuses; every day he led his wife and children in reciting the Buddha’s name ten thousand times. Emperor Xiaozong...
The Emperor personally inscribed the two characters "Lian-she" (Lotus Society) and bestowed them upon him.
Lu Yuan’s religious name was Sheng’an; he resided at Hengxi in Ming. Rising at dawn, he burned incense and sat in meditation with his eyes fixed, not glancing elsewhere.
He first chanted this verse: "Washing my hands at the break of day, the *palm-leaf* scrolls unfold. I seek no blessings, nor do I avert calamities. The world..."

When the conditions for his departure were severed, he withdrew from others. He performed a single dance amidst the fires at the end of the kalpa, and thereafter recited his mantras, neither too slowly nor too hurriedly, with a voice like a string of pearls.
Every day he recited the Lotus Sūtra once and the name of Amitābha ten thousand times, his mind solely directed toward the West.
At the age of eighty-five, he bathed, adjusted his robes, and passed away. Upon his enshrouding, the fragrance of lotus flowers was suddenly perceived; everyone [perceived it].
He did not know where it had come from; upon drawing near to examine it, he found it was emerging from his mouth.
Wang Rixiu was a native of Longshu and a national university jinshi. He authored several hundred thousand words of commentaries and exegeses on the Six Classics.
One morning he renounced them all, saying: "These are all merely habitual karmic tendencies; they are not the ultimate Dharma. I shall instead seek my return to the Western Land.
Thereupon, he wore simple clothing and ate coarse vegetables, contemplating only the Buddha. He performed a thousand prostrations daily and slept only at the final watch of the night.

He once composed ten volumes of *Writings on the Pure Land*, which were concise, clear, and straightforward; those who read them could not help but be moved to faith and submission. One night, he recited the name of the Buddha with a resolute voice.
After a long time, he suddenly said, "The Buddha has come to receive me," and he passed away while standing upright. The local people dreamed that a young boy led him away toward the west.
Fan Zhu died suddenly and entered the underworld; the King of the Underworld said, "According to the register of good deeds, you once exhorted an elderly man to recite the name of the Buddha."

"He has already attained rebirth in the Pure Land. By virtue of this merit, you too ought to attain rebirth there. Zhi said, "I still wish to recite ten thousand scrolls of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
He was then released and sent back. Later, he fulfilled his vow; at the time of his death, he manifested extraordinary signs, not deviating from his prior prediction.
Sun Bian was a native of Wulin. He styled himself the Layman Without Dispute (*Muzheng Jushi*). In his youth, he studied the *Yi* (Book of Changes), whereupon he remarked:

"The *Yi* is for the purpose of exhausting principle and perfecting one's nature; why must one be preoccupied with schemes for advancement? He closed his door to hide his traces, living apart from worldly affairs. The śramaṇa Shouning befriended him and said to him:
"Bai Juyi cultivated himself through Confucianism and regulated his nature through Buddhism. You have heard of this, have you not?"
"Is it so? Bi deeply resonated with the monk’s words. Daily he read the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Vajracchedikā*, and the *Amitābha Sūtra*.
He once dreamed that he reached a lotus pond and stood beside Qingzhao and Vinaya Master Heng. Again, he dreamed of a person holding a book with golden characters in Sanskrit script;
though he could not understand what was written, the person said, "I merely ask that you observe a fast on the thirteenth day. On the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, suddenly—
He fell ill and invited Master Miaoguang to perform prayers for his recovery. Huan said, "Birth and death are already predetermined; why pray for them?
He then instructed him on the principles of rebirth in the Pure Land. Thereupon, he assumed the full lotus posture, formed the mudrā, and sat facing west to pass away.

The following day, Qingzhao arrived to place [the remains] in the sarcophagus. He returned to his hermitage and passed away while seated after three days; this seems to correspond to the prophecy regarding the establishment of the Lotus Pond.
Wang Tian was a native of Cixi in Siming; he styled himself the "Old Man of No Merit" (Wugong Sǒu). Regarding all the fundamental tenets of the Chan school and the teachings of the Tiantai school...
There was nothing he did not thoroughly penetrate. He authored the *Jingtu Zixin Lu* (Record of Self-Confidence in the Pure Land) to clarify the principles of the three bodies and four lands.

In his later years, he devoted himself exclusively to the recitation of the Buddha’s name. Facing west in the full lotus posture, he passed away amidst a fragrance that filled the room. When his coffin was cremated, one hundred and eight grains of śarīra, the size of soybeans, were recovered.
Sun Zhong was a native of Siming. He maintained a vegetarian diet and observed the precepts, having long admired the Western Pure Land.

To the east of the prefectural city, he built a hermitage and excavated two ponds, planting white lotuses therein. He constructed a pavilion overlooking the pond and gathered monastics and laypeople monthly to recite the Buddha’s name for a period of three days.
Later, while ill, he requested a hundred monastics and laypeople to focus their mindfulness upon him; suddenly, looking up into the void, he joined his palms in greeting and raised his hand—
He formed the double mudrā and passed away with a serene countenance. The entire city heard the sound of celestial music and the scent of extraordinary incense; he gradually vanished toward the west.
His two sons followed in succession, reciting the Buddha’s name as they sat and passed away. Once, while reciting the Buddha’s name, they saw the Buddha’s body appear in the sky.

They immediately addressed the Buddha, saying, "We pray only that our Buddha will pause for a moment, so that we two sons may together obtain the honor of beholding you. They then ran outside to seek their two [parents].
When the Master returned home, the Buddha stood waiting for him for a long while. Later, people named the place "Zhufu Xiang" (Buddha’s Waiting Lane).

Zan Dingguo, whose courtesy name was Shengzhai, served as a lecturer at the prefectural school. He constantly recited the Buddha's name and read various sutras on the Pure Land, establishing a "Western Rebirth Society" to encourage others.
At the beginning of the Jiatai era, he built the Pure Land Temple at Huiguang in Xiaojiang and constructed a stone pagoda.

At the center of the pond was the site where the bones of a local villager who had been burned by fire were enshrined. He printed and distributed images for the practice of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation).
Every second and eighth day of the month, he gathered monastics and laypeople at Jingtuyuan to chant the *Amitābha Sūtra* and recite the Buddha’s name, making this a regular practice.

In the fourth year of the Jiading era, he dreamed that a youth in blue robes told him, "The Buddha has sent for you; on the third day, you shall be reborn in that land. On that day, he bathed and changed his clothes.
He passed away while sitting upright in mindfulness of the Buddha.

Lou Fen hailed from the Zhumin (Distinguished Achievement) clan of Siming, a family of great renown. Because of his elder brother Baozhou, he thoroughly investigated and clarified the principles of the Buddha-dharma.

Whenever he discussed the Way with śramaṇas, Fen would invariably sit by his side, listening with joy. At the age of twenty-two, he suddenly fell ill; thereupon, he resolved his will entirely upon the West.
He returned and said to his parents, "To be born in the Pure Land and see the Buddha—this path is the most supreme.

He further instructed them to invite monks to preach the Dharma for his guidance and to recite the *Amitābha Sūtra*. He set up an image of the Buddha opposite his bed and said with joy, "This is truly my teacher.

He again requested the monks to recite the Buddha’s name one thousand times, whereupon he declared, "I am already in the Western Land," and then closed his eyes, facing west, and focused his mind on the Buddha.
The Buddha manifested a transformation.
Wei Shizi (Wei Shizi) was a native of Liang Commandery during the Song dynasty. He served the Buddha with diligent devotion, though his wife alone did not believe.

When their daughter fell ill and died, she revived again on the seventh day. She immediately ascended a high seat and recited the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*. Upon descending, she addressed her father, saying: "I am leaving; I shall now go."
"In the Land of Immeasurable Life, the son, along with his father and elder brother, already has large lotus flowers within the pond where they shall be reborn;

only the mother alone has none. Unable to bear this grief, she has returned to inform you. Having finished speaking, she fell silent once more. From that time on, the mother also came to believe in the teachings of the Dharma.
Ge Zhi was a native of Juong County and the grandson of Ge Zhizhuan; consequently, his family had served the immortals for generations.
His wife, surnamed Ji, maintained her sincerity in the Buddha-dharma without ceasing day or night. While she was weaving, she saw the clouds part to reveal the light of the sun.

She cast aside her shuttle and looked upward, beholding the true form of the Tathāgata of the West with banners and canopies reflecting against the sky. Her heart was filled with singular joy, and she said, "The sutras speak of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life."
Having now obtained the opportunity to behold him, she prostrated herself with her head at his feet. As she was being led away by Ji, they still saw half of his body;
suddenly, it vanished. Subsequently, the husband and wife recited the Buddha’s name together and passed away one after the other.
Zuo Shen was a native of Tiantai. He received the Bodhisattva precepts from Shenzhao.

He carved images of the Three Sages and recited the Lotus Sūtra three thousand four hundred times and the Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra twenty thousand times. Later, while suffering from illness, he instructed his son, the śramaṇa Jingyuan, to chant the opening verses of the Lotus Sūtra and to receive the Bodhisattva precepts anew.
In a dream, three majestic figures stood on the riverbank and summoned Shen to board a boat; furthermore—
He requested a monk to recite the *Amitābha Sūtra*. Suddenly he said, "I have already seen the light of the Buddha," and immediately sat upright, formed a mudrā, and passed away.
Fan Yan was from Wulin; he had severed his ties to worldly affairs. When his son could not manage the household, Yan paid it no mind, saying only, "I am merely a guest here.
He recited the *Lotus Sūtra* daily and invoked Amitābha Buddha with single-minded devotion and without slackening.
Suddenly, he saw Samantabhadra Bodhisattva riding a six-tusked white elephant and emitting golden light.
The Bodhisattva informed Yan, saying, "At the hour of the rabbit tomorrow, you shall be reborn in the Pure Land. After one night had passed, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas came to welcome him.
His family heard him humbly declining, saying, "Who is this person? He is truly difficult to withstand. Then, sitting upright with palms joined, he passed away.
Yan Bangrong was a native of Chizhou. Encouraged by a monk to cultivate the Western Paradise, he recited the *Jueding wangsheng zhou* (Dhāraṇī for Certain Rebirth).
Every morning, facing west, he would recite it a thousand times, sometimes leading a group in its recitation. He continued this practice for twenty years.

In the spring of the first year of the Shaohui era, he suddenly smelled a wondrous fragrance that did not dissipate for several days. That night, his family members dreamed that two youths dressed in blue robes were standing in attendance beside Bangrong.
Beside him, his son again dreamed that Amitābha emitted light that illuminated the entire hall, turning everything into gold.

For several days, he sat cross-legged facing west reciting the Buddha’s name. Suddenly he rose and said, "I am going. After walking a few steps, he extended his hand, formed a mudrā, and with a smile, passed away while standing.

Yao Yue lived by Xiantan in Zechuan. He devoted himself to the inner scriptures (Buddhist texts). Whenever a monk came to visit him, he would invariably yield the seat of honor to the east, believing that a layperson should not take precedence over a monastic.
Master Juehai You encouraged the villagers to form a society for the practice of Pure Land Buddhism, and Yao Yue took charge of the actual organization of the matter.
Suddenly, he told Master You, "I have long grown weary of this fleeting life; I shall depart for the West before long. You may assist me."
Yue focused his mindfulness on this. His friend subsequently recited the mantra with him every day. One day, while sitting in meditation, Yue passed away.
Shortly thereafter, he appeared in a dream to his friend and said, "I have already been reborn; this is due to the power of the Master. The friend asked, "May I follow you to that realm?

Yue replied, "The Master's worldly lifespan is not yet exhausted. Jingyi of the temple shall go there first. A month later, Jingyi indeed passed away; he was a fellow member of the same religious society.
Shen Quan was a native of Qiantang. Together with his wife, Shi, he devoted himself single-mindedly to the Pure Land. He dedicated all his ordinary acts of merit toward this goal.
Later, both husband and wife passed away; on each occasion, they were moved by the appearance of a transformation Buddha holding a monk’s staff, who came to welcome and lead them away.
Mei Fu was a native of Songjiang. He recited the sutras and observed the precepts, constantly directing his mindfulness toward the Pure Land.

Knowing the time of his death was imminent, he immediately ceased eating and took only water, while reciting the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. On the seventh day, he bathed, changed his robes, and sat upright.
Addressing the assembly, he said, "Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva has now come to welcome me," and he passed away from his seat.
Sūn Liángjiā was from Qiántáng. He lived in seclusion and studied the Great Canon (*Mahāpiṭaka*), attaining a profound mastery of the essential principles of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.

He once received the Bodhisattva precepts under the Vinaya Master Dàzhì and daily recited the name of the Buddha ten thousand times, never ceasing for twenty years. Suddenly, he spoke to his family members:

He requested that the monks recite the Buddha’s name to assist him in his rebirth. At the midpoint of the day, he faced the sky with palms joined and said, "The World-Honored One and the Bodhisattvas have already graciously descended.
He then withdrew from his seat and passed away.

Hu Gao’s family resided in Zechuan. During his lifetime, he frequently performed Buddhist services. Suddenly, he dreamed that the Buddha called out to him, saying, "You may build a hall to welcome me.
Gao then went to Ming and constructed a Maitreya Pavilion (or Amitābha Hall) to fulfill this dream.
On the evening of his death, he suddenly said, "The Buddha has emitted light to illuminate me," and having finished speaking, he passed away.
Tang Shiliang was a native of Kuaiji during the Tang dynasty. He observed the precepts and maintained a vegetarian diet, reciting the Buddha’s name and performing prostrations.
Though he grew old and became ill, he would not even lie upon a pillow. He recited the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* one hundred thousand times and told his family, "The Buddha has come to receive me.

Having said this, he prostrated himself and immediately passed away while sitting upright. Later, while traveling to visit sacred sites, he was at Mount Daowei when he dreamed of a strange light from the West at night.
A light appeared, and amidst banners, flowers, and celestial music, a voice from the sky proclaimed: "Tang Shiliang has already returned to the Pure Land.
Lu Wei was a native of Qiantang who served as a district magistrate’s clerk (*duyuan*). In his middle years, he grew weary of the world and took to reciting the Buddha’s name.

He led a group to establish two religious associations for the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, each consisting of some one hundred members. Their practice was that every member, while remaining at home, would recite one scroll of the sūtra at the end of each day.
He would go to the monastery to recite the scriptures, dispersing only at the end of each day. In this manner, for twenty years, he eventually established a great assembly.
He once personally transcribed such sutras as the Lotus, the Flower Garland, the Śūraṅgama, the Perfect Enlightenment, the Diamond, and the Golden Light.

In his later years, his descendants passed away one after another, leaving him with no further worldly attachments. One day, he suddenly changed his robes, sat upright, and passed away while reciting the Buddha’s name.

Li Bing was an official during the Xianzhong era of the Shaoxing period. He served as the Director of the Imperial Pharmacy. Initially, he studied Chan under Huì of Jingci Monastery and attained a realization.
Later, he read the *Longshu Jingtuzhuan* (The Pure Land Texts of Longshu) and daily recited the Buddha’s name.
Together with his sons, Gechang Yuánměi and Diàncháng Lín Shīwén, and several dozen others, he established a Pure Land Society at Chuánfǎ Temple. This continued for a long time.
He fell ill. Suddenly, he saw Amitābha Buddha wearing a golden circular halo upon his head. After seven days had passed, he again saw golden lotuses filling his room.
He then entrusted his affairs to his relatives, wrote a verse, sat upright, formed the meditative mudrā, and passed away.

Shao Biao, courtesy name Xiwen, was a native of Zhenjiang. While he was still a scholar, he dreamed that he arrived at an official government office where everyone was addressed as "Anfu" (Consul-General).
Delighted, Biao said to himself, "Is this not because I shall become an Anfu after passing the imperial examinations?
As he walked forward, he saw an official who asked him, "Do you know why you have not yet passed the examinations? Biao replied, "I do not know. The official then ordered someone to lead Biao away.
He saw a large cauldron boiling clams. Seeing this, Piao called out his own name in a human voice.
Piao then recited the name of Amitābha Buddha; as soon as he had uttered it once, all the clams transformed into yellow sparrows and flew away.

Piao subsequently passed the imperial examinations and rose to the rank of Pacification Commissioner (*anfu shi*). From this, one sees that killing living beings obstructs one's future prospects; therefore, one must be cautious.
Furthermore, one sees that the power of the Buddha is vast and great; it must not be disregarded. Official rank has its own fixed destiny and must not be sought through improper means.
Chen Qi of Wangjiang once killed someone unjustly. Later, he encountered the manifestation of a ghost. Terrified, Qi urgently recited the name of Amitābha Buddha; the ghost did not dare approach him.
As Qi continued to recite the Buddha’s name without ceasing, the ghost eventually vanished. Thereafter, he constantly recited the Buddha’s name until his death.

She passed away while seated in meditation. Half a year later, she appeared to a granddaughter of her family named Miaoguang and said, "Because I have been mindful of Amitābha Buddha, I have already been reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Her movements and speech were exactly as they had been during her lifetime.
Relatives and acquaintances all came to visit her; after two or three days, her family members remarked, "It is a pity that during your life you did not transmit the joy [of the Dharma]."

He made offerings to the deity. Eventually, [the deity] appeared with a solemn countenance as if alive, though his face was slightly smaller than usual and his head resembled the spiral hair-tuft (*śikhā*) of a Buddha.
Liu Huizhong, a native of Changxing in Huzhou, frequently experienced fear in his nightly dreams; the Layman of Longshu exhorted him that—
He recited the name of Amitābha Buddha. Huizhong recited it with utmost sincerity and in a loud voice one hundred and eight times. That night, he was able to sleep peacefully.
On the following day, he recited as before, and from then on, they were all able to sleep in peace. Through this, one sees that the power of the Buddha is vast and great.
There was nothing he would not do.
Li Qing resided in Xiuzhou and was quite fond of the Daoist teachings; he had once studied under Wang Longshu. For a long time, he suffered from chronic feverish illness (shen-jie).
Longshu told him, "I only fear that you will not believe me; if you believe me, it will surely be effective. He then bestowed upon him [the following]:
On the other hand, he instructed [Zi Qing] to single-mindedly recite the name of Amitābha Buddha while taking this medicine. Zi Qing followed his instructions;
on that day, his illness was cured by eighty percent. On the following day, it was likewise, until he was completely healed.
From this, Zi Qing came to have profound faith in the principles of Buddhism and constantly kept a text on the Pure Land in the fold of his robe.

Li Yantong was from Kuaiji and served as a blacksmith. Having participated in the Kaiyuan Xilian (Recollection of the Buddha) assembly, he suddenly realized that the world is impermanent and turned his heart toward pure practice.
One day, he fell ill and suddenly said, "I am traveling through the Pure Land and see two gates with locks fastened very securely.
While I hesitate, I see a person of virtuous conduct open the gates and lead me inside, where I behold a lotus pond."

The Buddha and his assembly of Bodhisattvas in the multi-storied pavilion then invited the two practitioners, Xi Jing and Dao Guo, to the bedside. They preached the Dharma and exhorted them on the Path.
The entire family recited the Buddha’s name, and they passed away while seated facing west.
Lu Jun was a native of Qiantang. In his youth, he served at the imperial court, but after a long time, he abandoned that life to devote himself to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism.
He joined the "West Lake Recitation Assembly" and would always weep as he performed repentance before the Buddha.

Whenever fellow practitioners of the Way met him and spoke of the causes and conditions of the Pure Land practice, they would become choked with emotion and sigh with deep feeling within just ten or so sentences, fearing lest they not attain deliverance in this very life. [He attained] samādhi.
His [spiritual] cultivation was not yet perfected, and his rebirth in the Pure Land had not yet been realized; thus, he had not yet beheld our Buddha.

When he fell ill at the end of his life, he invited Vinaya Master Yuanjing to preach the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land. As they recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* up to the section on the Highest Grade of Rebirth, Yuanjing said to him, "It is time for you to depart.
Xu replied, "The assembly of sages has not yet gathered; let us wait a short while longer. He then rose, went to his bamboo bed, and sat facing west with dignified composure.
He sat down and passed away in an instant.
Weishi Zan was a native of Yongzhou; while still a novice monk, he was fourteen years old when he recited the Buddha’s name without ceasing. He encountered an illness and died.
Suddenly reviving once more, he said to his parents, "Amitābha Buddha has come here; I shall follow him.
A neighbor saw a jeweled platform in the sky accompanied by five-colored, extraordinary light, which vanished toward the west.
He Tantuan was a native of Qiantang. He constantly observed the Bodhisattva precepts and devoted himself exclusively to the practice of the Pure Land.

One night, while reciting the Buddha’s name, he suddenly said to his teacher, "I see the Buddha’s body, golden in color and radiating light, with banners and flowers filling the sky and a wondrous fragrance pervading the room.
Shortly thereafter, he passed away.
At Dai-zōzen-ji Temple, the novice monk Jōgyō constantly followed his teacher Zenkei, reciting the Buddha’s name and performing prostrations.
One night, he dreamed of a woman selling prayer beads. The boy said, "I wish to buy one string, but I regret that I have no money. The woman replied, "I shall give it to you."
"Open your mouth," he said, and immediately cast the rosary into his mouth. The boy reported this to his teacher, who said, "This is the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta;

he has bestowed upon you the *nien-fo* samādhi. After several days had passed, the boy saw two Great Beings holding a flower seat and giving it to him, saying, "In seven days, you shall mount this and be born in the Pure Land. Whenever the boy encountered anyone, he would say, "I..."
"He shall be reborn [in the Pure Land] in seven days. When the appointed time arrived, he suddenly exclaimed, "The Great Bodhisattva is coming! and passed away while sitting upright and composed.

The practitioner Ni was a native of Renhe who abandoned his home to become a seeker of the Way. He built a small hermitage and devoted himself exclusively to the recitation of the Buddha's name, intending to cremate [himself].
She vowed to substitute herself for all sentient beings suffering in the realms of misery and to make offerings to all Buddhas.
After a long time, three clusters of red creepers grew before her couch. She said to the assembly, "If these vines wither, I shall depart for the West.

Half a month before her death, she gathered the assembly to recite the Buddha’s name until ten thousand people had joined. On the eve of her self-immolation, the ground suddenly filled with golden light, rising high—
It was about half a foot [in height]. He cupped it in his hands, and it floated within his palms.
He then addressed the assembly, saying, "When I cremate my body, there will surely be purple and blue clouds passing from the northeast to the southwest; this shall be the sign of my rebirth.
Thereupon, he lit torches on all four sides and sat upright amidst them. Indeed, there appeared auspicious clouds of two colors.
Feng Min was a native of Shangyu. In his youth, he pursued a life of hunting. There was a giant serpent that caused harm to the local people; Min took up a spear and went after it.
He saw the serpent at the foot of a cliff, locked in combat with a yellow ox. Min pushed down a massive boulder to crush it, and the serpent eventually died.

Later, whenever he thought of it, he feared the serpent would become a vengeful adversary. He therefore sought the Buddha for absolution and dedicated his will to the Western Paradise to practice [the Way].

He practiced the repentance and mindfulness of the Buddha in this manner for ten years. One night, he invited his fellow practitioners of the society to assist him in chanting the *Amitābha Sūtra* and reciting the Buddha’s name.
Following this, he recited the Verses on Repenting of Sins by Samantabhadra and the Verses on the Vow for Rebirth. He then sat upright with palms joined and passed away.

Huang the Blacksmith of Tanzhou constantly recited the Buddha’s name without ceasing whenever he was at work. One day, while free from illness, he entrusted a neighbor to write a verse for him, which said:
"Day and night, the rhythmic clanging; long tempered, it becomes steel. Peace is drawing near; I am going to the Western Land.
He then passed away on that very seat.
Master Ji was an ironworker from Tiaoyuan in Siming. He was nearly seventy years old and had lost his sight in both eyes.
A local scholar, Zan Xue, instructed him to distribute large-character block-printed charts (*bèikē tú*) and encouraged people to recite the Buddha’s name. Master Ji initially received one chart;

after he had completed three hundred and sixty thousand recitations, his two eyes became clear upon reaching the fourth chart. He continued in this manner for three years until he had completed ten million recitations.
Seven scrolls. One day, while reciting the Buddha’s name, he suddenly lost consciousness.

After half a day, he revived and said, "I saw the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, who commanded that six scrolls be given to Academician Zan; he was the primary person who exhorted me. Give one scroll to Mr. Li Er;
he was the person who distributed the scrolls. He instructed his son to go and thank the Academician. Having finished speaking, he bathed, sat facing west, and passed away.
Xu Liugong was a farmer from Jiaxing. He and his wife lived on a vegetarian diet and maintained constant mindfulness before a Buddha image for forty years.

He frequently dreamed of traveling to the Pure Land. He prepared a burial niche in advance; on the day he was to depart, he changed into coarse cloth and grass sandals, entered the niche, and sat upright.
After a short while, he said, "The Buddha has come to welcome me," and passed away peacefully.
Shen Sanlang was from Lin’an and made his living as a merchant. In his later years, he turned his heart toward the recitation of the Buddha’s name.
One day, falling ill, he invited a monk to lecture on the *Amitābha Sūtra* and set up a sacred image. Day and night, he gazed toward the west. Suddenly, he changed his clothes and passed away.

A moment later, his knees drew together as if he were about to sit up; his two sons, finding it difficult to move him into the coffin, dragged his legs straight. After half a day had passed, they were about to close the casket.
Suddenly, he raised his hand and drew out a silken shroud; startled, he sat upright. The entire family was so alarmed that they fled in retreat.
His two sons hurried forward to support and protect him, fearing he might drag his legs, and struck him with their elbows and knees. The son said, "I am merely helping my father sit for his passing.
When his body was cremated, twenty-nine white cranes flew through the clouds; after a long while, they departed toward the west.
At the age of eighteen, Hetan Ji observed the Bodhisattva precepts and practiced mindfulness of the Buddha. At the fourth watch of one night, he rose immediately to recite the name of the Buddha.
Others remarked that it was too early, to which he replied, "I see the golden form of the Buddha coming to welcome me with banners and flowers," whereupon he passed away.

Zhu Gang was a native of the capital. He pursued the Confucian path and passed the provincial examination; however, after three attempts at the Imperial Academy, he did not attain the highest degree. Consequently, he took office and later retired from the two ministries.
He devoted himself exclusively to the Pure Land practice, reciting the Buddha’s name thirty thousand times daily for fifteen years without the slightest slackening.

At the time of his death, while sitting upon his bed, he held a rosary in both hands and continued chanting the Buddha’s name without ceasing. A wondrous fragrance filled the room, and he said, "The Buddha has come."
He passed away while continuously chanting the name.

Master Gao Baodang, whose name was Yuan, was dedicated to the cultivation of Pure Land practices and was on good terms with his Dharma friend, the layman Zhang Laoshi. When his illness became critical, he...

The assembly of monastics and laypeople chanted the name of Amitābha Buddha ten times in succession, singing in harmony. Zhang was among them. The official said, "At this moment, I still do not perceive any movement.
Zhang replied, "You are greatly mistaken. Why harbor such doubts? You must apply yourself with single-minded intensity and rouse your spirit to recite the Buddha's name.
After a short while, the assembly suddenly smelled a wondrous fragrance filling the room; the official saw for himself that his own body was sitting upon a lotus flower.
In the midst [of this], his sons were overcome with grief and longing. He exhorted them, saying: "Where do you think I am going?
Wherever it may be, it is this very place. The Buddhas welcome me. As the third watch begins, I shall set forth. Since my own vow has been fulfilled, your vows shall likewise be comforted."
When the appointed time arrived, he departed with a smile. Zhu Yuanzheng was a native of Haiyan.
While still a student, he lectured on the teachings of Confucius and Mencus; he was upright and did not act with levity.

After the age of sixty, he immersed himself deeply in the joy of Chan practice. He shut himself away in three dilapidated rooms behind his residence and no longer attended to family affairs. At the gate—
The heading above reads: "For example, I have already died," in six characters.

His daily practice was to recite one scroll of the *Lotus Sūtra* before noon and chant the Buddha’s name one thousand times after noon. In the fourth month of the Gengshen year, Tang Yizhi visited him together with his disciple Chen Zeliang.
Master Gong said to Zeliang, "Yizhi previously sent you a letter, exhorting you to cultivate the Pure Land."
"Listen carefully to my words. Thereupon, Liang said, "The Master is advanced in years; why not slightly relax the prohibition on wine?
The Master replied, "Do you think that in my declining years I must rely on several cups of wine to regulate my breath and nourish my blood?
You do not know that my life and death have already been decisively settled. Why speak of such things again? When the Master spoke of having "decisively settled" [his fate], he used his hand to—

On the table, he drew a single line; it was as if he had already finalized his departure from life and death. In the seventh month, being free from ailment, he suddenly said to his son, "I have no further business here;
I may now depart. His son asked, "Where will you go? He replied, "To the West. Although his son and grandson earnestly entreated him to stay, he granted their request.
On the first day of the twelfth month, he manifested illness and ceased eating. As his family members were in a state of panic preparing for his funeral arrangements, the Master said:

"Do not be in haste; this is a matter for the midnight of the eighth day of the twelfth month. He gave these instructions in advance to his family members. At the time of his departure, he forbade women from coming.
After two or three hours had passed, even if they arrived, they were not to weep. When the appointed time came, he sat upright and passed away. It was then just the crowing of the cock.
By dawn, when his kinsmen finally arrived to offer their lamentations, the Master had already regained consciousness and opened his eyes, yet he did not speak; he merely shook his head.
He ordered his wife to leave, and then passed away with his eyes closed.

Ding Mingdeng, whose courtesy name was Jianhong, was a native of Jiangpu. In the *Jiyou* year of the Wanli era, he took refuge with the Great Master Yunqi and placed firm faith in the Pure Land Dharma-gate, changing his style name to Lianlü (Lotus Companion).
In the *Benchen* year, he passed the imperial examinations and served as an official in Wenling, where he constantly [encouraged others] to...

This was a great matter for the world. He transformed both the clergy and the laity, leading many to profound realization. While serving as the Magistrate of Quzhou, he exerted great effort to prohibit the slaughter of oxen.
When a lawless man who had committed a crime was pursued with urgency, he realized that the official respected monks; the man immediately shaved his head and presented himself.

The official ordered the local headman to monitor the day he returned to lay life so that he might be severely punished. That man resolved to practice diligently and eventually became a renowned monk. He first served as the Governor of Quanzhou.

The official Li Xian was sentenced to have his neck bound in a cangue as punishment. Gong established a regulation, allowing those who wished to do so to contribute rice, using it to provide for the indigent prisoners in the jail.

During the summer months, he renovated the prison cells and provided *xiangru* (calendula) decoy and *huīshàn* (mugwort) fans. In the winter months, he installed warming boxes containing pepper and ginger.

He selected physicians to attend to the sick and further purchased over a hundred strings of plain prayer beads to distribute among the prisoners so they might recite the Buddha’s name. He would often say to others: "People..."

Those who resolve their minds [to seek enlightenment] are many when in times of hardship and calamity. I took advantage of his remorse to guide him toward the practice of *nienfo* (Buddha-recollection).

Fortunately, he was released from prison and became a virtuous citizen. Distressed that the women within the inner chambers did not hear the Buddha-dharma, he requested the Zen Master to expound upon the Mahāyāna, so that they might listen from behind the curtains.
At that time, four members of his family shaved their heads and received the precepts. Upon hearing the Great Master Lianchi’s...
The Master said: "There was an old woman who claimed her husband had recited the Buddha’s name with single-minded concentration and without distraction until the moment of his passing.
He bid her farewell with a single request, and from that, the woman gained deep faith in the Pure Land. The Great Master himself also resolved to leave the household life from this point on.

The official painted a picture titled "A Single Request" and hung it in his study, inscribing a poem upon it: "With you I have made one request; in a flash, you have departed. Cherish our meeting—how many times shall we encounter again?"

A Collection of Lotus Verses. In the winter of the year Wuyou (1845), his illness became severe. On the first day of the eleventh month, he prepared a written petition to inform the Buddha, expressing his firm resolve and aspiration for rebirth in the Pure Land.
He burned one petition each day; by the tenth day, his consumption of rice gruel and drink was as usual, and his facial complexion was radiant and lustrous.

He repeatedly exhorted his relatives and acquaintances to be born together in the Western Paradise. Reclining slightly upon his bed, he passed away peacefully and silently. This collection has been compiled accordingly.

News from the countryside: The clear resonance of the lotus-water clock and the subtle fragrance of the mustard-seed lamp have been transmitted through more than ten kinds of gentle discourses that have circulated in the world.
During the Tang dynasty, there was a man named Yizhi, a native of Huzhou. He attended upon Master Lianchi and diligently cultivated the Pure Land practices.
