Initially, he served as a Vice-Governor (Biejia) of Shouyang by virtue of his mastery of the classics; subsequently, he assisted the state of Xiangguo. His entire family and kinsmen all took refuge in the Triple Gem. Each morning, they...

He maintained the recitation of the sutra texts. In the evening, they would gather together to practice *nienfo* (Buddha-recollection). In the second month of spring in the *Xinsi* year of the Chongzhen era, the rebel Chang broke into Xiangyang.
He threw himself into a well to the left of the Duanli Gate; his family members pulled him out, but his breath had already ceased.

He revived, was summoned for interrogation by imperial decree, and was granted leniency under the broad amnesty. Shortly thereafter, he requested leave to return to his hometown. However, on the fifth day of the twelfth month, [the rebels] returned to Xiangyang.
He was trapped. First he did not die at the hands of bandits; next he did not die in the well; and finally he did not die by the Dharma.

Is this not proof that the compassionate, silent protection of his inconceivable merit and virtue is indeed such? The Duke himself described how, over several years, his practice and the Way had interacted in resonance.

On the eighth day of the twelfth month of the Dinghai year, while reciting the Buddha’s name and paying homage at the stupa in Changgan Temple, he beheld the form of the Buddha within the light of the stupa.
The Buddha was golden-hued, his radiance like snow or ice, like a bright mirror.

On the fifth day of the seventh month in the year Wuzi, while recollecting the Buddha in the meditation hall, he suddenly saw Mount Zhong floating upon a vast ocean. The golden Buddha stood majestic and lofty, his auspicious light dazzlingly brilliant.
All tiles, rubble, walls, and enclosures, as well as the tall trees and thickets, vanished entirely into emptiness. At the moment of his passing, these auspicious responses were manifest and clear.

The works he compiled include the *Lotus World Scripture* (*Lianhua shijie shu*) and the *Dharma-Sound Kalaviṅka Sound* (*Fayin pingyaya yin*), which were carved into woodblocks and circulated in the world.
Liu Tongzhi was a native of the capital; he was diligent and sincere in his recitation of the Buddha’s name. At the age of fifty-two, he fell ill, and his mindfulness became even more earnest.
A neighbor, Li Buzhai, had previously passed away; when Tongzhi’s breath ceased, it was from morning until noon before he revived again. He said to his family: "Just now..."
He saw a boat approaching from the Pure Land. Thirty-six people were aboard the boat, including Bai Zhai; he himself was also among their number.
However, his clothes were not fresh and clean, and he had forgotten to bring his prayer beads. Consequently, the boat stopped specifically to wait for him.
His family hurriedly changed his clothes and hung the beads around his neck. A short while later, he passed away.

Tang Tingren, courtesy name Tiru, was a native of Lanxi. His filial piety and fraternal kindness were pure and sincere, arising from his very nature. In his youth, he traveled among the schools and gained a reputation for excellence;

however, later realizing that the world is impermanent, he turned his heart toward the Ultimate Way. He studied under Yunqi and received the *nienfo* samādhi, which he subsequently practiced with great diligence.
For thirteen years, he remained as steadfast as on a single day. Devoted to the Western Pure Land, [he passed away] in the Gui-mao year of the Wanli era.
In the middle of winter, on the occasion of his sixtieth birthday, he suddenly said to his sons, "On the eleventh day of the new year, I shall return.
Several days prior, his ritual recitations were as they had always been. When the appointed time arrived, he washed and rinsed his mouth, adjusted his robes, and sat upright.
With his hands forming mudrās and his lips uttering the names of the Buddhas, he passed away with a smile, as if entering meditative absorption.
Yang Jiawei (style name Banghua) was a native of Taihe County. He was the son of a prominent family. At the age of thirteen, he observed the precept against killing;
even fleas and lice were not harmed by him. He devoted himself to the Pure Land school of Dharma and recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* daily.

At twenty-three, while studying at the Southern Capital Academy (Nanyong), he suddenly fell ill and passed away on the nineteenth day of the second month of winter in the year Wanyli Basi (1585). Prior to his death—
He dreamed that he was wandering through hell and saw the Great Being Kṣitigarbha in the Hall of the Living and the Dead.

Upon waking, he released many living beings, invited monks to recite sutras and chant the Buddha’s name, and said to his attendants, "I am about to pass away. A blue lotus flower has appeared before me;

could this not be the realm of the Pure Land? Thereupon, he chanted the Buddha’s name day and night without ceasing. He ordered the candles to be extinguished, saying, "You all rely on candles for [your vision]..."
[The Master] said, "It is bright. I have no need for a candle; I am always within the light. [The monk] asked, "What do you see? He replied, "Lotuses opening in four colors.
[The monk] asked, "Do you see Amitābha? He replied, "I see Amitābha manifesting a body one thousand *zhang* tall. [The monk] asked about Guanyin. He replied, "His body is equal in size to Amitābha's.
[The monk] asked about Shizhi. He replied, "I do not see him. Having finished speaking, he suddenly leaped up, took up incense, and spoke in a continuous stream:
"The merits of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* are unspeakably unspeakable. I have already attained the highest grade [of rebirth]. Having spoken thus, he passed away in silence.
His elder brother, Jiazuo, recorded these events and made a vow, saying: 'If I have uttered any deceptive words, may I fall into the Hell of the Plucked Tongue.'"
How truly did he perceive this, and how earnest was his expression! Those who do not believe in the Pure Land should reflect upon this.
Hao Xizai was a native of Qiantang; his Dharma name was Guangding. Throughout his life, he was loyal, trustworthy, and free from deceit, renowned for his virtuous conduct within the schools.

In his later years, he returned to the Buddha and took up the recitation of scriptures, increasing his devotion day and night. In the second month of the spring of the辛亥 year of the Wanli era, he attained [enlightenment].

He fell ill. Every time he awoke from sleep, he would say, "In my dreams, I have gone into the mountains seeking to see the Buddha. Before I can see the Buddha, I see hundreds of birds gathering there. This continued for several days.
On the night of the twenty-seventh, at the hour of midnight, he suddenly said, "Two youths have come to welcome me.
The Buddha is seated upon a lotus pedestal, appearing before me. I am going now. He passed away peacefully and auspiciously.

Go was a native of Qiantang, whose Dharma name was Guangtai. He was profoundly filial by nature and had long accumulated virtuous deeds, yet he remained deeply self-effacing, seeking no recognition from others.

In his later years, he served the Buddha with refined sincerity; together with the Lingzhi monk Xuansu, he formed two seasonal associations for the practice of *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation) and the recitation of the five scriptures of the *Avataṃsaka*. Suddenly, he said to those around him: "My great life-limit is approaching. When he...
To prepare the provisions for his western journey, he performed his daily recitations in his chamber, never ceasing from morning until night.
He fixed the date of his departure for the evening of the twenty-first day of the twelfth lunar month. On the eve of that day, mother and son looked around one another, choked with grief.
The Layman smiled and said, "Birth must inevitably end in extinction; why grieve? I am now concentrating my spirit on the Pure Land to behold Amitābha face to face. You all must be careful not to—"

Affectionate attachments disturbed his right mindfulness. He repeatedly and earnestly exhorted [his attendants] to assist him with recitation, ensuring there were no distracting words. When the appointed time arrived, he passed away in silence.
His grandson, Shu Zi, whose Dharma name was Dayu, had been clever and fond of learning since childhood; at the age of twelve, he followed his father, Jingwu.
The Duke brought an image of Amitābha Buddha adorned with the Forty-eight Vows and entered Yunqi. Thereupon, he received the five precepts and renounced meat and alcohol for life.
He vowed to practice *nienfo* (Buddha-recitation) and pledged to attain rebirth on the Golden Terrace. Through diligent and arduous effort, he disregarded even his own body and life.

Suddenly, he saw two bhikṣus holding lotus flowers, who certified his single-minded devotion to the Pure Land. Furthermore, he saw a transformed person reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for a full day and night.

He then sat up abruptly and said, "Amitābha and Avalokiteśvara have both come to welcome me. He formed the *vajra-muṣṭi-mudrā* (the adamantine fist seal) and called out "Amitābha Buddha" several times.
Then, he passed away in stillness. This occurred on the eleventh day of the second month of winter in the *xinhai* year of the Wanli era.
A "Song of the Twelve Hours of the Pure Land" was subsequently transmitted to the world.

Dai Baihu and Tao Baihu served together in administrative affairs. At one time, while the Provincial Governor was under his command, there was a notorious murderer and bandit on the Qiantang River known as Manjianghong (Full-River-Red).
His faction was so powerful that local officials dared not arrest him.

The Governor secretly summoned the two men, personally handing each a warrant and ordering them to capture Manjianghong. The two threw themselves into the midst of the bandits and employed various means...
He lured them in. At the moment of their execution, he felt such bitter resentment that he vowed to take their lives.

The two men, fearing for their own safety, resigned their posts, observed the fast, and recited sutras and the Buddha’s name to resolve their karmic enmity. Dai Baohu suddenly took leave of his relatives;

when the appointed time arrived and he sat down, he fell unconscious for a long while, then revived and said: "When my brother Tao was about to depart, his right mindfulness faltered for a moment because he lost his way. I have come to [correct this]."

"You all may speak now; I shall depart tomorrow. Early the next morning, he sat again and passed away. His nose hung down like a jade pillar, and a wondrous fragrance filled the room without dispersing.

Hua the Layman was a man from the banks of the Jiang River; he was honest, simple, and without guile, never engaging in formalities with others. In his middle years, he devoted himself to various [religious] practices.
The son lived alone in a single room, avoiding all worldly affairs; from morning until evening, he did nothing but diligently recite the Buddha’s name.
Later, as his end approached, he knew for himself that the time had come. He changed his clothes, adjusted his cap, and sat upright. He bid farewell to the assembly and passed away.

His son had already prepared a coffin, so they moved the remains to the shrine according to the traditional rites of a śramaṇa. On the day the shrine was carried forth, spectators gathered like a wall, both near and far.
People looked up to him with admiration.
Liánhuá Tàigōng was a man from Yùe who was simple and honest throughout his life; he spent his days and nights reciting the Buddha’s name without ceasing.
After his death, a single lotus flower suddenly sprouted upon his coffin. His relatives were struck with wonder and amazement, and for this reason he was called Liánhuá Tàigōng.
Guo Dalin was a native of Tangyin. Throughout his life, he maintained a life of integrity, purity, and refined simplicity, harboring a deep aspiration for transcendence.

Upon meeting a monk who instructed him in the practice of *nianfo* (reciting the Buddha’s name), he subsequently devoted himself single-mindedly to the Pure Land. At the age of seventy-six, one day without prior illness, he took leave of his son, saying, "I shall depart at noon tomorrow.
When the time arrived, he sat upright and passed away.
An old man who carried sugar lived in Hangzhou. He made his living by selling sugar and was constantly reciting the Buddha’s name.
One day, as he was carrying his sugar basket out, he saw someone and said, "Eat my sugar early; I am going home.
He went to several other acquaintances' homes and requested of them, "I trouble you to come tomorrow to carry my coffin; I wish to go home. Those who recognized him...
He marveled at this, feeling both faith and doubt. The next morning, he said to his wife, "Prepare food and drink to await the visitor.
At the appointed hour, those who recognized him all arrived. The old man led him to lift the coffin; once home, he bathed, changed his clothes, and stood with hands clasped in reverence.
He addressed the assembly, saying, "I shall sleep within the coffin myself; do not trouble yourselves. He sat his body within the coffin and, with a serene expression, went to sleep.
Thereupon, he passed away forever. The assembly was filled with wonder and astonishment.
At the shores of Lake Tai in Wujiang, there was an old man who, throughout his life, took pleasure only in reciting the Buddha’s name and practicing the release of living beings (*fangsheng*).
He knew nothing else. Whenever he traveled, he would pick up snails and clams from the shore and place them back into the water, regardless of how busy he might be.

On ordinary days, whenever he encountered living creatures, he would immediately take off his clothes, cut away his own flesh to buy their freedom, and release them, never once showing signs of weariness or indolence. One day, he suddenly said:
His family said, "I am about to pass away in the west; you may gather our relatives and friends to see me off. Thereupon, they assembled the multitude to recite the Buddha's name.
He sat peacefully and passed away. A wondrous fragrance lingered for an entire night without dispersing.

There was a commoner in Suzhou surnamed Wu who made a living by pouring wax over candles, for which he became well known. He rented a single room at Loumen Gate and lived there alone, observing a lifelong vow of celibacy and reciting the Buddha’s name day and night.
Because he was considered a man of utmost sincerity, the dozens of large candle shops both inside and outside Wuchang in Suzhou all vied to invite him to pour wax for their candles.
Since these candles were intended as offerings to the deities, Buddhas, and the Triple Gem, he would invariably recite the Buddha’s name several times before each application.
[He] poured a ladle of oil [upon the flame]. He lived like this for his entire life until he was over seventy years old. Suddenly, he said to the shopkeeper:

"I have accumulated some meager wealth, originally intended to provide for my old age. Now that the merit of my *nianfo* (recitation of the Buddha's name) has been perfected, on such-and-such a day I shall pass away and be reborn in a good realm;
there will be no further use for this. I respectfully offer it to you. The shopkeeper said: "What you have accumulated belongs to the community..."
"These goods do not belong to my family alone; how could I dare accept them? If they truly have no use for you, please allow me to perform a meritorious act on your behalf.
Lord Wu was greatly pleased and handed over the keys to the host, instructing him to go to the cellar at his residence and retrieve them.

There were approximately one thousand taels of silver. The master distributed these among the great monasteries of Suzhou for the purpose of providing vegetarian meals to the monks and for the various hermitages and guesthouses, bestowing them all as offerings to cultivate merit.
When the appointed time arrived, Master Wu joined his palms, recited the Buddha’s name, and passed away while sitting upright and composed.
Hundreds of thousands of people, both monastics and laypeople from the Wu Gate region, escorted his coffin to the cremation site.

Wu Shubo, whose name was Minggong, was a student at the Shangshe Academy in Taicang. His family wealth was abundant and he had long been fond of doing good, frequently participating in *fangsheng* (releasing living beings) assemblies;
however, he was not particularly well-versed in the Buddha-dharma. At over sixty years of age, he declared his desire to undergo spiritual transformation.

Suddenly, he bathed himself and ordered the invitation of Master Yinchu of Longfu Temple to bestow upon him the Three Refuges and Five Precepts. Upon their completion, he shouted loudly, "Go forth! twice.
With palms joined, he passed away. After a short while, he opened his eyes again and spoke to his brother-in-law, Mr. Wang Yen-ke:

"I have just made the vow to forever sever ties with the mundane world and have courageously recited the name of Amitābha Buddha. As soon as I leaped from beneath my bed, I found myself in the Lotus World.
Reflecting upon my past life, what good deed has led me to this place? Let the people of the world exert themselves! Having finished speaking, he asked for water.
He looked at himself. At midnight, he suddenly attained awakening and said, "In this life I am Wu Shubo; in my previous life I was Master Xu.
He then cried out, "How wonderful! and passed away, while a wondrous fragrance emanated from his room.

In his later years, Wu Zhanlou of Taicang entrusted his household affairs to his two sons. He devoted himself earnestly to the Pure Land, focusing single-mindedly on the Western Paradise without engaging in any other activities.

In addition to reciting the Buddha’s name nearly ten thousand times each day, he recorded his daily practice of the *Amitābha Sūtra* (both the longer and shorter versions), the *Dharani for Rebirth*, and the *Contemplation of the Western Paradise* in a register. He practiced without interruption through both winter and summer for twelve years.
For more than seventy years thereafter, he never diminished his fixed daily recitations. Holy scenes from the Western Paradise repeatedly appeared before his eyes;
he personally saw that in every compartment of the offering boxes, there were brocade linings beneath and exquisite fruits piled upon them. The stand was as large as one mu of farmland.
Before his bed, white lotuses would frequently emerge, as large as stone mortars, which all the children witnessed. Thereupon, he passed away with a serene expression.

Huang She-liu, styled Ziyu, was a native of Taicang known as Yingsheng. He was originally an eminent friend within the Lotus Society (*liánshè*). Although born of a noble lineage, he was profoundly learned, refined, and pure in conduct.
He held Yunqi’s teachings in the highest regard and practiced them with single-minded devotion. Through recommendation and appointment, he served as the magistrate of Xindu in Shu.

He governed the people with compassion and benevolence, and his reputation for virtuous administration spread far and wide. It is passed down that he provided meals for monks in the county hall and personally practiced the seven [precepts].

He offered a *gui* vessel, distributed alms, and followed this with prostrations. Those who heard of it found it strange. Later, when the rebel Xian invaded Western Sichuan, he slaughtered everyone in his path, and the corpses were piled as high as mountains, numbering in the thousands.
The monk, moved by the magistrate’s virtue, vowed to climb the city walls to strike the wooden board and recite the Buddha’s name.
In the middle of the night, the sound of the Buddha’s name shook the heavens. When the rebel Xian asked why this was happening, the local people replied, "Because of Magistrate Huang’s usual..."

He delighted in providing fine meals for the monastics, who would strike the wooden board to call the assembly for reciting the Buddha’s name as a means of guarding the city. The rebels were instructed not to cause disturbance, and they passed by in silence;

even the chickens and dogs were not startled. Later, he returned to his fields and resolutely cultivated the Pure Land practices. In the tenth month of the Jihai year, his illness grew somewhat more severe.
The monk Jie Xian of Lingyin, together with his brother-in-law Wang Yanweng, braved the cold to visit his dwelling. There, they found the four walls adorned with images of Amitābha;

he had made preparations for his western departure. He requested that Jie Xian confer upon him the Bodhisattva precepts at the third watch of the night, whereupon Jie Xian gave him an exhaustive discourse on the contemplation of the purity of the mind.
The Master said, "My spiritual faculties are increasingly robust and my vows are increasingly firm; I have full confidence."

"It is certain that he will be reborn in the Western Paradise. He must depart on the eighth day. When the appointed time arrived, he passed away with auspicious signs. At that time, I was in prison for having committed an offense;
I led the way in chanting the Buddha’s name, and many others followed me as I resolved to meet him. On the appointed day, we gathered together, chanting without ceasing day or night.
Suddenly, the entire wall appeared to be filled with the radiance of the Buddha’s image. Subsequently, I received an imperial edict regarding the decline of the Dharma at the end of the age.
Jinguang was originally from Wujun; he was illiterate, yet whenever he encountered matters of moral significance, he would invariably apply himself with keen resolve.
His wife, Lady Gong, was the daughter of a filial scholar from Luzhou. Having suffered deeply during the chaos of the civil wars, she turned her heart toward the Western Paradise;
moreover, she had a rudimentary knowledge of books and history, and whenever she encountered Buddhist scriptures, she would recite them morning and night. Jinguang was moved by her devotion.

He moved with deep conviction. In the winter of the *guisi* year of the Shunzhi era, while accompanying the imperial forces on their campaign against those who did not submit to court, he traveled together through the road to Fuzhou and passed through Wulin.
There, hearing that Master Juede was preaching the Dharma at Lingyin Monastery, they went together to seek instruction.

Having personally received his guidance, he thereafter applied himself to the practice of *nianfo* (reciting the Buddha’s name) with ever-increasing intensity and steadfastness. In the summer of the *xinchou* year, he returned to the capital and halted at the banks of the Qiantang River.
Suddenly, he manifested illness. Gong invited a physician, but Guangqian stopped him, saying, "In the past, I visited Lingyin with you in person;
now I precisely wish to make my 'turning-over' arrangements right here, seeking only the Master’s certification. What need is there for medicine?
Gong laughed heartily and said, "I did not expect that Guangqian would also reach such a state," and he then moved his tent inside.
At Chongsheng Hermitage, she intended that her death might find its proper place. After residing in the hermitage for ten days, Gong had two coffins made and said to the people:
"I and Master Jin shall travel together; it is only that there is no one to complete his funeral rites.

Once those matters are finished, I shall depart. When Guangqian heard this, he immediately passed away with a serene countenance. After completing the funeral arrangements, Gong ceased all food and drink.
Day and night he did not lie down. For one day he focused his mind single-mindedly on the Buddha; feeling his body slightly weary, he leaned against the coffin and fell asleep.
After a short while, he awoke and said, "The time has come. He then passed into stillness with a dignified posture, his countenance as if alive.

Han Chengshan was a native of Puhang County. He was a man of sincerity and simplicity who devoted himself to agriculture and sericulture, accumulating family wealth until his fields and gardens were valued at approximately one thousand *jin*.
He lived his life constantly observing the fasts and reciting the Buddha’s name.
At the age of eighty-one, in the fourth month of the first year of the Kangxi era, he suddenly said to his son: "Tomorrow you may invite all your relatives to come; I wish to [meet them] with them."

At their parting, the Master followed the instructions and was invited to attend. He addressed the assembly, saying, "I have only seven days remaining in this world; I have come specifically to bid you all farewell.
When the appointed time arrived, he bathed, changed his robes, and sat upright. He then had his children and grandchildren sit in a circle around him to recite the Buddha's name.
He himself also practiced mindfulness of the Buddha. After a long while, he remained motionless. Upon approaching to look closely, he had already cast off his mortal remains.
Qiao Zhongwo was a native of Changxing who made his living by selling bamboo wares; with both hands he would carve bamboo, yet he never ceased reciting the Buddha’s name from his mouth.
He paid homage to Master Wuzhan Pumen and would regularly attend the summer retreat at Mount Zhan, entering the meditation hall as well. (The first year of the Kangxi era).
Three days prior to his passing, he announced to his relatives, friends, children, and grandchildren, saying, "I am about to depart.

On the first day of the tenth month, he changed his robes, turned toward the west, and sat upright in mindfulness of the Buddha. To those who came to visit him, he instructed them to assist him by reciting the Buddha's name.
Addressing his fellow practitioners and monks, he said, "Now we part; we shall meet again within the Lotus Pond. Having spoken these words, he passed away peacefully.
Zhai Mengli, whose Dharma name was Jingzhen, was a native of Linjiang. Her conduct had always been sincere and simple, and she possessed deep faith in the Pure Land.
Although she was over seventy years old, her spirit remained vigorous and alert. She never failed in her daily recitations and also regularly chanted the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

In the seventh month of the Wushen year of the Kangxi era, she suddenly fell ill. On the thirteenth day of the eighth month, when monastics and laypeople, as well as her relatives and friends, all came to visit her, she said:

The assembly said, "We are deeply grateful for your compassionate visit; we must now recite the Buddha's name to assist you in your rebirth. She personally turned her prayer beads without the slightest sign of weariness.
A short while later, she said, "I shall depart tomorrow morning. When the appointed time arrived, she passed away while reciting the Buddha's name.
Shenyang Su, whose Dharma name was Zhien, was a native of Linjiang. She devoted herself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism, never ceasing regardless of cold or heat.

Having reached the age of seventy-six, she traversed perilous paths as if they were level ground. At that time, she would frequently recite the Buddha’s name and chant the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

She had once completed thirty or more recitations of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. In the eighth month of the Wushen year of the Kangxi era, she suddenly fell slightly ill and said, "I shall follow in the footsteps of Zhai Mengli."
He said to his son, "On the fifteenth day of the ninth month, I shall depart. His son remarked, "The fifteenth is not auspicious; the sixteenth would be better.
He raised his voice and said, "It is better to advance forward than to retreat. On the fourteenth day, he passed away while reciting the Buddha’s name.
A wondrous fragrance emanated from his body and did not dissipate for several days.
Dai Tongzi, whose courtesy name was Gonglie, was a native of Xiuyi who had settled as a sojourner in Tangqi, at the northern boundary of the town.
Born into a Confucian family, he lost his mother at the age of one. Even during his childhood play, he never transgressed the bounds of propriety.

At twelve, he began to study for the civil service examinations; his brilliance shone forth like emerging sprouts. By thirteen, he became even more intelligent and acute, and his deportment resembled that of an adult. Nevertheless, his natural constitution was delicate and frail.
Due to a rash caused by medical treatment, his stomach qi was impaired, and he sought medical attention at his lodging in Wumen.
There, among several volumes of Master Lianchi’s *Zhuchuang suibi*, he would frequently take up the books and read them over and over with great care;

whenever he experienced a resonance in his heart, on the sixth day of the seventh month, he suddenly sat upright and said to his grandfather, "Help me recite the Buddha's name," whereupon he clearly and loudly chanted the name of the Buddha. His grandfather...

He harmonized with it. At first the sound was high; gradually it became low; finally there was no sound at all, yet his lips were still seen to move. After a short while, even his lips ceased to move;
he became motionless, as if transformed into nothingness.
Shen Jingfu, whose courtesy name was Bing, was a native of Changzhou. In his youth, he suffered from asthma, which became severe after he reached the age of thirty;

this led him to develop a resolve for world-transcendence, and he recited the Buddha’s name with great earnestness. By the time he was fifty, his illness grew even more acute, persisting from the first month until the ninth month.
His breath was barely sustained for a moment, yet he then made a vow to abstain from meat. His friend Yang Guangwen visited him and urged him to uphold the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
He helped him up and received the scripture; having read through one fascicle, three days later he had recited it up to the third fascicle.

After half a month, his illness was cured. Thereafter, he made it his constant practice to recite three fascicles daily. He would chant the names of the Buddhas without ceasing throughout the night, sitting until dawn, though he remained gasping for breath.

His illness was subsequently cured. He then received the five precepts. As for Master Lüting: in the eleventh month of the forty-sixth year of the Qianlong era, he manifested a slight ailment for several days.
On the final day of that month, having finished washing and bathing upon rising in the morning, his breathing became very labored; he turned his head toward the west.
He sat in the full lotus posture recollecting the Buddha. His wife was by his side; he brushed her away, and having become silent, he passed away while seated.
He left instructions that he should be enshrined in a coffin and cremated according to the *chāya* (cremation) rite. His wife subsequently left the household life to become a nun.
Gu Tianrui was a man from Dacun. In his old age and childless, he and his wife, Lady Lu, maintained a lifelong fast and cultivated the Pure Land practice.

When there was a Buddha-recitation assembly at a monastery, the couple joined it. In the second month of the thirty-fifth year of the Qianlong era, Tianrui passed away while reciting the names of the Buddhas without any illness, at the age of seventy-two.

Lu Shiquan, whose style name was Jintang, was a native of Yuanhe. Initially at Yutan, he prayed for a friend’s illness; a deity instructed him to perform the *Lianghuang Chan* (Repentance of the Imperial Sovereign).
Following this, Jintang performed the repentance rite and resolved to travel to Tianning An to receive the Bodhisattva precepts.

There, he maintained the Buddha’s name, practiced meditative contemplation, and recited the *Lotus Sūtra*. In the fifty-second year of the Qianlong era, he contracted a chronic ulcerous disease with persistent discharge, and he lay bedridden.
Unable to rise from his bed, as he was about to pass away, his gaze turned upward as if seeing something;

he uttered the names "White Lotus," "White Crane," and various great virtuous persons, repeatedly calling out, "Buddha! Buddha! He then passed away lying on his right side, while a wondrous fragrance filled the room.
Ma Rongliang, courtesy name Rongzu, was a native of Xiushui. He served as a tutor for students to support himself while he was still a *zhusheng* (commoner student). He was over thirty years of age.

He contracted a disease characterized by coughing up blood. Upon meeting Master Wen of Xiangfeng Peak, he was exhorted to practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name. His illness was promptly cured, whereupon he undertook a lifelong fast and received the five precepts.
He daily recited the Buddha’s name thirty thousand times. After doing so for over ten years, his illness flared up again, and he lay bedridden for more than a month.

He himself declared that the Three Sages appeared before him and preached the Dharma; that he was constantly within a great radiance; and that at the time of his death, he saw the Buddha coming to welcome him.
He repeatedly invoked the Buddha’s name and passed away lying on his right side. This occurred in the fifty-sixth year of the Qianlong era.

Guichengcao was the Empress Dowager of Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty. Although she resided within the royal palace, she deeply loathed her female nature and constantly recited the name of Amitābha Buddha.
On the day of Jiazi in the eighth month, she passed away. At that time, to the north of the Yong’an Palace, various kinds of music manifested spontaneously.
There was a thunderous resonance. The nun Daming was the Empress’s favorite. Whenever she practiced mindfulness of the Buddha, she would first don pure robes and hold aloeswood incense in her mouth.
Suddenly, the multitude smelled the fragrance of the aloeswood filling the chamber in an extraordinary manner. After a short while, a radiance appeared, like clouds coming to welcome her.
They departed toward the west. The Emperor asked the Tripiṭaka Master Śāitisna, "What auspicious omen is this?
He replied, "In the west there is a Buddha named Amitābha. Because the Empress’s merit is sublime, she shall transcend to that land; therefore, this auspicious sign has appeared."
Because the nun Fanxing had exhorted her to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, when Yaopó was approaching the end of her life, she saw the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas coming to welcome her.

She said to the Buddha, "I have not yet taken my leave of the nun Fanxing; I request that you, World-Honored One, remain suspended in mid-air for a moment. When Fanxing arrived, Yaopó attained parinirvāṇa standing upright.

Lady Wang, the consort of the King of Jing, during the Yuanyou era, served the West with the utmost sincerity and devotion. She had a single concubine who was negligent and disrespectful; the Lady intended to dismiss her.
The concubine, filled with grief and remorse, redoubled her diligent practice. One night, a wondrous fragrance pervaded the chamber, and she passed away without illness.
Suddenly, the Lady dreamed that the concubine was attending to her daily needs and offering thanks, saying: "Because of your reprimands and instructions, I have now attained rebirth."
When they reached the birthplace, the lady asked, "May we proceed to the West? Her handmaiden replied, "Simply follow me.

The lady followed her and saw two ponds, both filled with white lotuses, some flourishing and others withered. The handmaiden said, "These are all those from the world who have resolved their minds to cultivate the Western Land.
As soon as a single thought of aspiration arises in the human realm, a flower immediately grows in the pond; according to their diligence or indolence, they flourish or wither."
Their withered appearances were each different. Among them was one flower; it sat dressed in court robes, its garments fluttering and scattering thin in the wind.
Immediately, one saw a precious crown and necklaces adorning its body. The concubine said, "This is Yang Jie. There was another flower, sitting upon a seat in court robes;
this flower was somewhat more withered. She said, "This is Ma Yu. They proceeded forward for several li, and from afar they gazed toward the gold.
The light from the altar shone through clearly. The lady said, "This is the place where the noble lady was reborn by transformation; this is the highest grade of the highest birth.
She then went to visit Yang Jie, but he had already passed away, while Ma Yu was still alive and well. Later, on the lady's birthday, she held the incense burner and burned incense.
Guanyin Ge stood upright and passed away (she was the daughter of Emperor Huizong and Princess Jingwang).

Lady Wu, née Rǔ, was the wife of Lǚ Hóng, an Official of the Department of State Affairs. Because Lǚ Hóng had been exhorted by an extraordinary monk, he attained a wondrous realization of Buddhist principles.

Lady Wu read the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and its commentaries, and likewise attained accord with emptiness and stillness. The couple observed the fasts and precepts for forty years. Then, suddenly, Lady Wu—
He saw three pairs of giant footprints, all upon golden lotus flowers. After several days, he saw his knees; after another few days, he saw his body;
and after several more days, he saw his face and features. These were the Three Holy Ones: the Buddha and two Bodhisattvas.

When he also saw the pure male figures within the palace and its precincts, people asked him, "That Buddha teaches the Dharma in such a manner. He replied, "I have attained the supernormal power of the divine eye, yet I have not [yet attained the divine ear]."
She possessed the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*). Thus it was for three years. One night, she manifested signs of illness and said of herself, "I am about to return to the West.
Having finished speaking, she passed away. She had formerly served Avalokiteśvara; she arranged dozens of jars and bowls, filling them with water, and held willow branches in her hands.

Whenever she recited mantras, she would invariably see Avalokiteśvara emit light that poured into the vessels. Those who drank from them were invariably cured. Consequently, the world came to call her Guanyin (Avalokiteśvarī).
Lady Wang, the wife of Magistrate Ma Chao-feng Yu, practiced the method of the ten recitations and maintained the mantra for shattering hell.
She once dreamed that the Lord of Hell thanked her for bestowing the gift of these verses and mantras upon her. Later, when she fell ill, she died while reciting the Buddha’s name. Her relatives...
Her concubine Qi and her maidservant both dreamed that Lady Wang told them they would be reborn in the Pure Land.

Lady Cai, the Countess, resided in Wulin; she had been a widow since early years and maintained her practice of reciting sutras and chanting the Buddha’s name. Every morning she performed prostrations before the sacred images for more than twenty years.
Suddenly, she saw golden lotus flowers appear in the sky, whereupon she immediately requested the scroll of her regular daily recitation manual.
She carried [the fetus] in her womb and passed away while sitting peacefully.

She was the daughter of Feng Shisheng Xun and the wife of Chen Sigong, a Commander of the Imperial Household. Having been ill since her youth, she received instruction from the Chan Master Cishou Shen;
she observed the fasts and recited the Buddha’s name for over ten years, becoming increasingly diligent in her practice. She said to her kinsmen:
Within the Pure Land, he lost mindfulness and arrived here; his karmic conditions in China having been exhausted, his practice led him back to the West.

One night, he said to his attendant, "My spirit has traveled to the Pure Land, where I was able to pay homage to the Three Holy Ones. Upon hearing these words, Fu immediately accompanied him in the recitation of the Buddha's name.
She passed away while lying on her right side. For three days, a wondrous fragrance wafted through the air.
Zheng was a native of Qiantang who daily recited the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra and never ceased her mindfulness of the Buddha.

Later, while ill, she requested a bath, sat facing west, and asked her family members, "Do you hear the sound of the chime? The sages of the Pure Land are about to arrive. Thereupon, she joined her palms in reverence.
Xi said, "The Buddha and Bodhisattvas have come; Avalokiteśvara holds a golden platform in his hand, and the Tathāgata receives me to ascend the seat.
Thereupon, she passed away peacefully.
Lady Lu was a native of Qiantang and the wife of Wang Yu, a Court Petitioner; she regularly recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and became even more devoted to it in her later years.
He performed the ritual of repentance for the Pure Land and recited the Buddha’s name ten thousand times in a single session for thirty years.
Due to a slight illness, he suddenly heard the celestial drums resound on their own; as people were struck with wonder, he sat upright facing west and passed away, his two hands forming a mudrā.
Lu Shishou, who continued the *Jingtu zhuan* (Biographies of the Pure Land), was his nephew.
Zhu Ruyiqin was the niece of Empress Zhu. She married Xue Jun of Siming and embroidered one copy of the *Lotus Sūtra*, completing it over ten years.
Upon reaching the "Parable of the City of Illusion" chapter, she inserted *śarīra* relics the size of chestnuts onto the needle points; she obtained dozens of such grains in succession.
She performed one prostration for each character. Having thus paid homage to the *Lotus Sūtra* three times, she separately added eighty-four thousand [prostrations] at the title of the scripture.

He performed a thousand prostrations daily and recited the Lotus Sūtra for three months until he had mastered it. He carved large-character woodblock illustrations and exhorted others to practice nianfo (recitation of the Buddha’s name) until they reached one hundred thousand recitations.
Among those he converted, numbering two hundred thousand people, only the Lady Zhu recited it morning and night beyond count.

In the fourth year of the Shaoxi era, he commissioned embroidered sūtras for a precious stupa and brought them back to Nanhu, where he provided a meal for a thousand monks to celebrate the occasion. This is...

In his later years, he suffered from a slight illness and invited monks to recite the Buddha’s name. Suddenly, he rose and sat in the full lotus posture. Xue Jun remarked, "There is no such practice in my family.
Thereupon, he passed away in the auspicious posture with his right side down. His family members dreamed that he was riding on a multicolored cloud, departing toward the west.
Liu Shi Huijing was the granddaughter of Lou Shu, the Military Commissioner of Yangming. She married Zhou Yuanqing, a Director of the Bureau of Sacrifices.

She had frequently studied and savored the *Chuan deng lu* (Transmission of the Lamp), thereby clarifying her realization of the Buddha-ground. She was particularly devoted to the practice of Pure Land as her true cultivation.

In her later years, when she fell ill, she suddenly beheld a purple lotus pedestal with countless transformation Buddhas and an extraordinary fragrance filling the room. She spoke of this to her family members and immediately urged them to recite the Buddha’s name.
She was transformed in an instant.
Zhou Miaocong, the daughter of Zhou Yuanqing, was constantly moved by the auspicious signs of her mother’s rebirth in the Flower Terrace Pure Land.

She regularly recited the sutras and chanted the Buddha’s name, vowing to be born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*). While ill, she requested a monk to perform a repentance ritual; she then saw herself wearing new [robes].
Wearing clean robes, she stood upon the pavilion, paid homage, and recited the Buddha’s name. She said to her family members, "You all should diligently cultivate pure karma;
I shall await you in the Pure Land. She then passed away while lying on her right side in the auspicious posture, facing west.
Qin Jingjian was from Songjiang. Disgusted with her female body, she lived separately from her husband and maintained the precepts and fasts with diligence.

She read the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, the Lotus Sūtra, the Prabhāsa Sūtra, and the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra every day without fail. Morning and evening she performed the Amitābha Repentance and prostrated to the Buddha a thousand times daily.
After a long time, a radiance entered her room. Facing west, she recited the Buddha’s name and passed away while sitting peacefully.
Zheng Jing'an of Qiantang was pure in his conduct; he spent every day in the recitation of the Buddha’s name and the chanting of sutras, never letting a single day pass in vain.
Later, he fell ill and prayed to the Buddha. He heard a voice from the air saying, "Your time has come; do not be indolent.
He also beheld the golden body of the Buddha, whereupon he rose with vigor and sat upright facing west. He instructed his son, the monk Yixiu, to chant the *Amitābha Sūtra*. Suddenly—
However, she was transformed. In her dream, her mother informed her, saying, "I have already attained rebirth in the Pure Land; you may tell your teacher so that he may know.
Regarding the Buddhist disciple Qin Shi Jingle: her family resided in Qiantang. Her husband’s surname was Yu, and his occupation was selling fish. She had a son.
A merchant who traded in private goods frequently encountered legal trouble with the authorities. The Qin family was filled with grief and suffering;
they were on the verge of throwing themselves into the river when they met Master Zhao of Jingzhu Temple, who exhorted them, saying: "To have such afflictions is to harbor enemies from past lives.

To throw yourselves into the river pointlessly is not as good as reciting the Buddha’s name. The Qin family was awakened and changed their minds; they immediately burned off a finger and vowed to observe the three-month fast and recite the Buddha’s name ten times daily.

Throughout her life she was never indolent. Whenever she saw anyone, she addressed them all as "sons of the Buddha. One day, she invited practitioners of the precepts to recite the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*.
For each visualization (*dhyāna*), she would chant the name of the Buddha a thousand times. When they reached the visualization of the Buddha’s image, she suddenly passed away.

Huang of Siming lost her husband early; she returned to her father’s house and cultivated the Pure Land practice. At the time of her death, she chanted the name of the Buddha and formed mudrās, passing away with her feet firmly planted [upon the ground].

The boat was moored in the middle of the harbor. While Li went elsewhere, Liu suddenly saw a large fish on the boat shaking its mane and head while chanting "Namo Amitābha Buddha.
Startled, Liu ran to the shore. Immediately, he heard ten thousand fish leaping together, all chanting the Buddha's name, their voices shaking heaven and earth.
Liu was terrified and threw all the fish back into the river. When Li returned and did not believe him, Liu used his own wealth to compensate him.
The next day, among the reeds, he found fifteen thousand coins (fifteen guan), with an inscription that read: "To repay you for the price of the fish.
Master Xueya of Wu served as the Judicial Commissioner of Fuzhou; throughout his life, he venerated the Tathāgata with devotion and frequently visited Kaiyuan Temple.

He paid homage to the Buddha and recited the sutras. Having long heard that the monks in the provincial temples frequently consumed meat and that his own temple in particular kept livestock for slaughter, he petitioned the Provincial Governor and the Commander-in-Chief to issue a strict edict and erect a stone monument to prohibit such practices; yet, this stubborn custom could not be entirely eradicated.
One day, while the Master was reciting the Buddha’s name in the meditation hall, a rooster heard him and also began to recite it.

The Master questioned him, saying, "You fellows have said that no livestock have been kept in this temple for a long time; how then can there be a rooster? He had the bird brought forth. As the Master recited the Buddha’s name, the rooster continued to recite it as well.
Thereupon, he severely rebuked the monks, saying, "Now I see that even animals still possess Buddha-nature. You, however, have shaved your heads and broken [the precepts]..."

"His observance of the precepts was not like that of common animals; how could his downfall be doubted? The monks all wept and prostrated themselves in repentance, saying, "We shall from this day forth make great vows and maintain our fasts and precepts with sincerity.
When the news spread throughout the province, everyone took it as a warning, and the community of śramaṇas underwent a complete transformation.
The official raised this rooster in his office and constantly recited the Buddha's name without ceasing. Later, when he was transferred to another post, he took it with him.

The Master erected a stupa to commemorate him.
Zou Ziyin of Jiangxi served as a Military Commissioner (Bingxian) in Guangdong. He had a subordinate Colonel who knew his own karmic causes from three lifetimes:
in one life he was a snake, in the second a scholar, and in the third his current office. While leading troops to campaign against the mountain-dwelling barbarians, they passed a certain mountain.
The Colonel addressed his soldiers, saying, "In my previous life, I once lived on this mountain as a snake; now I wish to enter the mountain to see it."
"Former colleagues, do not be afraid. He entered and saw countless snakes within the cave. The Colonel spoke to them in the language of snakes, saying:

"In the past, I was born here together with you all. It was only because I was able to recite the Buddha’s name once that I attained birth among humans and have now become a great general. Why do you not recite the Buddha’s name to seek deliverance from this suffering? The snakes—
He bowed his head, assuming the posture of one receiving instruction. On the day of his triumphant return, he entered again to observe closely;
all the snakes had died, having surely departed through the power of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation). When Lord Chū heard of this, he marveled at it and recorded the account for posterity.

A monk named T'ien-i of Puci Temple in Hangzhou kept a dog. Whenever the assembly of lay believers gathered at the Lotus Society to recite sutras and chant the Buddha’s name, the dog would immediately crouch down and listen quietly; this had been so for many years.

On the sixth day of the sixth month in the fifth year of the Kangxi era, according to secular custom, cats and dogs were bathed together. Following this custom, the dog was bathed in the pond. Early the next morning, it died in the latrine.
The monks took pity on him and recited the Three Refuges for him. As they chanted mantras intending to cremate him, the dog suddenly stood up;
having finished listening to the sound of the Dharma, he again joined his front paws together and prostrated himself as if in the gesture of *añjali*. The entire assembly marveled at this.

Since the dog manifested such a supernatural marvel, it is clear that while crouching in his daily life, he must have directed his utmost sincerity and faith toward the teaching. Though he could not speak with his mouth, his devotion was manifest.
He silently recited to himself: "There is no doubt that my rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss will make me a person of supreme goodness.
A verse by Tianyi says: In the vast, ancient garden, half is overgrown with weeds; Fortunately, the sacred ox has not failed its duty. Treading upon the moss, it welcomes the virtuous guest;
Barking at the moon through the vines, it warns the stubborn man. As he grasps his remains daily, his true heart is revealed; Who among you will investigate this kōan? Who will meet the Buddha?
Nature is non-existent. Having long borne the burden of sincerity, my life’s conditions have suddenly ended. My cremation shall not differ from that of the fox on the sea-mountain.
*Xifang Huizheng*, Volume Lower (End).
